units.la: CUM proximè in obitu sanctissimi viri, et grauissimi Theologi Petri Martyris Vermilij, orationem publicè in schola nostra habuissem, qua historiam uitæ illius breuiter complexus sum, petierunt à me complures mei pariter & Martyris amici, ut eam recognoscerem & si possem augerem, atque ita ederem, quibus id non modò ob eorum in me amorem, sed alias quoq; graues ob causas denegare non potui. Etsi enim mea oratio non ita ornata & compositá est, ut Martyrem dignis laudibus euehere queat, arbitror tamen eam ob rerum ipsarum ueram & simplicem commemorationem, multis qui Martyrem amarunt non omninò ingratam fore. Nihil enim à me narratur nisi quòd uel ipse uidi, uel à testibus fide dignis didici. Nam hac in re diligenter elaboraui ut omnem uitæ illius historiam exactè quantum fieri poterat, ab ijs qui cum illo uersati sunt cognoscerem. Qua in re cum alij mihi auxilio fuerunt, tum maximè omnium Iulius Terentianus, qui & in Italia Martyris discipulus fuit, & in exilio omnibusq; peregrinationibus ad obitum usque illius nunquàm ab eo diuelli potuit. Non pauca etiá cognoui ex Martyris uarijs scriptis, & ex literis itè ipsius ad amicos ac uicissim amicorum ad ipsum, quas diligenter inspexi, uoluntate & iussu hæredum easdem in ordinem colligens.
units.tr: When I had recently delivered a public oration in our school at the funeral of the most holy man and most serious theologian Peter Martyr Vermigli, in which I briefly summed up the history of his life, several of my friends, and friends of the Martyr alike, asked me to revise it and, if I could, to enlarge it and publish it. I could not refuse them, not only because of their affection for me but also for other weighty reasons. For although my oration is not so ornate and polished as to be able to raise the Martyr to the praise he deserves, I think that because of its true and plain account of the facts it will not be wholly unwelcome to the many who loved the Martyr. For I relate nothing except what I saw myself or learned from trustworthy witnesses. In this matter I took great pains to learn the whole history of his life as exactly as I could from those who lived with him. Several people helped me in this, but most of all Julius Terentianus, who was both a pupil of the Martyr in Italy and, in exile and on all his travels up to his death, was never parted from him. I also learned not a few things from the Martyr's various writings, and from letters of his to friends and of friends to him, which I examined carefully, gathering them into order with the will and at the command of his heirs.

units.la: Hanc igitur qualemcunque orationem (nam mea omnia quàm exilia & ieiuna sint, noui optimè & libenter fateor) ad te mittere Reuerende pater, & sub tui ornatissimi nominis auspicio in publicum exire uolui. Nam cùm Martyrem quoad uixit amaris & colueris, non dubito eius memoriam tibi gratam & iucundam esse, atque dolorem tuum, quem te incredibilem ex eius obitu percepisse arbitror, nulla re magis exhauriri posse existimo, quàm frequenti memoria & cogitatione diuinarum, quæ in illo fluxerunt uirtutum. Et quia tibi Martyris uita intimè perspecta &cognita fuit,poteris etiâ optimè de veritate narrationis meæ judicare. Vixisti in Anglia cum eo sub felicis & sanctæ memoriæ rege Edoardo,mutatis verò temporibus,cū imminentibus peri-culis & sævi-ente iam persecutione multi viri boni è patria exce-derent,rursus ad Martyrem quasi in portū quendam studiorum tuorū in exilio tuo appulisti,& ita cum eo vixisti,cū Argentinæ primum,tum pòst apud nos Tiguri,ut perpetuus studiorū & la-borū illius,qui maximi fuerunt,socius & adiutor fueris. Posteaquam verò singulari Dei beneficio, studio verò & voluntate ac diligētia serenissimæ reginæ Elizabethæ vera religio apud vos in integrum restitui cœpit, & tu cum multis aliis viris bonis & doctis patriæ restitutus es,& honoribus amplissimis,prout tuæ excellentes virtutes merebantur, auctus, absens literis assiduis & omni officiorū genere pristinā amicitiam semper studiosè & diligenter coluisti. Tu.n. illum patris loco habuisti, & ille vicissim tæ ætate sibi filium, dignitate patrem esse libentissimè prædicabat. Quare cum domestica familiaritate & diuturna consuetudine Martyris ingenium,eruditionem,pietatem,modestiam, humanitatem moresq; suavissimos perspexeris:multa etiam de vitā illius ex ipso audieris(solebat.n.quādoq; amicis petentibus ea commemorare, magna ipsorum delectatione, quæ sibi cum in Italia tum aliis in locis accidissent) optimè omnium de veritate huius narrationis judicabis. Et nisi fallor multa quæ ad eius laudes pertinebant, vel à me omissa, vel oratione mea depressa esse infra rei dignitatē,potius judicabis,quā ut statuas me quicquam falsæ laudis illi affinxisse.Fortasse etiā idem judicabunt cū hæc nostra viderint qui apud vos sunt veteres Martyris amici,cū generosi et nobiles viri tum etiam Reverendi episcopi atq; alij cōplu-res viri celebres,qui aliquando Martyre noverunt et amarunt,si modò aliqui eorum nostram hanc orationem sibi legenda exis-timabunt:quòd nonnullos tamen facturos puto,quorum animis altius impressa infixaq; hæret Martyris etiam mortui memoria. Horum verò judiciis refragari non ausim, quin potius culpam fateor ante judicium,& pœnam deprecor: partim quod justum arbitrer veniā meremeri,si ego unus non satis instructus ingenij & eloquentiæ viribus, & graui præterea mœrore ac dolore impeditus,eius viri laudes omnes oratione complecti nō potui, cuius unus virtutes aliquot seculis plures cū quibus cōferantur pares nō habuerunt: runt: partim quod existimem in me non modò successum, sed cōsilium & uoluntatem suscipiendi operis speƈtari debere. Nam ideò potissimum quæ ab amicis didiceram, & mediocri studio collegeram, publicare uolui, ut magni ac eloquētes uiri, studiosi & amantes Martyris, quales multos esse noui cum Italos & Anglos, tum etiā Germanos & Gallos, excitati meo exemplo, quod ego multis de causis non potui, ipsi quibus hoc facile erit, præstent, ut Martyris laudes splendida, eleganti, ornataq; oratione celebrent. Et hoc quidem munus mortuo Martyri à te pręstari multi uiri boni optant, qui & quid in dicendo possis norunt, & quantum amaris Martyrem perspectū habent: & huiusmodi orationes à uestro munere & dignitate nō alienas esse existimāt: quandoquidem & Nazianzenus Basilium ac Athanasiū, & Ambrosius Valentinianum ac Theodosium, atq; fratrē suum Satyrum, & alij episcopi alios præstantes uiros orationibus funebribus honorarūt: ne tamē hoc à te petant, Reuerēde pater, ea ratione mouentur, quod tibi non uoluntatem sed ocium & tempus deesse existimant. Quantos.n. labores perferas in regno Christi propagando, & quanto studio & assiduitate ueri Episcopi munus exequaris, nos quoq; quamuis longe disiti non ignoramus. Interea tamē si hac mea oratione te ad Martyris laudes ac uitam describendā prouocare potuero, sicuti sæpe optimi citharœdi ineptis aliorū cantionibus prouocantur, ut quadā ex indignatione qui antea noluerant q̄ optime deinde canant, satis magnum fructum ex meo labore percepero. Sin uero tibi tempus, alijs uoluntas hoc exequendi defuerit, cupio saltē meam hanc orationē extare, nō in memoriā illius quam ille proprijs scriptis & laboribus sempiternā sibi coparauit: sed ut nominis eius studiosi, saltē hāc uitę illius historiam qualēcunq; habeant: in qua cernere poterūt studiorū eius initia & progressus: & multarū ac magnarum uirtutum exempla hinc petere. A te uero peto Reuerende pater, ut hanc meę in te obseruantiæ significationem ęquo animo accipias, & non tā me quàm Martyrē ipsum de quo tota est narratio, in hac oratione cognoscenda speƈtes. Postulabat quidem tuus erga me amor, ut maius aliquod & luculentius meę in te obseruatię testimonium darem, uerum cum uires desint, tu R. pater uoluntatem potius meam speƈtato, & me uti soles amare & cōmendatum habere quæso pergito. Vale Pater reuerende. Datum Tiguri primaria Heluetiorum urbe, IIII. Cal. Ian. 1562.
units.tr: I wished, therefore, to send this oration, such as it is (for I know very well and freely admit how slight and meagre all my work is), to you, Reverend Father, and to bring it out into the public under the protection of your most distinguished name. For since you loved and cherished the Martyr while he lived, I do not doubt that his memory is pleasing and agreeable to you, and I think your grief, which I believe you have felt beyond measure at his death, can be relieved by nothing more than by frequent remembrance and reflection on the divine virtues that flowed in him. And since you knew the Martyr's life intimately and thoroughly, you will also be able to judge the truth of my account very well. You lived in England with him under the king of happy and holy memory, Edward; then, when the times changed, with dangers threatening and persecution already raging, many good men left their homeland, and in your exile you came back to the Martyr as to a harbour for your studies, and so lived with him, first at Strasbourg and afterwards with us at Zurich, that you were the constant companion and helper of his studies and labours, which were very great. Afterwards, by the singular benefit of God, and through the zeal, will and diligence of the most serene Queen Elizabeth, true religion began to be restored among you in its entirety, and you were restored to your country with many other good and learned men and raised to the most eminent honours, as your excellent virtues deserved; and though absent, you have always zealously and diligently kept up your former friendship by constant letters and every kind of service. For you regarded him in the place of a father, and he, in turn, most willingly declared that you were to him a son in age and a father in rank. Therefore, since through your close intimacy and long acquaintance with the Martyr you have observed his talent, learning, piety, modesty, courtesy and most pleasant manners; and since you have heard many things about his life from himself (for he would sometimes, when friends asked, recall these things, to their great delight, things that had happened to him both in Italy and in other places), you will judge better than anyone about the truth of this narrative. And unless I am mistaken, you will judge that many things which pertained to his praise have either been left out by me or lowered by my oration below the worth of the subject, rather than that I have added any false praise to him. Perhaps those who are your old friends of the Martyr in your country, both noble and distinguished men and also the Reverend bishops and several other famous men who once knew and loved the Martyr, will judge the same when they see this of ours, if indeed any of them think this oration of ours worth reading. I think some will do so, though in the minds of some the memory of the Martyr, even now that he is dead, cleaves deeply impressed and fixed. I would not dare to dispute the judgments of these men; rather, I confess my fault before their judgment and beg pardon for it. This is partly because I think I deserve forgiveness if I, alone, not sufficiently equipped with talent and the powers of eloquence, and moreover hindered by heavy grief and sorrow, could not comprise all the praises of that man in an oration, a man whose virtues, taken alone, several centuries have not produced equals to compare with them; and partly because I think that not only the outcome but also the intention and will in undertaking the work ought to be regarded in me. For I chose above all to publish what I had learned from friends and had gathered with moderate care, so that great and eloquent men who love and study the Martyr, of whom I know there are many, both Italians and English and also Germans and French, may be stirred up by my example (which I could not do for many reasons) and may themselves, to whom it will be easy, celebrate the Martyr's praises in a splendid, elegant and ornate oration. Indeed, many good men wish that this service be rendered to the dead Martyr by you, who both know what you can do in speaking and have a clear view of how much you loved the Martyr; and they think that such orations are not foreign to your office and dignity, since Gregory of Nazianzus honoured Basil and Athanasius, Ambrose honoured Valentinian and Theodosius and his own brother Satyrus, and other bishops honoured other outstanding men with funeral orations. Yet they do not ask this of you, Reverend Father, on the ground that they think you lack not the will but leisure and time. For we too, though far apart, are not unaware what great labours you undergo in spreading the kingdom of Christ, and with what zeal and constant effort you discharge the duty of a true bishop. Meanwhile, if by this oration of mine I can provoke you to describe the Martyr's praises and life, just as excellent lyre-players are often provoked by the clumsy songs of others, so that out of a certain indignation they who before were unwilling then sing best, I shall have reaped a fairly great fruit from my labour. But if you lack time, and others lack the will to do this, I at least desire that this oration of mine should exist, not as a memorial of him, which he has obtained for himself as everlasting by his own writings and labours, but so that those who are zealous for his name may at least have this history of his life, such as it is, in which they can see the beginnings and progress of his studies and draw from it examples of many great virtues. And from you, Reverend Father, I ask that you receive this token of my respect towards you in good part, and that in reading this oration you regard not so much me as the Martyr himself, of whom the whole narrative is. Your affection for me indeed required that I give some larger and more brilliant witness of my respect for you; but since my powers fail, I beg you, Reverend Father, to regard rather my good will, and to go on loving me and holding me in your esteem, as you are wont to do. Farewell, Reverend Father. Given at Zurich, the chief city of the Swiss, on the 4th day before the Kalends of January, 1562.

units.la: VELLEM Deo visum esse, Patres honorandi atque Auditores studiosi, ut saepe multumque adhuc de hoc loco dicentem virum optimum, Theologum gravissimum, communem nostrum praeceptorem Petrum Martyrem audire potuissemus. Sed quia Deo patriae omnia optime gubernanti, visum est eum nobis (indignis forte tanti viri praesentia) adimere, et in veram patriam evocare, quoniam illum uti optabamus audire iam non possumus, de illo saltem ego, quod praesens tempus et officii mei ratio postulat, ad vos verba faciam. Non tamen ignoro orationem meam non posse parem esse Petri Martyris virtutibus, quibus ille sic omnes alios antecelluit, ut summi oratoris voce vix satis pro dignitate celebrari possit. In me autem ingenium minus etiam quam mediocre est, exercitatio dicendi pene nulla, dolor autem tantus, qui etiam summi oratoris ingenium possit infringere. Doleo enim Auditores meo, doleo ipsius, doleo scholae vestrumq;[?] qui Martyrem amastis et coluistis omnium nomine: Meo, quod amisi officio quidem collegam, reipsa praeceptorem fidelissimum, aetate atque amore patrem charissimum, qui me unice diligebat, idque eo tempore quo minime omnium putabam: Ipsius, non tam quod mortuus sit, iamdiu enim semper optavit dissolui et esse cum Christo: et cum illo quis negarit bene actum esse, quod a morbis, a laboribus, a curis et doloribus quos ingentes ex piorum calamitatibus et ecclesiae dilaceratione capiebat, liberatus est, ac urbium direptiones, aut funesta prælia, captivitates & cædes bonorum virorum, quæ omnia quotidie audimus & metuimus, non audit, non videt, non novit, sed felix cœlestibus gaudijs frui-tur: illud autem doleo ipsum multa & præclara opera, multo-rum annorum labores, multarum noctium vigilias, cum iam prope ad finem perduxisset, non tamen potuisse penitus absol-vere & in lucem edere, & hoc gaudium & hunc quasi fructum suorum laborum percipere. Doleo scholæ nomine quæ eum do-ctorem amisit, cui par non potest substitui: quemcunq; enim patres Martyri nostro substitueritis, alterum Martyrem nō habebitis: neq; enim unus fuit è vulgo Theologorum, & ex gregario doctorum numero, sed tanto fuit ingenio, tam excellenti doctrina, ea præterea pietate, modestia, morumq;[?] facilitate, ut non modo ijs quibus cum vixit gratus, charus, reverendus fuerit, sed ab hostibus quoq; & adversarijs inter summos numeratus sit, & admirationi illis fuerit. Hæc cum & dolorem meum augeant, & præterea vos quoq; cernam demisso vultu, tristi fa-cie, humentibus oculis dolorem & ingentem animi molestiam ostendere, vincor magnitudine doloris, & quod principiū, quem exitum orationis meæ inveniam non video. Verumtamen ne officio meo desim, comprimam dolorem, & non committam ut in hoc meo munere obeundo, tantum in me possit luctus, ut ab officio impediat, & me ingratum erga præceptorem meum efficiat. Quoniam vero Martyris laudes sunt amplissimæ, ob excellentes & divinas eius virtutes, in me autem exigua est di-cendi facultas, eaq; magno & vehementi dolore constringitur, ne conabor quidē[?] splendidis & magnificis amplificationibus singula eius facta illustrare, ne forte oratione mea plus illis decedat quàm accedat dignitatis, sed tantum vitam atq; obitum illius historico more vobis exponam. Et contendam, si modo asequi potuero, ut ea quæ sparsim, quæ diversis temporibus de viro optimo & præstantissimo Theologo vel vidistis ipsi, vel au-ditis, omnia in ordinem collecta & disposita simul cognoscere possitis. positis. Quò ex his rebus quilibet vestrum præclara omnium virtutum exempla capere posset, cum ad aliorum eruditionem, tum ad suæ vitæ usum. Sequar autem rationem & ordinem usitatum illis qui aliorum vitas literis commendant, ac primùm patriam, parentes, & educationem eius exponam, deinde, his quasi initijs & fundamet[?]is positis reliquæ illius vitæ, quæ maximarum & amplissimarum uirtutum exemplis abundant, narratione aggrediar. Etenim ut in segetibus non tantùm messis copiosa & frugum ubertas nos delectat, verùm simul quoq; cognoscere iuuat, in quo solo seges facta sit, qua ratione agri sint culti, quo tempore sati, qua agricolæ industria adiuti ad tantam fertili-tatem peruenerint, sic in hominibus non tantùm virtutis quasi bonæ frugis contemplatio, sed parentum quoq; educationis q; no-titia nos multùm iuuat & delectat.
units.tr: I WOULD have wished it to please God, honoured Fathers and diligent hearers, that we might have been able to hear the most excellent man, the most grave theologian and our common teacher Peter Martyr, who spoke often and at length on this subject. But since God, who governs his native land in the best way, has seen fit to take him from us (perhaps we were unworthy of the presence of so great a man) and to call him to his true homeland, since we can no longer hear him as we wished, I shall at least speak to you about him in the way that the present time and the duty of my office require. Yet I am not unaware that my speech cannot match the virtues of Peter Martyr, by which he so far surpassed all others that his praise could hardly be celebrated as it deserves even by the voice of the greatest orator. In me, however, talent is less than mediocre, practice in speaking is almost nil, and my grief is so great that it could break even the talent of the greatest orator. For I grieve, hearers, I grieve on my own account, I grieve on his account, and I grieve on account of your school, you who loved and honoured Martyr in the name of all. On my own account, because I have lost a colleague in office, a most faithful teacher in fact, a most dear father by age and affection, who loved me uniquely, and that at a time when I least of all thought it would happen. On his account, not so much because he has died, for he long ago always desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, and who would deny that with him all went well, since he has been freed from diseases, labours, cares and sorrows, which he bore in great measure from the calamities of the godly and the tearing apart of the Church; and he neither hears nor sees nor knows of the sacking of cities, the deadly battles, the captivities and slaughters of good men, which we hear of and fear every day, but he is happy and enjoys heavenly joys. Rather, I grieve that he, when he had already brought his many distinguished works and the labours of many years and the watches of many nights almost to completion, was not able to finish them entirely and bring them to light, and to receive this joy and, as it were, the fruit of his labours. I grieve on behalf of the school, which has lost such a teacher as cannot be replaced; for whomever you appoint in place of our Martyr, you will not have another Martyr. He was not one of the common run of theologians nor one of the ordinary number of teachers, but he had such a great intellect, such an excellent learning, and besides such piety, modesty and gentleness of manner, that he was not only dear, pleasing and revered to those among whom he lived, but was also counted among the greatest even by enemies and adversaries, and was an object of their admiration. Since these things increase my grief, and since I see you too, with lowered countenance, sad faces and moist eyes, showing your sorrow and great distress of mind, I am overcome by the magnitude of my grief, and I do not see where I may find a beginning or an end for my speech. Nevertheless, lest I fail in my duty, I shall restrain my grief and not allow that, in discharging this office, my mourning should have such power over me that it hinders my duty and makes me ungrateful towards my teacher. Since, indeed, the praises of Martyr are most ample, on account of his excellent and divine virtues, while my faculty of speaking is slight and is constrained by great and vehement sorrow, I shall not try to illustrate each of his deeds with splendid and magnificent amplifications, lest by chance my speech should take away more dignity from them than it adds, but I shall set out for you his life and death in the manner of history only. And I shall strive, if only I can attain it, that you may be able to know together, gathered and arranged in order, the things about this excellent man and outstanding theologian that you have seen or heard at various times and in scattered places. So that from these things each of you may take the outstanding examples of all virtues, both for the instruction of others and for the practice of his own life. I shall follow the method and order customary for those who commend the lives of others in writing: first I shall set out his homeland, parents and education, and then, when these beginnings and foundations are laid, I shall proceed to the narrative of the rest of his life, which abounds in examples of the greatest and most ample virtues. For just as in fields we are delighted not only by the abundant harvest and fertility of the crops, but it also pleases us to know in what soil the crop was grown, by what method the fields were tilled, at what time it was sown, and with what diligence of the farmer it was helped to reach such fertility, so in men it greatly pleases and delights us not only to contemplate virtue, as it were a good crop, but also to learn of their parents and their upbringing.

units.la: Natus est igitur Petrus Martyr Florentiæ, urbe(ut omnes nouistis)non modò Hetru-riæ sed totius Italiæ longè florentissima, & quæ diutissimè antiquam suam libertatem retinuit & defendit. Annus tum agebatur à parta salute M. D. qui maximè celebris est Caroli V. Imperatoris potentissimi natiuitate. Dies autem erat sextus Iduum Septembris, quo die veteres memoriæ tradiderunt deiparam virginem natam esse, & urbem Hierosolymorum à Ti-to Vespasiani filio captam esse & euersam, sicuti Christus ser-uator quadraginta annos ante prædixerat. Parentes habuit Stephanum Vermilium & Mariam Fumantinam ambos ve-tustæ honestæ[?] familiæ, & quorum maiores plerosq; in urbe ma-gistratus gesserunt. Ab his puero nomen impositum est Petri Martyris ex voto quodam, quod pro more & consuetudine illorum temporum fecerant Petro Martyri Mediolanensi, qui quondam, ut ferunt, ob defensionem verae fidei ab Arrianis il-lius temporis occisus est: cuius etiam fanum non longè à pater-nis ædibus abfuit. Cum verò parentes ipsius unicum hunc ha-berent filiu, nam quos alioqui plures susceperant liberos, omnes ipso excepto & ipsius sorore gemina Felicitate, in pueritia morte obierunt, opes autem illis esset satis honestæ & amplæ, filium quem optimè erudiri cupiebant, fidelissimis præceptoribus commendarunt, & præterea domi suæ singulari diligentia ipsum erudierunt. Mater præsertim quæ Latinæ linguæ perita in eadē filium suum à prima pueritia instituit, & teneris adhuc annis optimi Latinæ linguæ auctoris, Pub. Terentij comœdias illi interpretata est. Neq; vero hæc muliebris disciplina contemnenda est, quandoquidem apud veteres auctores & principes huius linguæ, summi oratores Gracchi, Lælij, Catuli, Iulij, Curiones linguæ latinæ puritatem, & pronunciandi suauitatem à matribus acceptam, ab hac muliebri & domestica disciplina in forū attulerunt. Et nostra ætate clarissimæ fœminæ Iana Suffolcia Angla, & Olympia Morata Itala, ut de viuentibus taceā, suo exemplo docuerunt, quid muliebre studium in eloquentia possit efficere, si eò animum appellat. Ab hac domestica disciplina deductus est ad Marcellum Vergilium, virum doctum, & celebrem translato nuper Dioscoride & commentarijs illustrato: Is eo tempore reipublicæ Florētinæ ab epistolis operam præstabat, quod munus antea Aretini Poggij fuerat, & præterea nobilem iuuentutē Latinas literas de pulpito magna cum laude docebat. In hoc primo studiorum cursu socios & amicos habuit nobiles & patricios adolescentes Franciscum Mediceum, Alexandrum Caponium, Franciscum & Raphaelem Riccios, Angelum quoq; & Pandulphum Stuphas, & Petrum Victorium, cuius singularis & excellens eruditio omnibus nota est, ob vetustos auctores Græcos & Latinos aut commentarijs illustratos, aut alioquin suæ integritati restitutos. In hoc autem primo studiorum cursu, cùm vix dum à metis progressus esset, initiò statim egregia quædam & præclara indoles apparuit, quæ parentibus & præceptoribus summæ eruditionis summæq; virtutis non dubiam spem afferebat. Erat enim in eo primum magna in percipiendo & cognoscendo ingenij celeritas, in retinendo tanta vis memoriæ, vt quiduis comprehendere & custodire posset. Studium deinde discendi adeo ardens, ut nulla unquàm molestia, nullum audiendi & legendi fastidium in eo appareret.
units.tr: Peter Martyr was therefore born at Florence, a city (as you all know) by far the most flourishing not only in Tuscany but in all Italy, and one that most long retained and defended its ancient liberty. The year then being counted from the saving birth was 1500, which is most famous for the birth of the most powerful Emperor Charles V. The day was the sixth of the Ides of September, on which day the ancients have handed down in memory that the Virgin Mother of God was born, and that the city of Jerusalem was taken and overthrown by Titus, son of Vespasian, just as Christ our Saviour had foretold forty years before. His parents were Stephen Vermilius and Mary Fumantina, both of an ancient and honourable family, most of whose forebears had held magistracies in the city. By these parents he was given, as a boy, the name Peter Martyr, in fulfilment of a certain vow which, according to the custom and practice of those times, they had made to Peter Martyr of Milan, who, as they say, was once killed by the Arians of that time for the defence of the true faith; whose shrine also was not far from the paternal house. Now since his parents had this one son, for the others they had had, all of whom died in childhood except himself and his twin sister Felicitas, they had sufficient and ample means, and so they entrusted the son, whom they very much wished to be well educated, to most faithful teachers, and besides they educated him themselves at home with singular diligence. His mother especially, who was skilled in the Latin tongue, instructed her son in it from his earliest boyhood, and while he was still of tender years she explained to him the comedies of Publius Terence, the best author of the Latin language. Nor indeed is this womanly training to be despised, since among the ancient authors and chief men of this language, the great orators Gracchi, Laelii, Catuli, Iulii and Curiones brought into the forum the purity of the Latin tongue and the sweetness of pronunciation which they had received from their mothers, from this womanly and domestic training. And in our own age the most famous women, Jane Suffolk the Englishwoman and Olympia Morata the Italian, not to mention the living, have shown by their example what womanly zeal can achieve in eloquence if it directs its mind to it. From this domestic training he was led on to Marcellus Vergilius, a learned and renowned man, who had lately translated Dioscorides and illustrated him with commentaries. At that time he served the Florentine republic as secretary of its letters, an office which before had belonged to Poggio of Arezzo, and besides he taught the Latin letters to the noble youth from the lectern with great distinction. In this first course of studies he had as companions and friends the noble and patrician young men Francis Medici, Alexander Capponi, Francis and Raphael Riccio, also Angelo and Pandolfo Stufa, and Piero Vettori, whose singular and excellent learning is known to all, for the ancient Greek and Latin authors which he either illustrated with commentaries or otherwise restored to their integrity. In this first course of studies, when he had scarcely got beyond the starting posts, from the outset there at once appeared a certain distinguished and remarkable disposition, which promised his parents and teachers no doubtful hope of the highest learning and the highest virtue. For in him there was first of all a great quickness in apprehending and understanding, and such a power of memory in retaining that he could grasp and keep whatever was put before him. Then there was such an ardent zeal for learning that no weariness, no distaste for hearing and reading ever appeared in him.

units.la: Pudor praeterea qui illam ætatem maximè ornat, mirificus in eo semper fuit, itaq; & senes instar parentum reuerebatur, & æquales suos quamuis plerosq; ingenio excelleret, ita tamen amabat, ita modestia sua sibi devinciebat, ut nulla inter eos penitus oriretur æmulatio: quin eos quos puerilis consuetudo & familiaritas sibi coniunxit, quamdiu in patria & in Italia vixit amicissimos semper habuit. Quia vero in ætate lubrica, à voluptatum illecebris quas urbs opulenta & abundans suppeditat, non modò in præsens sibi temperare statuerat, verùm eadem in posterum cauere, decreuit omnibus delitijs spretis sese vitæ monasticæ quæ tum sola sancta habebatur, addicere.
units.tr: Moreover, the modesty that adorns that age was always remarkable in him: he revered the elderly as though they were his parents, and although he excelled most of his peers in talent, he so loved them and so bound them to himself by his modesty that no rivalry whatever arose among them. Indeed, those whom childhood companionship and familiarity had joined to him he always kept as his dearest friends, for as long as he lived in his homeland and in Italy. Since, however, at a slippery age, exposed to the allurements of pleasures that a wealthy and abounding city provides, he had resolved not only to restrain himself for the present but to guard against them for the future, he decided to devote himself, having spurned all delights, to the monastic life, which at that time alone was regarded as holy.

units.la: Quia vero ea ætate per Italiam maximè celebris erat familia Canonicorum Regularium D. Augustini, quòd cæteris monachis seueriore disciplina uterentur, & diligentius etiam studia literarum excolerent, statuit se huic familiæ adiungere.
units.tr: Since at that time the Order of Canons Regular of St Augustine was especially renowned throughout Italy, both because they observed a stricter discipline than the other monks and because they cultivated their literary studies more diligently, he resolved to join himself to this order.

units.la: Itaq; anno ætatis decimo sexto in collegium Fesulanum, quod in antiquæ Fesularū urbis ruinis extructum, unum à Florentia lapidem distat, cooptatus est, magno consensu & gratulatione sociorum eius collegij, quibus præclara ingenij eius indoles nota erat.
units.tr: Accordingly, in his sixteenth year he was admitted into the college at Fiesole, which was built among the ruins of the ancient city of Fiesole and lies one mile from Florence, with the great consent and congratulation of the fellows of that college, who knew well the outstanding promise of his talent.

units.la: Fratris consilium soror quoq; Felicitas imitata est, ac socia facta est earum virginum quæ monasterium D. Petri Martyris incolunt.
units.tr: His sister Felicita also imitated her brother's resolve, and became a member of those virgins who dwell in the convent of St Peter Martyr.

units.la: Fuit hoc utriusq; factum patri ingratū & molestum, vel quod voluisset familiam Vermiliam, in qua præter ipsos nemo alius superstites erat, à filio uxore ducta propagari, vel quod vulgi superstitionem, & monachorum fictam sanctimoniam, vir grauis improbaret.
units.tr: This decision of both of them was unwelcome and distressing to their father, either because he had wished the Vermigli family, of which no one else survived besides themselves, to be propagated by a son taking a wife, or because the serious man disapproved of the superstition of the common people and the feigned holiness of the monks.

units.la: Etenim Florentiæ iam olim Dantes & Petrarcha multos abusus in Ecclesia reprehenderunt, & ante paucos annos idem factum fuerat à Hieronymo Sauonarola, cuius conciones haud dubiè Vermilius senior audierat.
units.tr: Indeed, at Florence Dante and Petrarch had long before censured many abuses in the Church, and a few years earlier the same had been done by Girolamo Savonarola, whose sermons Vermigli the elder had doubtless heard.

units.la: Certè non omninò illi probatam fuisse vitam monasticam, ex eo colligimus quod testamento suo id quod in numerato argento habuit, uxori legauit, quam secundam post Fumantinæ obitum duxerat: reliqua vero bonorum Xenodochio cedere voluit in vsum pauperum, hac conditione vt filio quo ad viueret soluerentur aurei quinquaginta, quos à signo scutatos nominamus. Cumque liberi eius in cœnobijs vitam agerent, maluit tamen sua bona pauperum vsui cedere, quàm ab ignauis monachis consumi, qui scilicet preces quasdam non intellectas pro eo demurmurarent. Quæcunque tamen eius hac in re fuerit sententia, vicit voluntatem patris ardens in filio diuini vt putabatur obsequij studium. Credo equidem multos esse qui hoc eius consilium ineundæ vitæ monasticæ reprehendendum esse existiment, atq; hi non tantùm me, verùmetiam hunc ipsum qui id secutus est, sibi consentientem habebunt. Neq; enim cuiquam hoc factum vehementius displicuit quàm ipsi, qui quàm primùm errorem suum agnouit, eundem etiam emendauit. Quanquam si temporum conditionem spectemus, iudicium quidem reprehendi potest, voluntas verò laudem meretur. Nam in illa monachorum vita superstitiosa & inerti, fuerunt tamen olim multa quæ animum pietatis & literarum studiosum ad eam allicerent: magna primùm nomina sanctissimorum virorum qui monachi fuisse dicerentur, Basilij, Nazanzeni, Chrysostomi, Epiphanij, Hieronymi, Augustini, & aliorum, quorum vitam imitari & vestigijs ingredi quis non cuperet? deinde nomen religionis, & apud omnes peruulgata sanctitatis opinio: falsa quidem, fateor, sed quis hoc tum vidisset in tantis tenebris? quis etiamsi vidisset, ausus fuisset omnibus dissentientibus mendacij arguere, præsertim adolescens, cui ætati alioqui imbecillitas consilij propria est? Adde huc ea quæ vel maximè Martyrem ad hoc genus vitæ pertraxerunt, ocium non ignauum sed dicatum studijs, optimorumq; librorum magnam copiam. Nam cum pleraque collegia huius familiæ insignes Bibliothecas habent, tum vel maximè Fesulanum. Hoc enim Medicei veteres, qui maximo sumptu optimos libros non modò ex Italia, verumetiam ex Græcia, Asia & Ægypto gypto collegerunt, extruxerant & celebri bibliotheca ornarūt. Qua librorum copia cum quodammodo ad monasticam vitam illectus sit Martyr noster, accedente praeterea opinione divini cultus, condonemus judicij errorem illis temporibus, voluntatē vero laudemus, quod scilicet religiosè, quod sanctè, quod in bo-narum literarum studijs statim à pueritia aetatem suam transfi-gere voluit. Vixit in hoc collegio triennium, sic ut socij colle-gij eius modestiam probarent, morum facilitatem & concordiae studium amarent, ingenium vero laudarent & mirarentur. Exercuit se illo tempore non modo in artium dicendi praeceptis, quae junioribus socijs in hac familia diligenter tradebatur, ve-rumetiam in sacrarum literarum lectione. Laudabilis nanque mos fuit huius familiae, ut adolescentes qui memoria valerent, assuefierent quo quam plurima ex sacris literis memoriae man-darent: itaq; alij integras Pauli epistolas, alij librum Prouer-biorum Salomonis, nonnulli historiam Tobiae, aut aliquē alium ex libris sacris memoriter recitabant. Sub hac disciplina cum triennio absoluisset Martyr, ita & ingenium et diligentiā suam approbauit socijs eius collegij, ut omnes dignum judicarent qui ad praestantiores doctores mitteretur. Quare Patauium mis-sus Es[?], ut in celeberrima eius urbis Academia ampliorem in-genij cultum caperet. Est autem in ea urbe eiusdem familiae coenobium S. Joannis de Verdara, in quo annis fermè octo vixit, cum Alberto Abbate homine non indocto & qui aliorū studia libenter juvaret. Illo igitur tempore totum sese Philosophi-cis studijs addixit, & dies noctesq; in omnium artium meditatione versatus est: itaq; saepe referre solebat, se quicquid in phi-losophia, & illis literis quas humaniores nominant, sciret, quod ipse quidem parum esse dicebat, ego vero cum alijs multis magnum super judicabam, id se magna ex parte acceptum referre Patauinis studijs. Abundabat enim tum ocio quod omne in li-teris consumebat, habebat quos audiret Philosophos insignes, docebant enim tū in illa Academia celeberrimi Philosophi, Branda, Genua, Confalionerius, erat praeterea in ipso ingenium ex-cellens & singularis diligentia. Nam quotidie sese exercebat, legendo, meditando, scribendo, & potissimum disputando: qua in re eius diligentiam & acumen illi ipsi quos modo nominaui doctissimi Philosophi summopere approbarunt: sic vt in publicis congressibus saepenumero Branda Florentinum suum, sic enim Martyrem nominabat ad disputandum prouocaret. Tra-debatur tum temporis in Academijs omnibus Philosophia Aristotelea, hanc non tantum quod sola floreret est amplexus, sed vti in suis comentarijs testatur quos in moralem Aristotelis philosophiam conscribere aliquando caeperat, Aristoteleam Philosophiam maximè amauit & coluit ob methodum, & quod minus errorum haberet quam reliquae philosophorum sectae. Quia vero Aristotelis libri Latini quidem habebantur, sed tamen ita translati vt non vbiq; satis commodè Aristotelis sensum mentemq; exprimerent: quamuis enim doctissimi viri in Aristotele transferendo laborarint, pauci tamen Aristoteleam breuitatem & limatissimum orationis genus imitari & exprimere per omnia potuerunt: quia ergo Latini libri non vbiq; fideliter & perspicue Aristotelis sententiam exprimebant, statuit Graecam linguam addiscere, vt Aristotelem aliquando sua lingua loquentem audiret: & in hac re multum studij operæq; posuit. Carebat enim praeceptoribus idoneis, qui perspicuè ac diligenter rationem & vsum linguae docerent, itaq; priuato studio & assiduitate magna difficultates omnes illi superandae fuerunt. Audiui ex eius familiaribus eum saepe integras fere noctes in Bibliotheca, quae in illo caenobio locupletissima fuit, vigilasse cum Benedicto Gusano qui illi omnium studiorum socius fuit, ita vt alter alteri mutatis vicibus Graecum aliquem auctorem interpretaretur. Hac autem diligentia tantum profecit, vt non modo Graecos oratores & philosophos, sed poëtas quoq; omnes, quorum tamen aliud dicendi genus est, absq; vllo interprete exactè intelligeret. Debebam hoc loco Theologica quoq; illius studia commemorare,tres enim Patauij Theologos audiuit, Heremitanum unum & duos Dominicani ordinis: verùm quia postea aliud & exactius genus Theologiae secutus est, facile patiemini me hanc uerè Scholasticam Theologiam silentio praeterire, & ad alia atq; maiora progredi. Cùm ad annum aetatis peruenisset vigesimū & sextum visum esset socijs collegij illi publicè concionandi munus demandare, quo studia sua quae intra scholam & in coetu collegij hactenus[?] delituerant, in lucem tandem & in publicum ecclesiae usum proferret, & ordini seruiret, sibi verò auctoritatem ac nomen compararet. Nam in Italia non uti apud Germanos presbyteri concionantur, sed munus hoc universum ad monachos relegatum est, è quorum numero Dominicanae familiae socij singulis dominicis concionari solent, unde etiam Praedicatorum nomen acceperunt, qui verò ex alijs sunt familijs,hi plerunq; tantum in Aduentu & in Quadragesima (ut ipsorum nominibus utamur) concionantur ad populum. Quo autem rariores sunt conciones,eo maior & frequentior est concursus populi, praesertim in magnis & populosis urbibus. Deliguntur itaq; ex omnibus familijs monachorum ad hoc munus, qui maximè doctrina & eloquentia videntur excellere. Qui si approbarint se populo, magna est eorum gloria, & celebre nomen sortiuntur. Ad haec Canonicorum D. Augustini familia peculiaribus priuilegijs à Romanis pontificibus ornata est, ut omnes ex hac familia qui aliquando publicè hoc concionandi munus executi sunt, fruantur honoribus, titulis, dignitatibus, priuilegijs quae dantur illis quos Academiae solenni more doctores pronuntiarunt. His autem titulus quos alij iam senescentes vix merentur, Martyr anno ut diximus aetatis suae vigesimo sexto ornatus est: & ita ornatus, ut nō inane nomen haberet sicuti multi, sed doctrinam magnam & amplam studio indefatigabili comparatam: & munus ac laborem publicè docendi cum ipso nomine doctoris coniunxit. Coepit autem primum docere Brixiae in tē-plo D. Afrae, & deinde in celeberrimis Italiae & Galliae Cisalpinæ[?] vrbibus docuit, Romæ, Bononiæ, Firmi, Pisis, Venetijs, Mantuæ, Bergomi, Montferrati. Quodcunq; vero à concio-nandi munere ocium nactus erat, id omne in sacrarum literarū & Philosophiæ studijs ponebat: ac non tantum publicè conciona-batur, sed in collegijs suæ familiæ philosophiam & sacras lite-ras interpretatus est: Patauij, Rauennæ, Bononiæ, Vercellis, quain[?] vrbe, vt ea quæ in Græcis literis didicerat docendo con-firmaret, Homerum interpretatus est, petente hoc ab eo obni-xè Benedicto Gusano Vercellensi, quem supra diximus omnium eius studiorum socium fuisse. Eodem tempore frequenti exer-citio concionandi excitatus, qui pro scholarum consuetudine ha-ctenus[?] se potissimum in Scholasticis Theologis, Thoma præ-fertim & Ariminensi exercuerat, & interea quoq; patrum scri-pta cognouerat, diligentius quàm ante hac ipsos fontes Theo-logiæ sacras literas vtriusq; testamenti perscrutari cœpit. Quia uero experiebatur ad id sibi necessariam esse Hebrææ linguæ co-gnitionem, ad hanc animum adiecit, & Bononiæ in qua vrbe vicarius erat Prioris, ita enim collegiorum præsides ab ipsis no-minantur, illi operam dedit, nactus præceptorem Isaac quædam Hebræum Medicum. Quantò autem labore plerunq; hæc lin-gua ab Hebræis addiscatur, norunt qui huiusmodi præcepto-ribus vsi sunt: nam plerisq; eorum in tradendo fides, methodus vero deest omnibus: itaq; cum ordine recto progredi non possint, & suæ linguæ cognitionem nostris hominibus inuideant, non nisi magno labore & sumptu ( quicquid enim boni tradunt spe mer-cedis faciunt ) lingua sacra ab illis discitur. Attamen omnes has molestias Martyr singulari patientia & indefatigabili stu-dio superauit: tantus in eo ardor erat cognoscendi sacras lite-ras. Quem cum considero, non possum satis admirari progres-sum & ordinem, quo visum est cœlesti patri ipsum ad agnitio-nem cœlestis veritatis perducere. Primum enim ab ineunte ae-tate voluntatem eius excitauit, vt pro viribus conaretur Deo placere & seruire, quamuis interea passus sit eum aberrare in ratione divini cultus: deinde ita animum eius in-nocentia vitæ & iustitiae studeret, qua etsi Dei promereri non potuit, coram tamen hominibus se irreprehensibilem præstitit: postremo ipsum incredibili amore sacrarum literarum inflam-mavit & accendit: quarum dum literam aliquandiu sectatur, tandem patefaciente spiritu Dei, abdita & spiritualia myste-ria salutariter cognovit. Possem hac in re ipsum iure D. Pau-lo gentium doctori comparare, in cuius vita ante conversionem fuit studium divini cultus, & iustitiae quae est secundum legem, in qua irreprehensibilis fuit, & præterea lectio legis, sed adhuc velo obtectæ: verum brevitatis studium me ad alias narratio-nes his omissis revocat. Probabant principes familiæ ipsius in concionando & docendo diligentiam, erat iam nomen eius celebre in maximis Italiæ urbibus, quare statuerunt eum pro ut ipsius excellentes virtutes merebantur, ad ampliorem dignita-tem provehere, itaq; eum communi consensu fecerunt Abbatem Spoletanum. Quod munus administrandum cum suscepisset, ita præclarè se gessit, ut cuncti mirarentur hominem hactenus duntaxat in literis versatum, tanta pollere in omnibus rebus administrandis prudentia & dexteritate.
units.tr: Certainly we may infer that he did not wholly approve of the monastic life, from the fact that in his will he left his wife the cash he had in hand, the wife whom he had married as his second after the death of Fumantina. He wished the rest of his goods to pass to the hospice for the use of the poor, on condition that his son should receive fifty gold pieces, which we call scudi from the stamp on them, for as long as he lived. Although his children were living in the monasteries, he preferred that his goods go to the use of the poor rather than be consumed by idle monks, who would of course mutter some unintelligible prayers over him. Whatever his opinion in this matter, the ardent zeal of his son for what was thought to be the service of God prevailed over his father's wishes. I believe indeed that there are many who think this decision of his to enter the monastic life deserves blame, and they will have not only me but this very man who followed it as one who agrees with them. For no one was more displeased with this step than he himself, who, as soon as he recognised his error, also corrected it. Yet if we look at the conditions of the times, the judgement may indeed be blamed, but the intention deserves praise. For in that superstitious and idle monastic life there were nevertheless once many things that could draw a devout and studious mind to it: first, the great names of the most holy men who were said to have been monks, Basil, Nazianzen, Chrysostom, Epiphanius, Jerome, Augustine and others, whom who would not wish to imitate and follow in their footsteps? Then there was the name of religion and the widely spread opinion of holiness among all: false indeed, I admit, but who in such darkness would have seen this? And even if he had seen it, who would have dared, against everyone who disagreed, to accuse it of falsehood, especially as a young man, to whom weakness of judgement is otherwise natural at that age? Add to this the things that drew Martyr most strongly to this way of life: leisure, not idle but devoted to study, and a great abundance of the best books. For while most colleges of this order have notable libraries, the one at Fiesole is especially so. For the old Medici, who at great expense had gathered the best books not only from Italy but also from Greece, Asia and Egypt, had built it and adorned it with a famous library. Since our Martyr was in some measure drawn to the monastic life by this abundance of books, and with the added opinion of divine worship, let us pardon the error of judgement in those times, but praise the intention: that he wished, namely, to spend his life from boyhood religiously, piously and in the study of good letters. He lived in this college for three years, so that the fellows of the college approved his modesty, loved his easy manners and his zeal for harmony, and praised and admired his talent. At that time he exercised himself not only in the precepts of the art of speaking, which were diligently taught to the younger fellows in this order, but also in the reading of Holy Scripture. For it was a commendable custom of this order that young men with good memories should accustom themselves to commit as much of Holy Scripture to memory as possible; so some recited whole epistles of Paul from memory, others the book of Proverbs of Solomon, some the story of Tobias, or some other book of the sacred writings. Under this discipline, when Martyr had completed three years, he so recommended his talent and diligence to the fellows of that college that all judged him worthy to be sent to more distinguished teachers. Therefore he was sent to Padua, so that in the famous academy of that city he might receive a fuller cultivation of his mind. In that city there is a house of the same order, the monastery of St John of Verdara, where he lived for about eight years with Abbot Alberto, a man not unlearned and one who gladly helped the studies of others. At that time, then, he devoted himself wholly to philosophical studies, and he spent day and night in the contemplation of all the arts. So he often used to say that whatever he knew of philosophy and of those studies which they call the more humane, which he himself said was very little, but which I and many others judged to be great, he owed in large part to his studies at Padua. For he then had abundant leisure, which he spent entirely on letters; he had famous philosophers to hear, for at that academy the most celebrated philosophers taught then, Brandus, Genua and Confalonerius; and besides, he had an excellent talent in himself and singular diligence. For he exercised himself every day in reading, meditating, writing, and above all in disputation. In this matter the most learned philosophers I have just named greatly approved his diligence and acuteness, so that in public meetings Brandus often challenged his Florentine, for so he called Martyr, to dispute. At that time Aristotelian philosophy was taught in all the academies. He embraced it, not only because it alone flourished, but, as he bears witness in his commentaries which he had once begun to write on Aristotle's moral philosophy, he loved and cultivated Aristotelian philosophy above all for its method, and because it had fewer errors than the other schools of philosophers. But since the Latin books of Aristotle were indeed available, yet were so translated that they did not everywhere express Aristotle's sense and meaning sufficiently clearly: for although most learned men laboured at translating Aristotle, few have been able to imitate and fully express Aristotle's brevity and most polished style of expression; therefore, since the Latin books did not everywhere faithfully and clearly express Aristotle's opinion, he resolved to learn the Greek language, so that he might one day hear Aristotle speaking in his own tongue; and in this he put much effort and work. For he lacked suitable teachers who could teach the grammar and use of the language clearly and diligently, so all the difficulties had to be overcome by him through private study and great persistence. I have heard from his intimates that he often kept watch almost whole nights in the library, which in that monastery was very well stocked, with Benedetto Gusano, who was his companion in all his studies, so that each in turn interpreted some Greek author for the other. By this diligence he made such progress that he understood exactly, without any interpreter, not only the Greek orators and philosophers but all the poets too, although their manner of speaking is different. Here I ought also to mention his studies in theology, for he attended three theologians at Padua, one of the Hermits and two of the Dominican order; but since he afterwards followed a different and more exact kind of theology, you will readily allow me to pass over in silence that truly scholastic theology and to proceed to other and greater matters. When he had reached the age of twenty-six, the fellows of the college thought fit to entrust him with the office of preaching in public, so that the studies which had hitherto lain hidden within the school and in the company of the college might at last be brought into the light and into public use of the Church, and that he might serve the order and at the same time gain authority and a name for himself. For in Italy preaching is not done by presbyters as among the Germans; rather this whole office is assigned to monks, from whose number the fellows of the Dominican order usually preach to the people every Sunday, whence they also received the name Preachers; but those from other orders usually preach to the people only in Advent and in Lent (to use their own terms). Yet the rarer the sermons, the greater and more frequent the crowds of people, especially in large and populous cities. Therefore men are chosen for this office from all the orders of monks who seem to excel most in learning and eloquence. If they win the approval of the people, their glory is great and they acquire a famous name. Moreover the order of the Canons of St Augustine has been adorned by the Roman pontiffs with special privileges, so that all from this order who have at any time performed this office of preaching in public enjoy honours, titles, dignities and privileges, the same as are given to those whom the academies by solemn custom have declared doctors. Now these titles, which others scarcely deserve even when grown old, Martyr was honoured with at the age of twenty-six, as I have said; and he was so honoured that he did not hold an empty name, as many do, but had great and ample learning gained by tireless study; and he joined the office and labour of public teaching to the very name of doctor. He began to teach first at Brescia in the church of St Afra, and then he taught in the most famous cities of Italy and Cisalpine Gaul: at Rome, Bologna, Fermo, Pisa, Venice, Mantua, Bergamo and Monferrato. Whatever leisure he gained from the office of preaching, he spent wholly on the study of Holy Scripture and philosophy; and he not only preached in public but also expounded philosophy and Holy Scripture in the colleges of his order: at Padua, Ravenna, Bologna, Vercelli, and in that city, so that by teaching he might confirm what he had learned in Greek letters, he expounded Homer, at the earnest request of Benedetto Gusano of Vercelli, whom I said above was his companion in all his studies. At the same time, stirred by the frequent practice of preaching, he began to search the sacred letters of both Testaments more diligently than before, the very fountains of theology, whereas hitherto, according to the custom of the schools, he had chiefly exercised himself in the scholastic theologians, especially Thomas and Ariminensis, though he had also in the meantime become acquainted with the writings of the Fathers. Since he found that a knowledge of the Hebrew language was necessary to him for this, he applied his mind to it, and at Bologna, where he was vicar of the Prior (for so the heads of the colleges are named by their own people), he devoted himself to it, having obtained as his teacher a certain Hebrew physician, Isaac. How great a labour this language is usually to learn from the Hebrews, those know who have used teachers of this kind: for most of them lack faithfulness in teaching, and all lack method; and since they cannot proceed in right order, and begrudge our people the knowledge of their own language, the sacred tongue is learned from them only with great labour and expense (for whatever good they teach, they do in hope of reward). Yet Martyr overcame all these troubles with singular patience and tireless zeal: so great was his ardour for knowing the sacred letters. When I consider him, I cannot sufficiently admire the progress and order by which it pleased the heavenly Father to lead him to the knowledge of heavenly truth. For first, from his early age he stirred up his will to strive, as far as he could, to please and serve God, although meanwhile he allowed him to go astray in his understanding of divine worship; then he so inflamed his mind with innocence of life and zeal for righteousness that, although he could not merit God's favour by it, he showed himself blameless before men; and finally he kindled and set aflame in him an incredible love of Holy Scripture; and while for some time he pursued its letter, at last, with the Spirit of God opening the way, he came to know the hidden and spiritual mysteries to his salvation. In this matter I could rightly compare him to St Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, in whose life before his conversion there was zeal for the worship of God and for the righteousness which is according to the law, in which he was blameless, and besides the reading of the law, but still with the veil over it; but the desire for brevity calls me back from these matters to my other narratives. The leaders of his order approved his diligence in preaching and teaching, and his name was already famous in the greatest cities of Italy; so they resolved to advance him to a higher dignity, as his excellent virtues deserved, and by common consent they made him Abbot of Spoleto. When he had undertaken this office, he conducted himself so admirably that all wondered that a man hitherto engaged only in letters should excel in such prudence and dexterity in managing all affairs.

units.la: Nam ut alia ta-ceam, duabus in rebus quas nulli ante eum Abbates coficere valuerunt, singularis eius virtus enituit. Fuere Spoleti duo colle-gia virginum, & tertium in quo ipse agebat Canonicorum Au-gustiniana illius regularis ut nominant familiae, horum omnium disciplina superiorum Abbatum negligentia sic collapsa erat: ut ob eorum luxum & turpitudinem vitae, universa familia huius instituti magno odio apud omnes esset. Id cum Martyr videret, pro authoritate & officio suo docendo, monendo, hortando, & severius etiam castigando ita omnes in ordinem redegit, ut hinc non tantum sibi maximam laudem verumetiam universæ familiæ summam gratiam conciliarit. Atq; hoc quidem or-dinis & instituti eius proprium & quasi debitum officium fuit: illud autem alterum quod iam commemorabo longè præstantius & universæ reipublicæ collatum est. Spoletana respublica si-cut & multa aliæ in Italia, certas in factiones erat divisa, in-ter quas perpetuæ erant contentiones, quæ sæpe ad pugnas & cæ-des usq; progrediebantur: & quamuis hoc sæpè conati essent su-periores Abbates, nunquam tamen partes componere & civita-tem in concordiam redigere potuerunt. Id cum non ignoraret Martyr, secum autem cogitaret nihil magis officio suo convenire, quàm dissidentes in concordiam revocare, & mutua charitate, quam toties Christus commendavit, inter se conjungere, existimavit vitam potius sibi ponendam esse, quàm ut ulterius aspiceret civitatem, ita miserè proprio dissidio perire. Itaq; non ante destitit omnes publicè & privatim ad concordiam hortari, officia Christiani hominis docere, patriæ calamitatem & privata singulorum pericula ante oculos ponere, quousq; id quod con-tendebat efficeret. Tantum enim valuit eius auctoritas, prudentia, eloquentia, ut deinceps omni illo tempore quo in ea urbe vixit, non modo cædes & pugnæ nullæ committerentur: verum etiam nulla vestigia factionum apparerent: tantum unius viri excellens virtus & industria potuit. Habent in hoc viro Ab-bates omnes exemplum, quod si imitarentur, possemus forte ali-quam ab illis ecclesiæ emendationem sperare, nunc vero quan-do neq; manifestissimos abusus corrigunt, perpetuo autem cædes & bella spirant, quid quæso boni nobis de illis polliceri pos-sumus? Fuit Martyr Spoleti triennium, ac tum in publico con-uentu patrum totius familiæ præfectus est collegio Neapolitano S. Petri ad aram, quod sacerdotium ob loci amœnitatem, & amplos proventus magnæ dignitatis est. In hac urbe gratia divinæ illuminationis illustrius ac clarius illi affulgere cœpit. Nam quum hactenus in scholastica Theologia, in patribus etiā multum diuq; versatus esset, & tandem ad ipsos fontes se totum contulisset, magis magisq; quotidie à spiritu illustratus, errores, & abusus in ecclesia cœpit agnoscere. Itaq; quod multis religio-ni est, animum adjicere cœpit ad percipienda nostrorum quoq; hominum hominum scripta, atq; natus Buceri commentaria in euangelistas, & annotationes in Psalmos, quas ille sub Aretij Felini nomine ediderat, diligenter evoluit, Zuinglij quoq; librum de vera & falsa religione & alterum eiusdem de providentia Dei, nonnulla etiam Erasmi, & legit, & se horum omnium lectione multum profecisse saepe ingenuè confessus est. Interea quotidie pene cum amicis qui purae religionis studiosi erant aliquid ex sacris literis commentabatur, sic ut huiusmodi colloquijs multum utrinq; in vera religione aedificarentur. Inter hos verò quibus cum de religione conferebat praecipui fuere Benedictus Gusanus, cuius supra quoq; mentionem fecimus, M. Antonius Flaminius, & Ioannes Valdesius Hispanus. Fuit hic postremus nobili genere natus in Hispania, & dignitate equestri ornatus à Carolo Caesare, qui posteaquam à Deo verae religionis agnitione donatus est, vitam suam in Italia & praecipuè Neapoli egit, quo loco doctrina & sanctissimo vitae exemplo quamplurimos, praesertim nobiles, Christo lucrifecit, ac fuit eo tempore non spernenda ecclesia piorum hominum in urbe Neapolitana: nam in illo coetu multi viri erant nobiles & docti, multae etiam excellenti virtute foeminae, inter quas ut alias illustres ac verè heroinas omittam, silentio tamen praeterire non debeo nobilissimam heroinam Isabellam Manricam quae nunc Christi nomine à patria exulat. In hoc coetu piorum fuit itidem Christi nomine exul Galeazzius Caracciolus Marchio Vici & alij magni viri nunc exules, quos omnes nominare non necesse est, etc.
units.tr: To say nothing of other matters, his singular virtue shone out in two undertakings that no earlier Abbot had been able to accomplish. There were at Spoleto two colleges of virgins and a third, in which he himself served, of canons of the Augustinian rule, as they call it. The discipline of all three had collapsed under the negligence of the previous Abbots, so that because of their luxury and disgraceful way of life the whole community of this order was held in great hatred by everyone. When Martyr saw this, he used his authority and office to bring them all back into order, by teaching, admonishing, exhorting and, where necessary, rebuking them more severely. In this way he won for himself not only the highest praise but also the great favour of the whole community. This was indeed the proper and, as it were, the required duty of his order. The second matter, which I shall now mention, was far more outstanding and was of far greater benefit to the whole commonwealth. The republic of Spoleto, like many others in Italy, was divided into hostile factions, between which there were constant quarrels that often went on to fighting and slaughter. Although the previous Abbots had often tried, they had never been able to settle the parties and bring the city into harmony. Martyr, aware of this, and reflecting that nothing was more fitting to his office than to call the quarrelling back to concord and to unite them in that mutual love which Christ had so often commended, judged that he ought rather to lay down his own life than to watch the city perish in such miserable division. So he did not cease to urge everyone, publicly and privately, towards concord, to teach the duties of a Christian, and to set before their eyes the calamity of their country and the private dangers of each individual, until he achieved what he was striving for. So great was the power of his authority, prudence and eloquence that for the whole time he lived in that city no murders or battles were committed, and not even any traces of the factions were to be seen. Such was the power of one man's outstanding virtue and diligence. All the Abbots have in this man an example, and if they would imitate it we might perhaps hope for some reform of the Church from them. But now, since they neither correct the most manifest abuses and, on the contrary, breathe continual murder and war, what good, I ask, can we promise ourselves from them? Martyr was at Spoleto for three years, and then in the public assembly of the fathers of the whole community he was made head of the college of St Peter at the Altar of Naples, a priesthood of great dignity because of the pleasantness of the place and its ample revenues. In this city the grace of divine illumination began to shine upon him more brightly and clearly. For although he had hitherto long and deeply been versed in scholastic theology and in the Fathers, and had at last devoted himself wholly to the sources themselves, he was more and more illuminated by the Spirit every day, and began to recognise the errors and abuses in the Church. Therefore, as is the concern of many who are devoted to religion, he began to apply himself to reading the writings of our own people as well. He diligently read through the commentaries of Bucer on the Evangelists and his annotations on the Psalms, which Bucer had published under the name of Aretius Felinus, as well as Zwingli's book on the true and false religion and another of his on the providence of God, and some works of Erasmus. He read them, and he often openly confessed that he had made great progress from the reading of all these. Meanwhile, almost every day, he discussed something from the sacred writings with friends who were zealous for pure religion, so that by such conversations both sides were greatly built up in the true religion. Among those with whom he conferred on religion the most prominent were Benedetto Gusano, whom we have mentioned above, Marcantonio Flaminio, and Juan de Valdés of Spain. This last was born of noble family in Spain and was honoured with the knighthood by Charles Caesar. After God had granted him knowledge of the true religion, he lived his life in Italy, especially at Naples, where by his learning and most holy example he won very many to Christ, especially nobles. At that time the church of godly men in the city of Naples was no small one: in that company there were many men who were noble and learned, and many women of outstanding virtue, among whom, though I pass over the other illustrious and truly heroic women in silence, I must not omit the most noble heroine Isabella Manrique, who now lives in exile from her country for the name of Christ. In this company of the godly there was likewise Galeazzo Caracciolo, Marquis of Vico, an exile for the name of Christ, and other great men now in exile, whom it is not necessary to name all, etc.

units.la: Quamuis autem huius ecclesiae prima laus debeatur Valdesio, nihilominus tamen Martyris quoq; virtus commemoranda est qui posteaquam à Domino ampliori luce divinae veritatis donatus fuit, & se coetui piorum adiunxit, eam quam veram doctrinam esse norat statim aliis quoq; praedicare voluit. Etenim epistolam D. Pauli ad Corinthios priorē publicè interpretari coepit, idq; magno cum fructu: nanq; illum non tantum eius collegij socij audiebant, verumetiam aliquot Episcopi, & multi nobiles, nam vt nostis ea vrbs semper nobilium & clarorum viro-rum domicilium fuit. Verū posteaquam verba Pauli quæ tertio eius epistolæ capite habetur, Vniuscuiusq; opus quale sit ignis probabit. Si cuius opus manserit, quod superstruxit mercedem accipiet: si cuius opus exustum fuerit damnum patietur, ipse vero seruabitur sed sic tanquam per ignem: hæc inquam verba cū contra receptam opinionem interpretatus esset, multos sibi aduersarios & hostes concitauit. Vulgò enim persuasum est, his verbis à Paulo statui & confirmari ignem illum Purgatorium, quo vix aliquid fructuosius habent Papistarū sacrificuli. Martyr vero etsi nondum aperte oppugnabat illum Purgatorium quasi carcerem à monachis extructum, ostendit tamen idq; ex antiquis patribus, Paulum hic neutiquam de igne Purgatorio agere, quandoquidem ignem talem constituit quem pariter boni & mali ædificatores experiantur, sed eum hoc potius dicere, eos qui non recte ædificauerint posse quidem seruari, sed quasi per ignem, vt enim is qui euadit per incendia vix nudus exilit, ita hi doctrina sua confutata & damnata agnoscunt se lusisse operam, atq; ita iudicio Dei retecto eorum peccato, pœnitentiæ dolorem & magnam tristitiam sentiunt. Sanam hanc & orthodoxam huius loci interpretationem quædam Papæ simul & ven-tris proprij mancipia non poterant ferre, videbant enim si hoc fundamentum Purgatoriæ ipsorum officinæ conuelleretur, etiāsi eam nemo deinde impelleret, tamen ipsam sua infirmitate sponte collapsuram: norant præterea casum Purgatorij necessariò consequi interitum parentalium sacrorum, & indulgentiarum ex quibus quæstum hactenus fecissent vberrimum. Quare cum statuerent hæc non esse ferenda, Martyrem quem harum rerum auctorem fore metuebant accusarunt, atq; tandem effecerunt ut illi lectione interdiceretur. Sed Martyr huic interdicto obtemperare noluit, vt iniquo & iniusto, & causæ bonitate fretus Romam ad Pontificem prouocauit, & illic amicorum ope aduersarios superauit. Habuit enim tum in vrbe amicos potentes & gratiosos Herculem Gonzagam Cardinalem Mantuanum, Casparem Contarenum, Reginaldum Polum, Petrum Bembum, Fridericum Fregosium, omnes et doctos et apud Pontificem gratiosos, et qui tum viderentur aliquam reformationem ecclesiae desiderare. Horum gratia et opibus subnixus facile obtinuit, ut interdictum illud adversariorum tolleretur, et sibi concederetur pristina docendi libertas: qua tamen non diu frui potuit.
units.tr: Although the first praise of this Church is owed to Valdés, nevertheless the virtue of Martyr is also to be commemorated. After he had been granted by the Lord a fuller light of divine truth and had joined the company of the godly, he wished at once to preach to others also what he knew to be the true doctrine. Indeed he began to expound publicly the first Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, and with great profit, for not only his fellow members of the college heard him, but also several bishops and many nobles, for, as you know, that city had always been a home of noble and distinguished men. But when he expounded, against the accepted opinion, the words of Paul which occur in the third chapter of that epistle, "Each man's work will be made manifest; for the day will declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire, and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is. If any man's work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as by fire" (1 Cor. 3.), he stirred up many adversaries and enemies against himself. For it is commonly believed that by these words Paul establishes and confirms that purgatorial fire, from which the Papist priests have scarcely any more profitable income. Martyr, although he did not yet openly attack that purgatory, which is like a prison built by the monks, nevertheless showed, and this from the ancient Fathers, that Paul is by no means here speaking of purgatorial fire, since he sets up a fire which equally good and bad builders undergo; rather, he says that those who have not built rightly may indeed be saved, but as through fire. For just as one who escapes through a conflagration scarcely comes out naked, so these, when their teaching is refuted and condemned, acknowledge that they have wasted their labour, and thus, when their sin is laid bare by the judgement of God, they feel the pain of repentance and great sorrow. Certain servants of the Pope and of their own belly could not bear this sound and orthodox interpretation of the passage. For they saw that if this foundation of their purgatory workshop were overthrown, even if no one afterwards pushed it, it would collapse of its own weakness. Moreover, they knew that the overthrow of purgatory must necessarily bring about the ruin of the masses for the dead and of the indulgences, from which they had hitherto made very abundant profit. Therefore, deciding that these things were not to be tolerated, they accused Martyr, whom they feared would be the author of such matters, and at last they brought it about that he was forbidden to read. But Martyr refused to obey this prohibition as unjust and unfair, and, relying on the goodness of his cause, he appealed to the Pope at Rome, and there by the help of his friends he overcame his adversaries. For he then had at the city powerful and influential friends: Ercole Gonzaga, Cardinal of Mantua, Gaspare Contarini, Reginald Pole, Pietro Bembo, and Federico Fregoso, all learned men and influential with the Pope, and men who at that time seemed to desire some reformation of the Church. Supported by their favour and resources, he easily obtained that the prohibition of his adversaries was lifted, and that his former freedom to teach was restored to him. He was not, however, to enjoy it for long.

units.la: Nondum enim integrum triennium Neapoli egerat cum in gravem et lethalem morbum incidit, una cum perpetuo studiorum socio et integerrimo amico Benedicto Gusano, quo hic quidem obiit, Martyr vero singulari Dei beneficio, et diligenti optimorum medicorum cura difficulter evasit. Quamobrem ut eius valetudini consulerent principes familiae, cum viderent ipsum non posse ferre aërem Neapolitanum, in publico conventu declararunt ipsum generalem visitatorem totius ordinis. In hoc munere ita se gessit ut boni eius integritatem et constantiam ac gravitatem plurimum laudarent, reliqui eum metuerent, et quamuis eum odissent id tamen dissimularent. Erant tum multi qui in ordine tyrannidem quandam exercebant, et cum luxu et impuritate vitae maximam universae familiae invidiam conciliarent, nullis rationibus et admonitionibus hactenus ad sanitatem revocari potuerant. Hos in ordinem redigendos esse Martyr existimans, re cum Mantuano Cardinali qui totius familiae protector erat, communicata, eius auxilio nonnullos suis dignitatibus privavit, et generalem rectorem totius familiae cum aliquot sociis in Diomedea insula ad perpetuos carceres damnavit. Ut autem hac disciplinae severitate gratiam universo ordini et sibi ipsi magnam gloriam comparavit, ita eodem facto multorum odia et inimicitias sibi conciliavit. Itaque Mantuae celebrato conventu procerum familiae Prior S. Fridiani Lucae designatus est: quae quidem etsi ampla est dignitas in hac familia, nam episcopalia iura in mediam urbis partem obtinet Prior S. Fridiani: pauci tamen honoris causa Martyrem huc promouerunt, pleriq; vero quod eum odissent vel illi inviderent, & existimarent eum ob patriam omnibus invisum fore: Lucē-ses enim magnum & inveteratum quoddam in Florentinos odium habent, propterea quod eos libertati suae insidiari existimant.
units.tr: For he had not yet spent a full three years at Naples when he fell into a grave and deadly illness, together with his lifelong study companion and most upright friend Benedetto Gusano. Gusano died of it, but Martyr escaped with difficulty, by a singular blessing of God and the careful treatment of excellent physicians. Therefore, so that the leaders of the order might look after his health, since they saw he could not endure the Neapolitan air, they declared him general visitor of the whole order at a public assembly. In this office he conducted himself so that his good men praised his integrity, constancy and gravity greatly, while the rest feared him, and although they hated him, they concealed it. There were then many in the order who exercised a kind of tyranny and, by their luxury and impurity of life, won for the whole brotherhood the greatest ill will. Until then they had not been brought back to soundness by any arguments or admonitions. Martyr judged that these men had to be brought into line. He discussed the matter with the Cardinal of Mantua, who was protector of the whole brotherhood, and with his help he deprived some of them of their dignities, and condemned the general ruler of the whole brotherhood, with several companions, to perpetual imprisonment on the island of Diomedea. But just as by this severity in discipline he won favour for the whole order and great glory for himself, so by the same act he won for himself the hatred and enmity of many. Accordingly, when a meeting of the leading men of the brotherhood was held at Mantua, he was appointed Prior of St Frediano at Lucca. This is indeed a considerable dignity in this brotherhood, for the Prior of St Frediano holds episcopal rights over the central part of the city. Yet few promoted him to it out of respect; most did so because they hated him or envied him, and thought that, being a Florentine, he would be hated by everyone in that city. For the people of Lucca have a great and long-standing hatred of the Florentines, because they think them plotting against their liberty.

units.la: Verùm Martyr ita excellenti sua eruditione & virtute Lucensium animos sibi devinxit, ut contra aduersariorum & invidorum spem & opinionem ipse homo Florentinus civibus non minus gratus atque charus fuerit quam si Lucensis civis suis-set: ita ut postea legatione ad proceres familiæ missa enixè pe-tierint ne Martyr sibi auferatur. Cùm itaq; Lucæ ageret Martyr & in collegio suo haberet plures viros doctos, multos etiam optimæ indolis adolescentes, talem disciplinam instituit qua bonos mores, religionem & literarum studia quàm maximè pos-set promoveret. Nam primum hoc curavit ut in tribus linguis adolescentes erudirentur quam diligentissimè, & Latinam quidem docebat Paulus Lacisius Veronensis, Græcam Celsus ex illustri Comitum Martinengorum familia, Hebræam Emanuel Tremellius. Ipse verò Martyr quo iuniores simul et Græcam linguam & religionem addisceret, quotidie epistolas Pauli illius interpretabatur & rursus ab ijs lectionē exigebat. Publicè verò ante cænam Psalmum aliquem Davidicum explicare solebat, confluebant autem ad eum audiendum è tota civitate viri complures nobiles & docti, patricij Lucenses. Quò autem in universa republica veram religionem plantaret, singulis diebus dominicis ad populum concionatus est, & in quadragesima quidem atq; in adventu usitato more Evangelia iam olim his temporibus adscripta exposuit, reliquis autem anni partibus Pauli epistolas. Quantum verò docendo profecerit ego commemorare nolo, vos autem ipsi facilè hinc colligere potestis, quod post eius ex Italia discessum, intra unius anni spatium decem & octo socij collegium deseruerunt, & relicto Papatu profecti sunt ad ecclesias in quibus publicè pura Evangelij doctrina prædicatur, inter quos fuere vir nobilissimus Celsus Martinengus, qui Geneuæ ecclesiæ Italicæ magna cum laude præfuit, & D. Hie-ronymus Zanchus qui nunc sacras literas in celebri Argenti-nensi schola docet. Emanuel itē Tremellius celeberrimus He-braeæ linguæ interpres. Testatur magnus numerus patriciorū Lucensium qui pro Christi nomine sponte exilii subierunt, Mar-tyris conciones fructu non caruisse. Dum ita Martyr Lucæ ageret, conuenēre in ea vrbe Carolus Cæsar & Paulus III. Pō-tifex, venit etiam illuc è Germanica legatione rediens Gaspar Contarenus Cardinalis, qui pro veteri amicitia apud Mar-tyrem diuertit, vna cum Thoma Badia Mutinense Magistro sacri palatij & legationis suæ socio.
