Fuere illis diebus quoti-diana Martyris & Contareni de religione colloquia, vti inter amicos homines doctos & religionis studiosos. Redierat tum primùm Contarenus ex Germania, audierat nostrorum homi-num fidei confessionem, rationes & argumenta eorum cognoue-rat, & vt plerique iudicant non omninò malè de nostris homini-bus existimabat. Credendum quoq; est & Martyrem multa ex illo de nostris hominibus & doctoribus audiuisse, quæ eum in sententia confirmarent: & vicissim quoq; in multis Contarenū iuuisse, vt oculos aperire ac veritatem clarius agnoscere inciperet. Existimabant nonnulli ob aduentum Pontificis Martyrem in aliquo periculo fore, quod homines inuidi & malitiosi qui semper veræ virtutis hostes sunt, apud suspiciosum senem facilè aliquam calumniam confingere possent, vnde illi periculum crearetur. Quia verò propria auctoritate & eruditione firmus erat, & præterea pollebat populi gratia & amicorum præsidijs, tum quidem nihil contra eum mouerunt, sed re in aliud tempus dila-ta ipsum ex insidijs adoriri statuerunt. Quare vt primum pa-tientiam Lucensis populi explorarent, quendam Eremitanum Augustinianæ familiæ à confessionibus, iussu Romani Ponti-ficis in carcerem coiciunt, & in eum de religione violata accu-sationem instituunt: quàm rem indignè ferentes nobiles aliquot Lucenses, qui hominis pietatem & innocentiam nouerant, ipsum effractis carceribus ex urbe eductum fuga sibi consulere iusse-runt: in qua cum forte lapsu crus fregisset, denuò captus & Romam abductus est. Posteaquam igitur prima hæc quasi impressio illis ex voto successit, statuerunt deinceps Martyrē aggredi, itaq; omnibus in locis insidias illi ponunt, Romæ clam in eum accusationem instituunt, in singulis collegijs eius familiæ veteres eius inimicos excitant, tempus adesse ostendunt quo suam licentiam quam ipsi libertatem appellabant recuperare, & de Martyrē pœnas sumere possint: hortantur ne occasioni desint. Breui itaq; horum studio & opera Genuam coëunt, nō pro more principes tantum familiæ, verum illi maximè qui Martyrem odissent, aut illi inuiderent, qui omnem licentiam vitæ sibi restitui cuperent, quorum religio in superstitiosis ceremonijs, sanctimonia in hypocrisi posita erat. Euocatur ab his Martyr ut se Genuæ primo quoq; tempore sistat: verum cum insidias inimicorum non ignoraret, quas odio excæcati celare non poterant: & præterea amici veteres eum monerent sibi caveret, multos esse qui vitæ eius insidias struerent, re secum diligenter deliberata statuit conventum hunc omninō evitare, ac se alio conferre, ubi ab adversariorum vi & insidijs tutus esse queat. Itaq; primum suæ Bibliothecæ partem aliquam, hæc enim erant ipsius χειμήλια, Christophoro Trentæ patricio Lucensi, homini pio verę religionis studioso committit, qui eam postea in Germaniam ad illum pervehi curavit: reliquam partem legavit collegio: deinde rebus collegij ordine quantum poterat compositis, & cura eius vicario suo comissa, clam è collegio & ex urbe discessit, cum tribus tantum comitibus: Paulo Lacisio Veronensi, qui postea Argentinæ factus Græcarum literarum professor in ea urbe mortem obijt: Theodosio Trebellio & Iulio Terentiano, quem omneis nostris Martyri constanter & fideliter ad obitum usq; adhæsisse. Luca discedens, cum statuisset patriam primum adire, Pisas venit, & in ea urbe cum aliquot nobilibus Cœnā Domini Christiano ritu celebravit: nactus illic fidos homines mines literas de discessu suo conscripsit ad Reginaldum Polum, & alteras ad suos Lucenses quæ post mensem a discessu suo illis redderentur. In his ostendit qui & quam graves errores & abusus sint in omni pontificiorum religione, & separatim etiam in vita monastica, quibus communicare salva conscientia ulterius non potuerit: exposuit etiam alias sui discessus causas, odia scilicet & insidias inimicorum suorum: commemorabat suam in illis erudiendis & moderandis fidem & religionem, & sibi dolere testabatur quod non potuerit eos clarius & apertius in vera fide instituere: annulum quem insigne dignitatis gestare solebat, illis remisit, quo declararet se nihil bonorum collegij in privatos usus voluisse convertere.
units.tr: But Martyr so bound the hearts of the Lucchese to himself by his outstanding learning and virtue that, contrary to the hopes and expectations of his adversaries and envious rivals, he, a Florentine by birth, became no less welcome and dear to the citizens than if he had been a citizen of Lucca himself. So much so that afterwards they sent an embassy to the leaders of the brotherhood, earnestly begging that Martyr not be taken from them. When Martyr was therefore at Lucca, and had in his college several learned men and many young men of excellent disposition, he established a course of training by which he could promote good morals, religion and the study of letters as far as possible. For first he took care that the young men be taught in three languages as diligently as possible. Paolo Lacisio of Verona taught Latin, Celso of the distinguished family of the Counts Martinengo taught Greek, and Emanuel Tremellius taught Hebrew. Martyr himself, so that the younger men might at the same time learn both the Greek language and religion, expounded to them daily the Epistles of Paul, and in turn required an account of the reading from them. Publicly, before supper, he used to expound some Psalm of David, and many noble and learned men and patricians of Lucca flocked from the whole city to hear him. In order to plant the true religion throughout the commonwealth, he preached to the people on every Lord's Day. During Lent and in Advent he expounded, in the customary manner, the Gospels long since assigned to these seasons, and at other times of the year the Epistles of Paul. How much he advanced by teaching I do not wish to recount, but you yourselves can easily gather this from the fact that, within the space of a single year after his departure from Italy, eighteen fellows deserted the college, and, leaving Popery behind, went to those churches in which the pure doctrine of the Gospel is publicly preached. Among them were the most noble Celso Martinengo, who presided with great credit over the Italian church at Geneva, and Master Girolamo Zanchi, who now teaches sacred letters in the famous school at Strasbourg; also Emanuel Tremellius, the most celebrated interpreter of the Hebrew language. A large number of the Lucchese patricians, who willingly underwent exile for the name of Christ, bear witness that Martyr's sermons were not without fruit. While Martyr was thus at Lucca, Charles Caesar and Pope Paul III met in that city. Cardinal Gasparo Contarini also came there, returning from his embassy to Germany, and for old friendship he stayed with Martyr, together with Tommaso Badia of Modena, Master of the Sacred Palace and companion of his embassy. In those days there were daily conversations between Martyr and Contarini about religion, as is usual among friends who are learned and devoted to religion. Contarini had just returned from Germany; he had heard the confession of our people, had become acquainted with their reasons and arguments, and, as most judge, did not think ill of our people at all. It must also be believed that Martyr heard many things from him about our people and teachers which confirmed him in his opinion, and that in turn he helped Contarini in many matters, so that he began to open his eyes and recognise the truth more clearly. Some thought that on account of the Pope's arrival Martyr would be in some danger, since envious and malicious men, who are always enemies of true virtue, could easily invent some slander against him before a suspicious old man, whereby danger would be created for him. But because he was firm in his own authority and learning, and moreover was powerful in the favour of the people and the protection of friends, they at that time did nothing against him, but deferring the matter to another time, they resolved to attack him by treachery. Therefore, in order first to test the patience of the people of Lucca, they threw into prison, on the orders of the Roman Pontiff, a certain Hermit of the Augustinian order who was confessor to the brotherhood, and brought a charge against him of violating the faith. The leading men of Lucca, who knew the man's piety and innocence, took this badly, and some of them, having broken open the prison, led him out of the city and advised him to flee; but in the course of his flight he happened to break his leg, was recaptured, and led away to Rome. After this first, as it were, impression had succeeded to their wish, they resolved thereafter to assail Martyr. So they laid snares for him in every place, secretly brought accusations against him at Rome, roused his old enemies in each of the college houses of that brotherhood, and showed that the time had come when they could recover the licence which they called liberty, and take vengeance on Martyr; they urged them not to miss the opportunity. Soon, through their zeal and effort, they assembled at Genoa, not only the leaders of the brotherhood as usual, but chiefly those who hated Martyr or envied him, and who wished all licence of life to be restored to them, men whose religion lay in superstitious ceremonies and whose holiness lay in hypocrisy. Martyr was summoned by them to present himself at Genoa at the earliest opportunity. But since he was not ignorant of the plots of his enemies, which men blinded by hatred could not conceal, and since his old friends also warned him to be on his guard, because many were plotting against his life, he resolved, after carefully deliberating the matter with himself, to avoid this meeting altogether and to betake himself elsewhere, where he could be safe from the violence and treachery of his adversaries. So first he committed part of his library to Christoforo Trenta, a patrician of Lucca and a pious man devoted to the true religion (for these were his treasured possessions), and Trenta afterwards took care to have them conveyed to him in Germany. The remaining part he bequeathed to the college. Then, having put the affairs of the college in as good order as he could, and having entrusted their management to his deputy, he left the college and the city secretly, with only three companions: Paolo Lacisio of Verona, who afterwards became professor of Greek letters at Strasbourg and died there; Teodosio Trebellio; and Giulio Terenziano, who, we know, clung constantly and faithfully to our Martyr until his death. Leaving Lucca, and having decided first to visit his homeland, he came to Pisa, and in that city celebrated the Lord's Supper in the Christian manner with some noblemen. There he found faithful men, and wrote letters about his departure, one to Reginald Pole, and others to his Lucchese people, to be delivered to them a month after his departure. In these he showed what and how grave errors and abuses there are in the whole Papist religion, and separately also in monastic life, with which he could no longer communicate and keep his conscience clear. He also set out his other reasons for leaving, namely the hatred and plots of his enemies. He recalled his faith and religion in instructing and guiding them, and he declared that he grieved that he had not been able to instruct them more clearly and openly in the true faith. The ring which he used to wear as the sign of his dignity he sent back to them, to declare that he had not wished to turn any of the goods of the college to private use.

units.la: Et certe quod eius innocentiæ indicium est, exiguum peculium secum in Germaniam attulit, quod scilicet paucis annis quibus iam exilium meditabatur, ex proprio patrimonio collegerat. Postea quam vero sicuti destinauerat in patriam pervenit, reperit ibi virum optimum & doctissimum Bernardinum Ochinum qui Romam evocatus eo pergebat, sed postea quam ab amicis de periculo admonitus cum Martyre sua consilia contulit, ambo tandem communi consilio statuerunt deserta Italia & relicto patrio solo Germaniam petere. Et prior quidem Bernardinus inde discedens se Genevam primum, & postea Augustã Rheticam contulit: Biduo post Mar-tyr ipsum secutus est, & Bononiam primum, deinde Ferrariam, mox Veronam profectus ubiq̄ humaniter exceptus ab amicis veteribus, tandem per alpes Rheticas in Helvetiam pervenit. In hoc itinere cum Tigurum venisset, humaniter exceptus a Bullingero, Pellicano, Gualthero & cæteris ecclesiæ atq; scholæ nostræ ministris, suam illis operam obtulit, si ea uti placeret: verum quia nullus locus in schola eo tempore vacabat, ostende-runt se quod maximè vellent hoc tempore eius opera uti nō posse, attamen voluntatis eius se grato animo memores fore. Re-ferebat aliquando, si huius professionis mentio facta fuisset, se cum primum Tigurum venisset, multum & tu[?] & deinceps semper eam urbem amasse, ac optasse hanc esse certum & firmum exi-lij sui hospitium: cuius voti post compos factus est, quamuis prius diuinae prouidentiae visum fuerit, eum tanquam legatum Iesu Christi ad varias urbes & gentes mittere, ut tandem Deo ita procurante Tigurum rediret, & in ea urbe non longè ab Italiae finibus, post longas & difficiles peregrinationes conquieseret.
units.tr: And certainly, as evidence of his integrity, he brought with him to Germany only a small private sum, which he had gathered from his own patrimony in the few years in which he had already been contemplating exile. After he reached his homeland as he had intended, he found there the most excellent and learned man Bernardino Ochino, who was on his way to Rome, having been summoned there. But after friends warned him of the danger, and he had discussed the matter with Vermigli, the two of them finally resolved by common counsel to abandon Italy and their native soil and make for Germany. Bernardino left first, going to Geneva and then to Augsburg in Rhaetia. Two days later Vermigli followed him, setting out first for Bologna, then Ferrara, and soon Verona, everywhere received kindly by old friends, and at last came through the Rhaetian Alps into Helvetia. On this journey, when he came to Zurich, he was kindly received by Bullinger, Pellican, Gwalther and the other ministers of our church and school, and offered them his services, if they wished to use them. But since no place in the school was vacant at that time, they showed that they could not make use of his work just then, though they would remember his goodwill with a grateful mind. He used to recall, whenever mention was made of this professorship, that as soon as he came to Zurich he had loved that city greatly, and had always afterwards, and had hoped it would be a sure and firm haven for his exile. He afterwards attained this wish, although it had first seemed good to divine providence to send him as an ambassador of Jesus Christ to various cities and peoples, so that at last, with God thus arranging it, he returned to Zurich and, in that city not far from the borders of Italy, found rest after long and difficult wanderings.

units.la: Tiguro igitur tu discedens Basileam venit, & cum illic men-se uno fuisset, Argentinam una cum Paulo Lacisio vocatus est, id procurante viro optimo & doctissimo Martino Bucero, atq; ipsi quidem sacrarum literarum, Lacisio autem Graecae linguae professio demandata esset. Suscepto igitur docendi munere illis quinq; annis, quibus Argentinae ante discessum in Angliam do-cuit, plurimos libros sacros interpretatus est. Nam primum Ieremiae prophetae Lamentationem, deinde duodecim propheta-rum, qui minores nominantur, librū enarrauit. Postea ab ini-tio Bibliorum volumen incipiens Genesim, Exodum, & bonam partem Leuitici explicauit. Quanta autem eruditione fidè & diligentia hoc fecerit, testabuntur aliquando ipsius in hos libros commentarij si in publicum prodierint. Nam quamuis eos in priuatum usum conscripserit, & morte praeuentus non potuerit recognoscere, digni tamen sunt qui in manus studiosorum ve-niant. Praeterea quantum iam tum in docendo excelluerit,non modo ex his quae ipsi audiuistis & vidistis conijcere, sed hinc quoq; cognoscere poteris, quod cum haberet collegam Martinū Bucerum summum Theologum, qui, ut à viro quodam docto vere de illo scriptum est, praeter reconditam eruditionem copio-sam; multarum rerum scientiam, praeter ingenij perspicaciam, multam lectionem, aliasq; multas ac varias virtutes, hanc sibi propriam laudem habuit, quod vix alius hac memoria exactio-re diligentia in scripturae interpretatione versatus est: hunc in-quam talem ac tantum virum cum in docendo collegam habe-ret, nunquam tamen eo inferior esse visus est. Nam primum quod propter trium linguarū exactam peritiam felicissimè praestare poterat, ipsa verba sacrarum literarum sensum[?] genuinum diligenter explicabat: deinde inuestigabat & retegebat rationes & argumenta, quae sub verbis alioquin simplicibus & contractis delitescunt: & simplicius dicta alijs locis confirmabat, obscura cum apertis conferebat, ostendebat quae nam aduersari viderētur verbis propositis, & rationem ea conciliandi demonstrabat, quid item patres sensissent singulari felicitate memoriae ordine exponebat: & acri iudicio quod pondus & robur singulorum interpretationes haberent, examinabat: controuersias vero incidentes ita dextrè & dilucidè explicabat, vt nemo alius.
units.tr: So he left Zurich and came to Basel, and after he had spent one month there, he was called to Strasbourg together with Paul Lasicius, through the good offices of the excellent and learned man Martin Bucer. He was assigned the teaching of sacred letters, while Lasicius was given the chair of Greek. Having undertaken this teaching office, during the five years he taught at Strasbourg before his departure for England, he interpreted many sacred books. First he expounded the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah, then the book of the twelve prophets who are called the Minor Prophets. Afterwards, beginning the volume of the Bible from the start, he explained Genesis, Exodus and a good part of Leviticus. How learnedly, faithfully and diligently he did this will be attested one day by his commentaries on these books, if they are published. For although he wrote them for private use, and death prevented him from revising them, they are nonetheless worthy to come into the hands of students. Moreover, you can judge how greatly he already excelled in teaching then, not only from what you yourselves heard and saw, but also from this: though he had as colleague Martin Bucer, the supreme theologian, who, as a certain learned man has truly written of him, besides his deep learning and wide knowledge of many things, besides the keenness of his judgement, his wide reading and many other varied virtues, had this particular praise, that scarcely anyone else engaged in the interpretation of Scripture with such exact diligence and such a retentive memory, nevertheless Vermigli, having such a man and so great a man as colleague in teaching, never seemed inferior to him. For first, because of his exact mastery of the three languages, which enabled him to excel most happily, he carefully explained the genuine sense of the very words of Scripture. Then he investigated and brought to light the reasons and arguments that otherwise lie hidden beneath simple and compressed words; he confirmed plainer statements by other passages, compared obscure places with clear ones, showed which things seemed to conflict with the words proposed and demonstrated the way of reconciling them, and likewise set out, with singular felicity of memory and in order, what the Fathers had thought; and with keen judgement he weighed how much weight and strength each interpretation had. But he explained the controversies that arose so skilfully and clearly that no one else could match him.

units.la: In vniuersa autem tractatione duo praeterea afferebat quae cum maximè in docendo necessaria sint, methodus exacta, deinde oratio pura & dilucida, sic in his excellebat, vt Bucerū non modo æquare verumetiam omnium iudicio superare videret ur.
units.tr: Moreover, in his whole treatment of a subject he showed two further things which are most necessary in teaching: an exact method, and a pure and clear style. In these he so excelled that he was seen not only to equal Bucer but, in the judgement of all, to surpass him.

units.la: Nam ille methodi alioqui obseruantissimus, nonnunquam tamen multarum rerum scientia alio abductus, longius ab ordine instituto diuertebat: aut infinitis occupationibus distractus partitionis propositae non semper memor erat: adhæc fuit illi (sicuti agnouit & sæpe fassus est) peculiaris obscuritas orationis, vt non nisi ab attento auditore intelligi posset.
units.tr: For Bucer, though very careful about method in general, was nevertheless sometimes carried away by the wealth of his knowledge and wandered far from the order he had set; or, distracted by endless occupations, he was not always mindful of the division he had proposed. Besides this, he had (as he himself acknowledged and often confessed) a peculiar obscurity of style, so that he could be understood only by an attentive listener.

units.la: Martyr autem omnia quae tractanda erant cum apte in certas partes diuidebat, tum neq; vllius earum in quantumuis prolixa tractatione obliuiscebatur, neq; nouam aliquam in media tractatione inserebat, neque ordinem quem initiò proposuerat inuertebat, sed eum quem semel proposuisset partium numerum & ordinem constanter ad finem usq; persequebatur.
units.tr: Vermigli, on the other hand, when he had to treat everything, divided it aptly into definite parts, and never forgot any of those parts however lengthy the treatment, nor did he insert some new matter in the middle of the discussion, nor did he reverse the order he had first proposed; rather he followed through to the end, steadily, the number and order of the parts he had once laid down.

units.la: In dicendo verbis vtebatur puris, proprijs, Latinis: compositione praeterea tali, quae neq; contractione orationis aut verborum ambiguitate obscuritatē pareret, vel rursus orationis longitudine sententiam suspenderet, & intellectum ac memoriam auditoris turbaret.
units.tr: In speaking he used pure, proper, Latin words, and with a construction that caused neither obscurity through compression of expression or ambiguity of words, nor, on the other hand, through length of sentence, held back the meaning and confused the understanding and memory of the hearer.

units.la: Itaq; non modò rerum ipsarum grauitate, verùm orationis quoq; suauitate & elegantia animos auditorū demulcebat, & summa praeterea grauitate in ipsis lectionibus nunc ad piam vitam cohortabatur , nunc ad pœnitentiam grauiori increpatione commo-vebat, ut omnibus his rebus quasi conditæ eius lectiones, sum-mam eruditionem & eloquentiam cum singulari pietate coniu-ctam ostendentes, magnam illi gloriam omnium iudicio compa-rarent. Nunquam tamen doctior erat & magis admirandus, quàm in publicis disputationibus. Siue enim moderandi essent concertantes alij, tam se æquum iudicem præbebat, ac rationi-bus tantum quæ ad persuadendum valerent mouebatur, ut ne-mo unquam suspicaretur partibus eum studere: non adversa-riorum argumenta solida deprimebat: non conniuebat ad ami-corum errores & falsas rationes: si extra fines disputationis e-vagari vellent eos mansuete ad rem propositam revocabat: si ve-rò res ad rixas vergeret, sua authoritate eas sopiebat. Ita aut finiebat eos congressus, ut & semper primum maximè necessa-ria repeteret, & tum demum de integra causa pronūtiaret,quo & veritas victrix foret, & inde non exigua ad auditores re-dundaret utilitas. Quod si ipsi differendum esset,tam in propo-nendo quàm in respondendo,ita se semper gerebat, ut nulla esset suspicio cupiditatis, vel rixandi vel reportandæ victoriæ de pro-strato adversario: sed animo ab affectibus libero, quid verum esset docebat potius quàm ut cum ullo de verbis rixaretur. Itaq; cum postea sæpe cum acerrimis Pontificiæ religionis propugna-toribus congressus sit, neq; ipsorum convitijs ad iram unquam impulsus est, neq; nostrorum hominum laudibus & acclamatio-nibus gloriola tali elatior factus est: sed eandem modestiam & animi æquabilitatem perpetuò tenuit. Qua vero perspicui-tate dicendi in publicis prælectionibus usus est,eam multo stu-diosius in differendo consectabatur: iudicabat enim orationis ob-scuritatem & ambiguitatem verborum plurimarum cõtentio-num causam esse. Atq; huius rei apertum testimonium scripta illius præbent, nam cum multa de iustificatione hominis, de prae-destinatione divina non pauca, plurima vero scripserit de Cœna Domini, in cuius explicatione complures viri docti affectata quadam obscuritate utuntur, nihil nisi proprium, simplex, diluci-dum in eius scriptis legitur. Quin etiam cum Bucerus, quem coluit & admiratus esset, sæpe illum hortaretur ut in causa cœnæ Dominicæ obscuris quibusdā & ambiguis dicendi formulis uteretur, quibus ipse ideo vtebatur, quod vir bonus sibi persuasisset, posse hac ratione tolli grauem quæ esset de hac causa controuersiam, & ita ecclesiæ, pacem diu desideratam restitui: paruit tandem illi & eisdem cum eo loquendi formis vsus esset: sed mox periculo huius rei animaduersus, sententiam mutauit. Vidit enim hac ratione non posse illis satisfieri, qui crassam & carnalem præsentiam corporis Christi in Cœna statuunt, nisi etiam crassæ eorum locutiones cum plena crassaq; interpretatione recipiantur: rursus etiam expertus est fratres infirmiores hac orationis ambiguitate partim grauiter offendi, partim ita implicari & perturbari, ut vix norint quid sibi in hac causa sentiendū sit. Quare Bucero suas locutiones cōcedens, ipse eandē quam in aliis rebus in hoc quoq; dogmate perspicuitatem secutus esset, mansitq; nihilominus inter eos firma cōstansq; amicitia: nam neq; Martyris sententiā Bucerus improbabat, neq; Buceri sensum, quantumuis ambiguis locutionibus vteretur, Martyr ignorabat. Itaq;, etsi diuersa eorum in hac causa esset docendi ratio, fuit tamen summus eorum consensus in omni doctrina religionis, & perpetua amicitia vitæq; coniunctio: quam si explicare vellem, & omnia eorum officia quibus mutuum amorem declararunt commemorare, verba me citius quam res ipsæ deficerent. Quare his omissis ad priuata & ad domesticam illius vitam enarrandam me conuertam, Argentinæ enim primum domum & familiam habere cœpit. Vixit autem primum absq; vxore in eisdem ædibus cum amicis qui eum ex Italia secuti sunt, stipendio modico aut potius exiguo contentus, quod tamen illi postea auctum fuit: cum enim patriam & opes amplissimas summosq; honores Christi nomine reliquisset, existimabat sibi non conuenire vlli molestum esse de augendo stipendio: præsertim cum vita ita esset frugali,ut hoc quod haberet nō modò sibi sufficeret, sed aliquid etiā superesset ad amicos iuuandos. Cùm verò vitam cœlibem gra-uibus de causis improbaret, amicorum consilio sibi despondit honestam & nobilem virginem Catharinam Dampmartinā quae cum Metis ageret, & veram religionem amaret, à pijs viris Argentinam euocata & Martyri postea desponsata fuit. Obiit hac postea in Anglia absq; ulla prole, cum annos octo cum marito uixisset. Huic quicunq; eam nouerunt cuncti hanc laudem tribuunt quae optimae & praestantissimae matronae debetur: fuit enim imprimis Deum timens, mariti amans, in re domestica administranda prudens & industria, munifica erga egenos, & quae non modò suis facultatibus, verumetiam consilio & omni ope eos iuuaret, praeterea in omni vita pia, modesta, sobria. Ferunt plebeios homines Oxonii, illam non tantū ut beneficam ac matrem quodammodo egenorum amasse, verumetiam quasi sacro numine praeditam admiratos esse, propterea quod in morbis, & praesertim in partu uxores eorum illius consilio & auxilio certam plerunq; salutem consequerentur. Huius defunctae corpus Polus Cardinalis effodi & in sterquilinium abici iussit, & cùm aliud ut iure agere videretur accusare non posset, hanc causam adscripsit, quòd iuxta corpus sanctae Fridesuidae humata esset, et haeretici uxor fuisset. Etenim Cardinalis hic qui aliquando praecipuus Martyris amicus fuerat, postea eius discessum ex Italia non modò ab ipsius amicitia discesserat, verumetiam studiū verae religionis, quod ad tempus simulauerat, penitus abiecit, & acerrimus nostrorum hominum hostis & persecutor factus est. Itaq; cum Martyrem, quòd optabat & maiore voluptate aspexisset, flammis absumere non posset, in mortuum cadauer, quod uxoris eius fuerat, saeuit. Posteaquam verò Anglia sub serenissima regina Elizabetha pristinam Euangelii lucem recepit, ad hanc infamiae notam eluendam corpus iussu Episcoporū rursus è fimo & stercore erutum, & frequenti populo in honorificentissimo templi loco solenniter sepultum est. Et ne quid simile in posterum Papistæ tentare possent, ossa eius cum Fride-suidæ (quam olim religiose illi coluerūt) ossibus permixta sunt. Quamobrem quòd sanctissimæ fœminæ corpus turpiter & cotu-meliose abiectum est, illustre est monimetum Romanæ tyrannidis, quæ neq; viuis neq; mortuis fidelibus parcit: quòd verò hono-rificentissimè restitutū est veteri sepulchro, Anglorum erga suū præceptoré, cuius ea nuper uxor fuerat, pietate & gratitudiné testatur. Et quia huius rei occasione in metionem rerum Angli-carum deuenimus, ac satis ut uidetur dictum est de ijs quæ Argentinæ fecit & docuit, exponā deinceps quare in Anglia profectus sit & quid in eā effecerit. Mortuo Heinrico rege Angliæ Edoardus eius filius de consilio tutorum, & maxime Edoardi ducis Somersetensis auunculi sui, ac Thomæ Cranmeri archie-piscopi Cantuariensis & totius Angliæ primatis, pontificiā re-ligionem abolere, & ecclesias iuxta verbum Dei reformare sta-tuit. Et quia ex Academijs ministri ecclesiarum prodeunt, qui per universum regnum verbum Dei annuntient, eas cū primis diligenter reformadas esse statuit, quo deinde ex his purus suc-cus sanæ doctrinæ in singulas regni partes deriuetur. Quia verò Petrus Martyr doctorum virorum judicio, ob singularem eru-ditionem & incredibilem multarum rerum peritiam, unus omnium ad hoc munus maximè idoneus videbatur, ab archiepisco-po Cantuariensi de voluntate regis vocatus esset. Itaq; sub exi-tum Nouembris anni 1547. permissu senatus, Argentina ubi jam quinquennium docuerat in Angliam discessit, comitate eum Bernardino Ochino, qui & ipse quoque ab eodem Archie-piscopo vocatus fuerat. Cum autem aliquandiu eos Archiepi-scopus secum detinuisset, & omnibus humanitatis officijs prose-cutus esset, Martyr iussu regis sacris literis interpretandis Ox-onij præfectus ess.[?] In ea Academia primum enarrauit epi-stolam D. Pauli ad Corinthios priorem, eò quòd in ea tractēn-tur varia & multiplicia capita quæ ad nostrorum temporū co-trouersias faciunt, sic ut huius epistolæ doctrina si commodè dextreq[?], adhibita fuerit, omnibus vitijs quibus Ecclesia syncer-itas corrupta est, mederi possit: & omnes abusus atq; superstitio-nes Papisticas conuincere. Pontificij quorū adhuc Oxonij magnus erat numerus, initio quidem vtcunque patienter ferebant Martyrem docentem, & quidam etiam lectiones eius frequentabāt, & se illius eruditionem admirari prae se ferebant: alij verò ac praecipuè collegiorum praesides, suos arcebant à lectionibus, nihil tamen mouebant vlterius. Verùm posteaquam damnatis iam ante ipsorum votis, deinceps occasione verborum Apostoli de Cœna Domini tractare incœpit, existimarunt sibi nō vlterius esse quiescendum. Etenim cum maiores ipsorum obscurata primùm, deinde depravata doctrina huius dogmatis,in ecclesiam hac ianua erroris patefacta omnem superstitionem & idololatriam inuexerint, non poterant ferre Martyre, qui mirifico studio veritatem Eucharistiae ab eorum erroribus & corruptelis vindicabat. Quo vero non modò inuidiam, sed graue etiam periculum illi crearent, eum apud vulgus primùm vsitatis criminationibus traducebant,quod maiorum doctrinam impugnaret,ceremonias optimè constitutas conuelleret, sacrosanctū altaris sacramentum prophanaret, & tantum non pedibus conculcaret. Deinde omnibus rebus compositis,ipso ignorante,omnibus templis schedas Anglico sermone conscriptas affigunt,postridie publicè disputandum esse contra praesentia Christi in sacra Cœna. Die ergo sequenti hi auditoriū occupant, operas suas idoneis locis disponunt, easq; ad clamores & tumultum, & ad pugnam praeterea si vsus postulet paratas esse iubent. Concurrunt praeterea audiendi causa, non tantùm studiosi ex omnibus collegijs, verumetiam pars non exigua concitati populi, partim vt euentum rei spectarent,partim etiā vt alterutri parti adessent, si forte tumultus aliquis exoriretur. Martyr interea horum omnium ignarus sese domi parabat,vt hora constituta more solito lectionem faceret, cum interea amici permoti insolita concursatione populi, domum ad eum veniunt, ac illi omnē rem exponunt, hortanturq; ut se domi contineat,neq; aliquod periculum sibi conciliet, quandoquidem aduersarij ita parati sint, ut potius videantur armis quā argumentis concertare velle. Respondet ille, se nō posse officio suo deesse, & munus à rege demandatum sibi, negligere, se nullius tumultus auctorem vnquā fuisse, cuius rei ipsi optimi testes esse possint: nunc quoq; se nolle aduersarijs tumultuandi occasionem dare, sed more solito legere velle, esse haud dubiè multos in hoc cætu qui lectiones consuetas expetant, quos non possit negligere. Pergebat iam ad auditorium comitantibus illū amicorum fidelissimis, cùm illi in via obuius fit puer Smithæi, qui in hac tragœdia primas partes agebat, ac literas ei porrigit quibus ipsum herus suus ad disputandum provocabat. Ibi tum amici rursus monere, rogare, hortari ut domum redeat, commemorare pericula quæ ipsum manent, perstat tamen ille in sententia, pergit in auditorium ac provocantes aduersarios modesta oratione compescens quantum poterat, respondet, se disputationem non recusare, sed nunc non disputandi sed legendi causa huc venisse, atq; ita illis concedentibus lectionem more solito habet, magna omnium admiratione. Quippe qui ante singularem doctrinā & eloquentiam admirati, nunc quoq; incredibilem constantiam & fortitudinem in ipso suspicerent. In tanto enim murmure populi & fremitu aduersariorum, ita lectionem absoluit, ut nulla mutatio vultus & coloris in eo esset, non hæsitatio aliqua vocis, non linguæ titubatio, non denique tremor membrorum aut pallor aliquam opinionem timoris præbuit. Finita lectione acrius instant aduersarij, & eum magnis clamoribus ad disputandum provocant, neq; modestissimam eius excusationem recipiunt, quod se diceret disputaturum esse sed alio tempore, nunc se non esse paratum, cùm propositiones disputandas ita studiosè occultarint, neq; more solito publicè proposuerint, ut eas ad hunc usq; diem ignoret: aiebant enim eum qui nuper causam Cœnæ Domini, tam multis lectionibus tractasset, non posse imparatum esse quacunq; tādem in hac materia quæstiones proponerentur. Tum ille cùm eum urgere perseuerarent, denuò respondit, se primùm nolle inconsulta Re-gia maiestate tantam rem aggredi, præsertim cùm res ad sedi-tionem spectare videatur. Deinde ad legitimam disputationem requiri, ut proponatur certa quæstiones, constituantur judices & moderatores, quorum judicio atq; arbitrio tota res gubernetur, deniq; requiri notarios qui utriusq; partis argumenta & orationes, bona fide justaq; diligentia conscribant: cùm autem horum nihil nunc paratum & constitutum sit, se nec velle nec posse di-sputare, præsertim cum non satis temporis superfit, die iam in meridiem vergente, ad tantam rem excutiendam. Postea quam vero his rationibus quamuis æquissimis aduersarijs non satis-fiebat, & iam res ad pugnam & conflictum spectare videretur, in-terponit se Universitatis Oxoniensis Vicecancellarius (liceat enim mihi usitata nomina retinere) & his conditionibus pugnā dirimit, ut utrq; Martyr & Smythæus cum aliquot socijs in ipsius ædibus conueniant, propositiones disputandas, tempus, or-dinem & modum disputandi communi consilio constituant. Jubet deinde apparitores suos, Pedellos nominant, turbam sum-mouere, & ipse ad suggestum accedes Martyrem manu illi por-recta è turba populi abducit, & domum usq; comitatur, ac pro sua auctoritate tumultuantes compescit. Martyr liberatus ex hoc præsenti periculo, ne ideò quod causæ dissideret disputationē renuisse videretur, hora constituta ad domum Vicecancellarij venit, comitantibus ipsum cum alijs amicis, tum præsertim Sidallo & Curtopo, qui illo tempore eximij veritatis defensores erant, postea tamen Marianus temporibus eandem constantiam non retinuerunt. Facit idem aduersarius, & secù adducit Co-lum Oglethropum & tres alios Theologiæ doctores. Diu inter eos de disputatione constituenda disceptatum est, Martyr enim æquum esse aiebat, ipsos in confutando eum seruare ordine quæ ipse tenuisset in docendo, idq; tandem obtinuit. Abhorrebat præ-terea à vocibus peregrinis, barbaris & ambiguis, quæ tamen in scholis scholis receptae sunt, itaq; duabus tantum usus est carnaliter & corporaliter, quoniam scriptura in Cœna describenda tantū carnis & corporis, nō rei & substantiae meminit, attamen ne ambiguitate aliqua ludere ipsum existimaret, se illas accipere dixit, atq; si dictum esset realiter & substantialiter. Fuerunt etiam alijs de rebus disputationes aliquae inter ipsos, attamen cū demum de universa ratione disputandi inter ipsos convenisset, omnia quae tum constituta fuerunt, partium consensu ad Regiae Maiestatis consiliarios relata sunt, ut illi de tota controversia cognosce-rent: ab his disputationis dies constitutus est quarto Nonas Maij, ad quem diem affuturi sint legati Regij, qui disputationi praesint. Verum Smythaeus conscius sibi tumultus excitati, non expectata die constituta, fuga se subduxit, et in Scotiam pri-mum, deinde Louanium in Brabantiam abijt. Posteaquam vero praescripta dies adfuit, venerunt Oxonium Regij legati, R. D. Henricus Episcopus Lincolniensis, D. Richardus Coxus Universitatis Oxoniensis Cancellarius, D. Simon Haydes Decanus Oxoniensis. M. Richardus Morisinus Armiger, D. Christophorus Neuynsonus Iu. C. doctor. His praesentibus disputavit Martyr per quatriduum cum tribus Pontificiae re-ligionis Theologis, Treshamo & Cheadzeo Doctoribus, & Morgano artium Magistro. Quanta autem eruditione hos confutarint nō necesse est a me commemorari, quandoquidē acta huius disputationis in omnium manibus habentur. Nam Martyr quia aduersarij multa falsa & conficta de hac disputatione in vulgus spargebant, eorum improbitate & praeterea amicorum precibus qui hoc assiduè flagitabant, coactus, disputationem hanc in publicum edidit: qua autem fide ac diligentia hoc fecerit ostendit testimonium Regiorum legatorum libro ab ipsis additum.
units.tr: Thus he soothed the minds of his hearers not only by the weight of his subject matter but also by the charm and elegance of his speech. In his lectures he exhorted them, with great seriousness, to a godly life, and at other times moved them to repentance with a stern rebuke. All these qualities, which gave his lectures their character, showed his great learning and eloquence joined with singular piety, and so won him great glory in the judgement of everyone. Yet he was never more learned or more admirable than in public disputations. When other speakers were contending under his moderation, he showed himself so fair a judge, and was moved only by arguments that could persuade, that no one ever suspected him of favouring a party. He did not overthrow the solid arguments of his opponents, and he did not wink at the errors and false reasoning of his friends. If the disputants wandered beyond the limits of the debate, he gently recalled them to the matter proposed; if the discussion tended towards quarrels, he calmed them by his authority. He brought such encounters to an end in such a way that he always first returned to the most necessary points and only then pronounced upon the whole case, so that truth might be victorious and a considerable benefit might flow to the hearers. If he himself had to dispute, both in proposing and in answering, he so conducted himself that there was no suspicion of any desire either to quarrel or to win victory over a prostrate opponent. With a mind free from passions, he taught what was true rather than wrangle with anyone over words. Therefore, although he afterwards often engaged with the fiercest champions of the Papist religion, he was never provoked to anger by their insults, nor was he made more proud by the praises and acclamations of our own people. He always kept the same modesty and evenness of mind. Moreover, he pursued with even greater care in disputation the clarity of speech which he used in public lectures, for he judged that obscurity of language and ambiguity of words were the cause of very many controversies. The writings of his own hand give clear testimony to this. For although he wrote much on the justification of man, not a little on divine predestination, and most of all on the Lord's Supper, in the explanation of which many learned men use a certain affected obscurity, nothing in his writings is read but what is proper, plain and clear. Indeed, when Bucer, whom he cultivated and admired, often urged him to use in the cause of the Lord's Supper certain obscure and ambiguous forms of speech, which Bucer himself used because he was persuaded as a good man that by this means the grave controversy on this matter could be removed and the peace of the Church, long desired, restored, Martyr at last yielded to him and used the same forms of speech. But soon, warned by the danger of this course, he changed his opinion. He saw that by this method it was not possible to satisfy those who maintain a gross and carnal presence of Christ's body in the Supper, unless their crude expressions were also accepted with their full and crude interpretation. Again, he found that weaker brethren were, by this ambiguity of speech, partly gravely offended and partly so entangled and confused that they scarcely knew what they ought to think on this question. Therefore, granting Bucer his own forms of speech, he himself followed on this doctrine too the same clarity he had kept in other matters, and nevertheless a firm and constant friendship remained between them. For Bucer did not disapprove of Martyr's opinion, and Martyr did not fail to understand Bucer's meaning, however ambiguous his expressions. Thus, although their method of teaching in this matter was different, they had the highest agreement in all the doctrine of religion, and a lasting friendship and union of life. If I wished to explain this and recount all the services by which they showed their mutual love, words would fail me sooner than the things themselves. So, passing these over, I will turn to narrate his private and domestic life. For at Strasbourg he first began to have a house and a household. He lived at first without a wife, in the same dwelling with friends who had followed him from Italy, content with a modest or rather meagre stipend, which was afterwards increased. For when he had left his country, great wealth and the highest honours for the name of Christ, he thought it unsuitable for him to be troublesome to anyone by seeking an increase of his salary, especially since his life was so frugal that what he had not only sufficed for himself but left something over to help his friends. When, however, he disapproved of the celibate life for serious reasons, he betrothed himself, on the advice of friends, to the honourable and noble virgin Catharine Dampmartin, who was living at Metz, loved the true religion, and was summoned to Strasbourg by godly men and afterwards married to Martyr. She died afterwards in England without any offspring, after living eight years with her husband. All who knew her ascribe to her that praise which is due to the best and most excellent matron. For she was above all a fearer of God, a lover of her husband, prudent and diligent in managing the household, generous towards the needy, and one who helped them not only with her means but also with her counsel and every kind of aid; moreover, in all her life she was godly, modest and sober. It is said that the common people at Oxford loved her not only as a kind of benefactress and mother to the poor, but also admired her as if she were endowed with a sacred power, because in sickness, and especially in childbirth, their wives usually obtained sure health through her counsel and help. When she was dead, Cardinal Pole ordered her body to be dug up and thrown onto a dunghill; and since he could not accuse them of any other thing that might seem lawful, he gave as the reason that she had been buried near the body of St Frideswide and had been the wife of a heretic. Indeed this Cardinal, who had once been Martyr's chief friend, after Martyr's departure from Italy had not only withdrawn from his friendship but had also utterly cast off the zeal for true religion which he had pretended for a time, and became a most bitter enemy and persecutor of our people. So, since he could not consume Martyr with flames, as he desired and would have been more glad to see, he raged against the dead body, which had been his wife's. But after England, under the most serene queen Elizabeth, received again the former light of the gospel, the body, dug up again from the dung and muck by order of the bishops, to wipe away this mark of infamy, was solemnly buried in the most honourable place of the church before a large crowd of people. And so that the Papists might not be able to attempt anything similar in future, her bones were mingled with the bones of Frideswide (whom they had formerly worshipped with religious devotion). Therefore, that the body of this most holy woman was shamefully and contemptuously cast out is a notable warning of Roman tyranny, which spares neither the living nor the dead faithful; but that it was restored with the greatest honour to its former grave bears witness to the piety and gratitude of the English towards their teacher, whose wife she had recently been. And since, on the occasion of this matter, we have come to speak of English affairs, and enough, it seems, has been said about what he did and taught at Strasbourg, I will next set out why he went to England and what he accomplished there. King Henry of England having died, his son Edward, on the counsel of his guardians, and especially of Edward Duke of Somerset his uncle, and of Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury and primate of all England, resolved to abolish the papal religion and to reform the churches according to the word of God. And since ministers of the churches, who proclaim the word of God throughout the whole kingdom, come out of the universities, he resolved that these above all should be carefully reformed, so that from them the pure juice of sound doctrine might afterwards flow into every part of the kingdom. Since Peter Martyr, by the judgement of learned men, on account of his singular learning and his incredible skill in many matters, seemed the most suitable of all for this office, he was called by the Archbishop of Canterbury with the king's consent. Therefore, towards the end of November in the year 1547, with the permission of the senate, he left Strasbourg, where he had already taught for five years, for England, accompanied by Bernardino Ochino, who had also been summoned by the same Archbishop. When the Archbishop had kept them with him for some time and had shown them every kindness of humanity, Martyr, by the king's command, was made professor of sacred letters at Oxford. In that university he first expounded the First Epistle of St Paul to the Corinthians, because in it are treated various and manifold heads which bear upon the controversies of our times, so that the teaching of this epistle, if applied fittingly and skilfully, could remedy all the vices by which the purity of the Church has been corrupted, and could convict all the abuses and Papist superstitions. The Papists, who were still at Oxford in great number, at first bore Martyr's teaching with some patience, and some even attended his lectures and openly professed to admire his learning. But others, and especially the heads of the colleges, kept their own men away from his lectures, yet made no further move. But when, after their wishes had already been condemned, he began to treat the words of the Apostle about the Lord's Supper, they thought they could no longer keep quiet. For since their forefathers, having first obscured and then corrupted the doctrine of this dogma, had introduced into the Church by this door of error all superstition and idolatry, they could not bear Martyr, who with remarkable zeal was vindicating the truth of the Eucharist from their errors and corruptions. In order to create for him not only hatred but also serious danger, they first slandered him among the common people with the usual accusations: that he was attacking the doctrine of their forefathers, overthrowing ceremonies that had been most rightly established, profaning the most sacred sacrament of the altar, and all but trampling it underfoot. Then, having arranged everything, without his knowledge they fixed up on all the church doors papers written in English, announcing that a public disputation would take place the next day against the presence of Christ in the holy Supper. So on the following day these men occupied the lecture hall, arranged their forces in suitable places, and ordered them to be ready for shouting and tumult and, if the situation required it, for fighting too. Moreover, there gathered to hear, not only the students from all the colleges, but also a considerable part of the excited populace, partly to watch the outcome, and partly to be present on whichever side some tumult might arise. Meanwhile Martyr, ignorant of all this, was preparing himself at home to give his lecture at the appointed hour as usual. Then his friends, moved by the unusual crowding of the people, came to his house and explained the whole matter to him, urging him to stay at home and not bring any danger upon himself, since the adversaries were so prepared that they seemed rather to want to contend with weapons than with arguments. He replied that he could not fail in his duty and neglect the office entrusted to him by the king; that he had never been the author of any tumult, as the best witnesses of this could testify; that now too he did not wish to give his adversaries an occasion for tumult, but wished to lecture as usual, since there were without doubt many in this gathering who sought the customary lectures and whom he could not neglect. He was already on his way to the lecture hall, accompanied by the most faithful of his friends, when on the road there met him a servant of Smythe, who was playing the leading part in this tragedy, and handed him a letter in which his master challenged him to dispute. Then his friends again urged, begged and exhorted him to return home, recalling the dangers that awaited him. But he persisted in his purpose, went on to the lecture hall, and, restraining the challenging adversaries as far as he could with a modest speech, replied that he did not refuse disputation, but had come there now not to dispute but to lecture. And so, when they allowed him, he gave his lecture as usual, to the great admiration of all. For those who had previously admired his singular learning and eloquence now also beheld in him an incredible constancy and courage. For in such a great uproar of the people and clamour of the adversaries, he finished his lecture without any change of expression or colour, without any hesitation of voice, without any stumbling of tongue, and finally without any trembling of limbs or paleness that could give any impression of fear. When the lecture was over, the adversaries pressed harder, and with loud shouts challenged him to dispute; nor would they accept his most modest excuse, that he said he would dispute but at another time, since now he was not prepared, seeing that they had so carefully concealed the propositions to be disputed, and had not, as usual, published them openly, so that to this day he did not know them. For they said that a man who had lately treated the cause of the Lord's Supper in so many lectures could not be unprepared, whatever questions were proposed on this matter. Then, when they persisted in pressing him, he again replied that first he was unwilling to undertake so great a matter without consulting the royal majesty, especially since the affair seemed to tend towards sedition. Next, for a lawful disputation it was required that definite questions be proposed, judges and moderators be appointed, by whose judgement and arbitration the whole business should be governed, and finally that notaries be provided who would record in good faith and with proper diligence the arguments and speeches of both sides. Since none of these things was now ready and arranged, he said that he neither wished nor was able to dispute, especially since there was not enough time left, the day already drawing towards noon, to examine so great a matter. Afterwards, however, since the adversaries would not be satisfied by these reasons, however most just, and the affair already seemed to be heading towards fighting and conflict, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford intervened (for I may be allowed to keep the usual names) and stopped the fight on these conditions: that Martyr and Smythe, with some companions, should meet in his house and by common counsel settle the propositions to be disputed, the time, order and manner of disputing. He then ordered his attendants, whom they call pedels, to disperse the crowd, and himself went up to the platform, took Martyr by the hand, led him away from the throng of the people, escorted him right to his house, and by his authority restrained the rioters. Martyr, freed from this present danger, so that he should not seem to have refused the disputation because he distrusted his cause, came at the appointed hour to the Vice-Chancellor's house, accompanied by his other friends and especially by Sidall and Curtop, who at that time were outstanding defenders of the truth; but afterwards, in the reign of Mary, they did not keep the same constancy. The adversary did the same, bringing with him Colum Oglethorpe and three other doctors of theology. For a long time they argued among themselves about setting up the disputation, for Martyr said it was fair that they, in refuting him, should keep to the same order which he had kept in teaching; and this at last he obtained. Moreover, he shrank from foreign, barbarous and ambiguous terms, which nevertheless have been received in the schools; and so he used only two, "carnally" and "corporally", since Scripture, in describing the Supper, mentions only the flesh and body, not the thing and substance; yet, lest he should seem to be playing with some ambiguity, he said that he would accept those terms as if it had been said "really" and "substantially". There were also some other disputes between them on other matters, but when at last they agreed about the whole method of disputing, everything that had then been settled was, with the consent of both parties, referred to the counsellors of the royal majesty, so that they might take cognisance of the whole controversy. By them the day of the disputation was fixed for the fourth day before the Nones of May, on which day the royal commissioners were to be present to preside over the disputation. But Smythe, aware of the tumult he had stirred up, did not wait for the appointed day but withdrew by flight, and went first to Scotland and then to Louvain in Brabant. When the day appointed had arrived, the royal commissioners came to Oxford: the reverend Henry, Bishop of Lincoln; Dr Richard Cox, Chancellor of the University of Oxford; Dr Simon Haydes, Dean of Oxford; Master Richard Morrison, esquire; and Dr Christopher Nevinson, doctor of both laws. In their presence Martyr disputed for four days with three theologians of the Papist religion, Doctors Tresham and Cheadle, and Morgan, Master of Arts. How learnedly he refuted them need not be recounted by me, since the acts of this disputation are in everyone's hands. For Martyr, because his adversaries were spreading many false and invented things about this disputation among the common people, was compelled, by their wickedness and also by the entreaties of friends who constantly demanded it, to publish this disputation for the public. The testimony of the royal commissioners, added by them to the book, shows with what good faith and diligence he did this.

units.la: Non multo tempore post hanc disputationem rustici per Denoniam & in Oxoniensi agro tumultum excitarunt, in quo cum multi nominatim Martyri necem minarentur, cum non modo docere sed ne tuto quidem versari in urbe posset, amicorum praefidio incolumis Londinum deductus est, non absq; singulari regis gaudio, qui illum Richemondam venientem ex arce prospiciens lœto animo salutabat eiusq; incolumitati gratulabatur. Vxorem quoq; & familiam, quoniam domi tutò esse non poterant, amici occuluerunt, donec furiosa multitudo seditiosæ plebis, vrbe excederet. Nam à proceribus regni conscriptis duobus exercitibus seditio breui compressa est, præcipuus eius auctoribus capitali supplicio affectus. Ac tum Martyr rursus Oxonium ad solitos legendi & disputandi labores redijt: quo tempore cùm Papistæ se disputando dudum victos nossent, & armis palàm congredi non auderent, noctu sæpè tumultus aliquos ante ædes Martyris commouerunt, ac lapidibus nunc ostium impugnarunt, modò fenestrarum specularia perfregerunt. Quamobrem Regia maiestas, vt eius securitati & quieti consuleret, fecit eum Canonicum collegij Ecclesiæ Christi, & in illud collegium migrare iussit: assignatis illi splendidis ædibus vnà cum amœnissimo horto. Fuit in hoc collegio Decanus, facit enim vestra in me audiendo benignitas, vt hæc quoq; minutiora persequar, ac huius officij ratione et disputationib. præerat, & præterea Doctores Theologiæ publico Academiarū more promouebat. Ipse quoq;, cùm ante Pontificijs priuilegijs doctoris gradu haberet, denuò Oxonij solenniter doctor Theologiæ renuntiatus est. Habuit Martyr Oxonij amicos, vt breuiter dicam: omnes eos qui puram ac veram doctrinam amabant, & ob eruditionem, alicuius nominis erant in illa Academia. Præterea Reuerendi Episcopi Hugo Latimerus, Nicolaus Ridleus, Ioannes Ponetus, Ioannes Hoperus, ex aula etiam generosi ac magnifici viri Antonius Cokus, Ioannes Checus, Richardus Morisinus, atq; alij complures quos nominare non necesse est, Martyrem non tantum diligebat verùmetiam amabant. Inter omnes tamen Reuerendissimus Thomas Cranmerus Cantuariensis Archiepiscopus & Angliæ primas singulari amore Martyrem nostrum coplexus est. Qui cùm ipse doctissimus esset, Martyri tyri tamen tantum tribuit, ut in rebus quibusque gravissimis eius consilio uteretur. Itaq; quotiescunq; vacationem aliquam à publicis docendi laboribus Martyr haberet, eum ad se vocabat, & sua de rebus gravissimis consilia cum illo conferebat: Ac po-steaquàm à rege cura conscribendi leges ecclesiasticas primum XXXII, deinde XVI. viris commissa fuit, effecit ut Martyr in horum numero unus esset: ac tandem etiam cum munus hoc universum uni Cantuariensi à rege fuisset commissum, tribus tantum ad id desumptis sociis, Gualtero Haddono & Rolando Taylero I. C. tertium voluit esse Martyrem. Horū opera adiutus eas leges Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ præscripsit, quæ magnam etiam nunc laudem habent apud omnes pios & doctos. Fruebatur iam universa Anglia pace & tranquillitate, & felix erat religione, & legibus optimè institutis, in tanta quoque totius regni felicitate Martyr non poterat non etiam felix & beatus videri, qui uteretur optimorum virorum, sanctissimorumq; Episcoporum amicitia, verùm omnia hæc subito Mariani regni tempestate mutata & eversa fuerunt. Pura.n.religio è templis est eiecta, sancta Ecclesiæ politia deleta, legesq; illius abrogatæ sunt, optimi quiq; in carceres coniecti. In tanta rerum omnium mutatione Martyri docendi munere interdicitur, & denuntiatur præterea ne iniussu magistratus pedè moveat, neve quid inde rerum suarum asportet, graui denuntiato periculo si id faceret. Paruit ille edicto, verùm cùm moram interponi uideret, de suo statu regni consiliariis perscribit, petit si quid admiserit accusatorem sibi sisti & causam cognosci. Qui cùm nihil in eum statuere possent, discedendi potestatem illi faciunt. Quáobrem rectà Londinum proficiscitur, & illic Cantuariensem in-veniens eum plurimum suo adventu recreauit. Venerat hic tum temporis Londinum, ut quæ adversarii de ipso falsò in vulgus sparserant refelleret. Nam quia summa eius apud omnes erat auctoritas, per cocionatores suos Pontificii apud plebem invulgarunt, Cantuariæ ipsius mandato Missam restitutā esse, ipsum quod pollicitum esse reginae se Missam dicturum in funere regis: simul etiam de futura disputatione quaedam iactabant. Hoc ubi resciuit ille, edito scripto sese purgat: testatur quoque se paratum esse religionis formam ab Edoardo rege institutam publica disputatione defendere. Si, inquit, nobis libertatem det maiestas Reginae, ego cum Petro Martyre, atque aliis quatuor aut quinque quos mihi delegero, fauente Deo, confido nos omnibus approbaturos, non solum preces communes ecclesiasticas, et administrationem sacram, cum caeteris ritibus et ceremoniis: verum doctrinam quoque universam, ac religionis ordinem constitutum a supremo nostro domino rege Edoardo sexto, puriora haec esse, et verbo Dei magis consentanea, quam quicquid mille retro annis in Anglia usurpatum novimus. Tantum ut iudicentur omnia per verbum Dei. Protestationem hanc et consilium suum cum Martyri exposuisset, probavit ille, et ostendit se paratum esse disputationi, neque ullum periculum nomine religionis velle defugere. Verum dum in hac disputationis expectatione sunt, Cantuariensis et Eboracensis Archiepiscopi, Londinensis praeterea et Vuigorniensis Episcopi, in carcerem abducuntur: his enim rationibus adversarij cum illis disputare statuerant. Versabatur tum Martyr in magno periculo cum ob eandem religionem, tum etiam ob familiaritatem et amicitiam horum virorum, neque hoc ipse ignorabat, verum fretus sua innocentia, et quod in leges regni nihil commisisset, non discedendum putavit nisi missione impetrata. Quare causam denuo proponit Consiliarijs regni, ac se non privata voluntate venisse in Angliam demonstrat, sed vocatum a Seren. rege Edoardo, et missum ab amplissimo magistratu reipublicae Argentinensis, ac utriusque diplomata profererebat: cum vero nunc sua opera uti esse non posset, se dimitti postulabat. Quod postquam obtinuit, vix tamen credebant amici, etiam acceptis a regina literis, eum tuto posse discedere. Dicebant enim eius adversarij, tantum Pontificiae religionis hostem non esse e manibus dimittendum, sed vel ex ipsa navi in carcerem et ad supplicium retrahendum esse: monebatur quoq; ut sibi caue-ret ab insidijs, quae si Oceanum traijceret, illi in Flandria & Brabantia paratae essent. Verum Dei beneficio cuncta haec pericula, & certissimas insidias, admiranda ratione euasit. Cum enim peregrinorum alij in Frisiam, nonnulli vero in Dania discederent, nactus est ipse gubernatorem navis hominem pium & metuentem Deum, qui eum in Anglico littore clam domi suae detinuit integris quatuordecim diebus, ac iam omnes tam amici quam inimici eum cum caeteris peregrinis abnauigasse credebant, cum ipse demum ex Anglia soluit, & gubernatore suo Antuerpiam noctu sui causa appellente, ab eo ad amicos est deductus, & ab illis ante lucem currui impositus, per regiones sibi infestissimas incolumis Argentinam peruenit, omnesq; adversariorum insidias, Dei primum beneficio, deinde sua celeritate euitauit.
units.tr: Not long after this disputation, country folk stirred up a tumult in Devon and in the Oxford countryside. Many of them openly threatened Martyr's death, and he could no longer teach, or even live safely in the city. Under the protection of friends he was escorted unharmed to London, not without the singular joy of the king, who, watching from the palace as Martyr came toward Richmond, greeted him with a cheerful heart and congratulated him on his safety. His wife and household, since they could not be safe at home, were hidden by friends until the raging crowd of the seditious commons had left the city. For the rebellion was soon put down by two armies raised by the nobles of the realm, and its chief instigators were punished with death. Then Martyr returned to Oxford to his customary labours of lecturing and disputing. At that time the Papists, who knew they had long been defeated in disputation and did not dare to meet him openly in arms, often stirred up nocturnal riots before Martyr's house, and at times they attacked the door with stones, at other times they smashed the window panes. Therefore the royal majesty, to provide for his safety and peace, made him a canon of the college of Christ Church and ordered him to move into that college, assigning him a handsome house together with a most pleasant garden. In this college he was Dean, and as you kindly allow me to pursue even these smaller matters, he presided over its governance and its disputations, and besides this he promoted Doctors of Theology according to the public custom of the universities. He himself, although he had earlier held the doctorate under the Papal privileges, was again solemnly declared Doctor of Theology at Oxford. In short, Martyr had as friends at Oxford all those who loved pure and true doctrine and who were of any repute for learning in that university. Moreover, the Reverend Bishops Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley, John Ponet and John Hooper, and from the court also the noble and distinguished gentlemen Anthony Cooke, John Cheke, Richard Morison, and many others whom it is not necessary to name, not only esteemed Martyr but also loved him. Yet among them all the most Reverend Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of England, embraced our Martyr with singular affection. Although Cranmer himself was most learned, he so valued Martyr that he used his counsel in all the most weighty matters. Accordingly, whenever Martyr had some respite from his public teaching duties, Cranmer summoned him and conferred with him about his most serious plans. Afterwards, when the king committed the task of drafting the ecclesiastical laws, first to thirty-two men and then to sixteen, he saw to it that Martyr was one of their number. And finally, when this whole task was entrusted by the king to the Archbishop of Canterbury alone, he took only three colleagues for it, Walter Haddon and Roland Taylor, a doctor of civil law, and he wished Martyr to be the third. Aided by their labour, he drew up those laws of the English Church, which even now have great praise among all the godly and learned. All England was now enjoying peace and tranquillity, and was happy in its religion and in laws most well ordered. Amid such general happiness of the realm Martyr could not but seem happy and blessed too, as he enjoyed the friendship of the best men and the most holy bishops. But all these things were suddenly changed and overthrown by the storm of the reign of Mary. Pure religion was cast out of the churches, the holy polity of the Church was destroyed, and its laws were repealed; the best men were thrown into prison. In such a complete upheaval, Martyr was forbidden the office of teaching, and it was proclaimed to him besides that he must not move a foot without the magistrate's leave, nor carry anything of his property from there, under the threat of grave peril if he did so. He obeyed the edict, but when he saw that delay was being interposed, he wrote to the councillors of the realm about his situation, asking that if he had committed any offence, an accuser be brought before him and the case examined. Since they could find nothing to charge him with, they gave him leave to depart. Therefore he set out straight for London, and there finding the Archbishop of Canterbury, he greatly refreshed him by his arrival. The Archbishop had come to London at that time in order to refute what his adversaries had falsely spread about him among the people. For since his authority was very great with everyone, the Papists, through their preachers, had given it out among the common people that by his order the Mass had been restored at Canterbury, and that he himself had promised the queen that he would say Mass at the king's funeral; at the same time they were also making boasts about a future disputation. When he learned of this, he published a written statement clearing himself, and he testified that he was ready to defend by public disputation the form of religion established by King Edward. "If," he said, "Her Majesty the Queen grants us liberty, I, with Peter Martyr and four or five others whom I shall choose, trust, God favouring, that we shall prove to everyone that not only the common ecclesiastical prayers and the sacred administration, with the other rites and ceremonies, but also the whole doctrine and the order of religion established by our sovereign lord King Edward the Sixth are purer and more agreeable to the Word of God than whatever we know to have been practised in England for a thousand years past. Only let all things be judged by the Word of God." After he had explained this protestation and his plan to Martyr, Martyr approved it, and showed that he was ready for the disputation and did not wish to flee any danger on account of religion. But while they were waiting for this disputation, the Archbishops of Canterbury and of York, and also the Bishops of London and of Worcester, were led off to prison; for the adversaries had decided on these grounds to dispute with them. At that time Martyr was in great danger, both on account of the same religion and because of his familiarity and friendship with these men, and he was not unaware of this. Yet, relying on his innocence, and because he had done nothing against the laws of the realm, he thought he should not leave unless he obtained a dismissal. Therefore he again laid his case before the councillors of the realm, and showed that he had come into England not of his own private will but at the summons of the most serene King Edward and sent by the most honourable magistracy of the Republic of Strasbourg; and he produced the documents of both. Since he could no longer be of use to them, he asked to be dismissed. When he had obtained this, his friends could scarcely believe, even after letters had been received from the queen, that he could leave safely. For his adversaries said that a foe of the Papist religion so great must not be let out of their hands, but must be dragged back into prison and to execution even from the ship itself; he was also warned to beware of plots, which, should he cross the ocean, were ready for him in Flanders and Brabant. But by God's benefit he escaped all these dangers and very certain snares in a wonderful manner. For while some of the foreigners were departing for Friesland and some for Denmark, he found a shipmaster, a pious man who feared God, who kept him secretly at his home on the English shore for a full fourteen days. And by now both friends and enemies all believed that he had sailed away with the other foreigners, when at last he set out from England. His shipmaster, at Martyr's request, put in at Antwerp by night, and from there he was conducted by the shipmaster to friends, who placed him in a cart before dawn; and through regions most hostile to him he came safely to Strasbourg, avoiding all the snares of his adversaries, first by God's benefit and then by his own speed.

units.la: Excepere eum Argentinae veteres amici viri optimi atq; doctissimi Sturmius, Sleidanus, Zanchus, Herlinus, Dasypodius, Sapidus, Hubertus & reliqui, magna laetitia. Quo.n. in maiori periculo ipsum versari nouerant, eo salus ipsius, & inopinatus aduetus, maius gaudium illis adferebant. Senatus quoq; cum eius virtutem & doctrinam optime nosset, iussit illi quam primum reddi pristinum locum, quem ante discessum in Anglia habuerat.
units.tr: At Strasbourg his old friends, the excellent and most learned men Sturm, Sleidan, Zanchi, Herlin, Dasypodius, Sapidus, Hubert and the rest, received him with great joy. For the more they had known him to be in danger, the more his safety and unexpected arrival brought them gladness. The Senate too, since it knew his virtue and learning very well, ordered that his former post, which he had held before leaving for England, be restored to him as soon as possible.

units.la: Interea vero nonnulli, qui illi male vellent, de eo sinistros rumores spargebant, quod in doctrina de Coena Domini a sententia Augustanae confessionis discessisset, ideoq; timendum esse, ne aliquas in ecclesia turbas excitaret. Admonitus ergo huius rei ab inimicis, Senatui scripto oblato sese purgat, & docet, confessionem Augustanam & alias quae ab ea non discrepent, si recte atq; commode intelligantur se libenter amplecti, profiteri, ac si opus fuerit velle pro viribus tueri. Promittit deinde per se nullas lites aut contentiones excitatum iri. Imo si locus aliquis pertractandus sit in scripturis, aut quaepiam alia necessitas requisiuerit, ut circa huiusmodi quaestionem suam sententiam explicet, id se facturum cum omni modestia, & citra cuiusquam amaram infestationem. Quæ vero sua sit sententia,ex libellis, inquit àse iam editis facilè posse cognosci, quibus hoc scripto seu promisso nil detractum seu immutatum velit, quoad per scriptu-ras diuinas edoctus aliter esse cognouerit.Et quia præter Augustanam confessionem,à quibusdam proferebatur concordia inita inter D. Bucerum & D. Lutherum eorumque symmistas, re-spondit se huic non subscripsisse, quòd per verbum Dei & coscien-tiam dare nequeat, destitutos vera fide, percipiendo sacramen-ta corpus Christi sumere. Addebat autem non debere hoc illis mirum videri quod assentiri nollet,cùm ipsemet D. Bucerus in Argentinensi schola secus docuerit,dum Acta Apostolorum ex-plicaret. Idemq; cum esset in Anglia( quod ex quibusdam eius articulis ostendi possit) longè aliter scripserit: & quidem rectè. Nam cum fides vnicum sit instrumentum quo à nobis Christus ipse ,corpus & sanguis eius percipiuntur , ea submota os corporis nil nisi sacramentum corporis & sanguinis percipere,pa-nem inquam & vinum instituto domini consecrata. Quemad-modum etiam ætatis adultæ homo si absque fide ad baptismum accesserit, nihil dicitur præter sacramentum, hoc est aquam & ecclesiæ preces , habere. Siquidem nullus dum non credit gra-tiam regenerationis adipiscitur: ita etiam citra fidem neminem ad communionem corporis & sanguinis Christi aditum habere. Vt enim dicit Augustinus,manducare & bibere nihil aliud est quàm credere.Postremò addebat,se vererine concordiæ huic ad se allatæ subscribendo videatur ecclesias Tigurinâ, Bernatem, Basiliensem, Geneuensem, Lausanensem & Anglicanam, om-nesq; per Italiam & Galliam dispersos fratres damnare , quòd sane per verbum Dei & charitate erga eos sibi non liceret.Pro-inde vt Saxonicas ecclesias omnesq; illis consentientes venere-tur & suspiciat, sic & alias quas commemorauerit se amplecti[?] in domino ac vehementer diligere. Non.n.hanc quæstione tan-ti esse, vt inter fideles communionem & charitatem soluere de-beat. Hoc eius seu scripto seu promisso Senatus Argentinensis, qui Martyrem mirificè amabat, contentus fuit, reiectis aliorum clancularijs accusationibus. Restitutus itaq; pristino muneri Iudicum librū interpretatus est. Et quia tum idoneo philosophiae professore schola destituebatur, decretum fuit ut duo Theologi, sicut sacras literas, ita quoq; Aristotelis philosophiam alternis septimanis docerent, itaq; Martyr laborem hunc non defugiens Aristotelis libros de moribus ad Nicomachum interpretari coepit, & in eorum explicatione in tertium usq; librum progressus est. Collega vero eius, is autem erat D. Hieronymus Zanchus, Martyri amicissimus & qui illum ex Italia ut diximus secutus est, libros Aristotelis de natura sibi interpre-tādos desumpsit. At vero adversarij illius & maleuoli, de quibus supra diximus: etsi palam se illi non opponerent, quotidie tamen clàm & quasi per cuniculos eum oppugnare non cessabãt. Nam & per literas, & in lectionibus atq; cōcionibus suis eū ita aperte perstringebant, ut iustae accusationi nihil nisi Martyris nomen deesset. Quin & è studiosis quidam publicè in schola orationem de eucharistia habuit, in hoc compositam, ut Martyrē & doctrinam illius ex professo damnaret. Quare cùm animaduerteret adversarios quotidie apertius bellū contra se gerere, & se nominatim libellis perstringere, ut etiam Sleidanus in sua historia commemorat, de discessu secum deliberare coepit, cū subitò diuinitus occasio opportunissima illi oblata est. Nam cùm apud nos mortuus eo tempore esset vir optimus & sanctissimus Conradus Pellicanus, amplissimus Tigurinae reipublicae Senatus, de voluntate ministrorum ecclesiae illi Petrum Martyrem substituit, & ea de re cum ad ipsum, tum etiam ad amplissimū Senatum Argētinensem[?] literas dedit, quibus ipsum Tigurum mitti postulabat. Fuit haec vocatio Martyri gratissima: quā-vis enim Argent. Rempub. amaret, & ei se multa debere agnosceret, quia tamen controversiam hanc Sacramentariam quotidie maiori animorum acerbitate agitari videbat, gaudebat sibi occasionem datam esse, qua se posset turbis eximere. Itaq; cùm à
units.tr: Meanwhile, some who wished him ill spread malicious rumours about him, claiming that on the doctrine of the Lord's Supper he had departed from the teaching of the Augsburg Confession, and that for this reason it was to be feared he would stir up some disturbance in the Church. Warned of this by his enemies, he cleared himself by presenting a written statement to the Senate. In it he explained that he gladly embraces and professes the Augsburg Confession, and the other confessions that do not disagree with it, provided they are rightly and fairly understood, and that he would, if necessary, be willing to defend them with all his strength. He then promised that he would not himself provoke any quarrels or disputes. Indeed, if some passage of Scripture needed to be treated, or some other necessity arose requiring him to set out his opinion on such a question, he would do so with all modesty and without any bitter attack on anyone. As for what his opinion was, he said, it could easily be learned from the books he had already published; and by this statement or promise he did not wish anything in them to be withdrawn or changed, so long as he was not taught by the divine Scriptures to think otherwise. Again, since some were putting forward the agreement made between Master Bucer and Master Luther and their associates, he replied that he had not subscribed to it, because he could not, in good conscience and according to the Word of God, grant that those who lack true faith receive the body of Christ in receiving the sacraments. He added that it ought not to seem strange to them that he would not assent, since Bucer himself had taught otherwise in the Strasbourg school when he expounded the Acts of the Apostles. And when he was in England (as can be shown from some of his articles) Bucer had written quite differently, and rightly so. For since faith is the one instrument by which Christ himself, his body and blood, are received by us, then, with faith removed, the mouth receives nothing but the sacrament of the body and blood, that is, bread and wine consecrated by the Lord's institution. Just as a grown man who comes to baptism without faith is said to receive nothing but the sacrament, that is, water and the prayers of the Church; for no one obtains the grace of regeneration who does not believe, so likewise no one without faith has access to communion in the body and blood of Christ. For, as Augustine says, to eat and to drink is nothing other than to believe.
