Finally, he added that he feared that by subscribing to this agreement, which had been brought to him, he would appear to condemn the churches of Zurich, Bern, Basel, Geneva, Lausanne and England, and all the brethren scattered through Italy and France; and this, he said, he could not do with a clear conscience before God and in charity towards them. Therefore, just as he revered and esteemed the Saxon churches and all who agreed with them, so too he embraced and most dearly loved the churches he had mentioned, in the Lord. For this question was not so important that it ought to break communion and charity among the faithful. The Senate of Strasbourg, which loved the Martyr greatly, was content with this statement or promise of his, and set aside the secret accusations of others. Restored therefore to his former office, he expounded the Book of Judges. And since at that time the school lacked a suitable professor of philosophy, it was decided that the two theologians should teach Aristotle's philosophy in alternate weeks, just as they taught the sacred letters. Accordingly Martyr, not shrinking from this labour, began to expound Aristotle's books on morals addressed to Nicomachus, and in their explanation he advanced as far as the third book. His colleague, who was Master Jerome Zanchi, a close friend of Martyr and one who had followed him from Italy as we said, took on the books of Aristotle on natural philosophy to expound. But his adversaries and ill-wishers, of whom we spoke above, although they did not openly oppose him, nonetheless never ceased to attack him daily in secret and, as it were, by underground tunnels. For they assailed him so openly in their letters, lectures and sermons that a just accusation lacked nothing but Martyr's name. Indeed, one of the students even delivered a public oration in the school on the Eucharist, composed for the express purpose of condemning Martyr and his teaching. Therefore, when he perceived that his adversaries were waging open war against him every day, and attacking him by name in pamphlets, as Sleidan also records in his history, he began to consider leaving, when suddenly, by God's providence, a most opportune occasion was offered to him. For when Conrad Pellican, an excellent and most holy man, had died among us at that time, the most distinguished Senate of the Zurich commonwealth, with the consent of the ministers of the Church, appointed Peter Martyr in his place, and on this matter wrote letters both to him and to the most distinguished Senate of Strasbourg, asking that he be sent to Zurich. This call was most welcome to Martyr. For although he loved the commonwealth of Strasbourg and acknowledged that he owed it much, yet, seeing that this Sacramentarian controversy was being waged daily with ever greater bitterness of spirits, he rejoiced that an occasion had been given him by which he could free himself from the disturbances.

units.la: Magnifico Illustriq[?] Senatu de sua voluntate rogatus esset, ni-hil dissimulans ostendit missionem sibi fore gratissimam, ac prolixè testatus de suo in Remp. animo: quo minus cum ipsis ma-nere posset, ideò fieri inquit, quòd videat se hoc tempore non posse apud ipsos habere eam quam cupiat docendi, disputandi, & scri-bendi libertatem. Ut autem hanc appetat se primum sua vo-catione urgeri, & minis etiam atq; comminationibus percelli.
units.tr: When he was asked by the Magnificent and Illustrious Senate about his wishes, he concealed nothing, and showed that his dismissal would be most welcome to him; and he testified at length to his good will towards the commonwealth. The reason, he said, why he could not remain with them any longer was that he saw that at this time he could not have among them the freedom to teach, to dispute and to write that he desired. Yet, he said, he was being pressed first by his own calling, and was also terrified by threats and menaces.

units.la: Deinde se vereri iudicia grauissimorum virorum qui sua scri-pta legerint & se docetem audiuerint, si veritatem alias usq; ad capitis periculum defensam, nunc multiplicibus & variis modis clàm & palàm oppugnatam, suo silentio non tantum dese-re sed quasi prodere videatur. Ab his.n.quorum aliqui ob hanc eandem causam vel ignibus cremari voluerunt, vel adhuc su-perstites magna cū utilitate ecclesijs Christi praesunt, se non pos-se nisi graviter coargui, ut vel qui à sententia vera defecerit, quòd inconstantiae crimen in homine Christiano minimè ferendū sit, vel qui tacitus velit praeterire quae ad salutem conducere & necessaria esse non ignoret.
units.tr: Next, he said, he feared the judgement of the most serious men who had read his writings and heard him teach: if he were to appear by his silence not merely to desert, but almost to betray, the truth which he had defended hitherto even to the peril of his life, and which was now being assailed in manifold and various ways, secretly and openly. For by those of whom some, for this very cause, wished even to be burned with fire, and others still living preside over the churches of Christ with great benefit, he could not but be seriously condemned: either as one who had fallen away from the true opinion, since inconstancy is in no way to be tolerated in a Christian man; or as one who would silently pass over things which he well knew to be conducive to salvation and necessary.

units.la: Cum itaq; Deus velit ut suam do-ctrinam vniuersam, & fide amplectamur & profiteamur: se hanc conditionem in qua nunc uersetur non posse salua conscientia re-tinere, nisi sibi quae scripto petierit concedantur: neq; hoc iniquum esse, ut tantum sibi liceat, quantum alij sui ordinis cum in con-cionibus tum in scholis liberum sibi volunt. Proinde cùm munus suum necessariò libertatem in docendo postulet, quam tamen ipsi certis de causis, quas non dubitet grauissimas esse, hoc tempore concedere nolint aut non possint, rogare se ut bona ipsorū venia sibi eò quo vocetur concedere liceat.
units.tr: Therefore, since God wills that we embrace and profess his whole doctrine both in faith, he said, he could not, with a clear conscience, remain in the situation in which he now stood, unless what he had asked for in writing were granted to him. Nor was it unjust, he said, that he should have as much liberty as the others of his order wished for themselves, both in sermons and in schools. Accordingly, since his office necessarily demanded freedom in teaching, which they, for certain reasons that he did not doubt were very weighty, were unwilling or unable to grant at this time, he asked them, with their kind pardon, to allow him to go where he was being called.

units.la: Ostendit praeterea nullam spem conciliationis per colloquium aut aliam viam sibi affulge-re, si quid tamen instituatur, se etiamsi alibi agat non defuturū suo officio.
units.tr: He further showed that no hope of reconciliation through a conference or any other way seemed to shine upon him; but if anything were arranged, he said, he would not fail in his duty even though he might be working elsewhere.

units.la: Senatus qui Martyrem amabat, & eum certis con-ditionibus retinere voluisset, cum videret ipsum in hac senten-tia persistere, sibi verò non integrum esse hoc tempore hanc quàm petebat docendi, disputandi, & scribendi libertatem illi concedere,inuito animo eum dimisit. Discesit itaque Argentina tertio Idus Iulij, anno partæ salutis M. D. LVI. magno cum dolore & gemitu bonorum omnium, quibus gratus, charus & reuerendus fuit, cum ab eximias virtutes, summum ingenium, & doctrinam singularem, tum etiam ob morum facilitatem summāq; concordiam, quàm cum omnibus bonis & doctis perpetuo coluit.
units.tr: The Senate, which loved Martyr and would have wished to keep him on certain conditions, when it saw that he persisted in this opinion, and that it was not in its power at this time to grant him the freedom of teaching, disputing and writing that he sought, let him go with an unwilling mind. And so he left Strasbourg on the third day before the Ides of July, in the year of the saved world 1556, to the great grief and lamentation of all good men, by whom he was welcomed, loved and revered, both for his outstanding virtues, his supreme talent and his singular learning, and also for his easy manners and the highest harmony which he always maintained with all good and learned men.

units.la: Tigurum cùm venisset vnà cum Cl. viro Ioanne Iuello Anglo, qui nunc Dei gratia est Sarisburiensis Episcopus: magna gratulatione exceptus est à Senatu, à schola, ab ecclesiæ mini-stris, deniq; à bonis omnibus.
units.tr: When he had come to Zurich, together with the distinguished Englishman John Jewel, who by God's grace is now Bishop of Salisbury, he was welcomed with great rejoicing by the Senate, by the school, by the ministers of the Church, and finally by all good men.

units.la: Cum autem ad Bullingerum veterem suum amicum diuertisset, donec familia, hoc est Iulius cū vxore sua & filiolo ipsum sequeretur, ita vterque alterum ab eo tempore cōplexus est, vt quamuis antea summa inter eos suis-set coniunctio, ea tamen ex hac familiaritate accessione magna aucta sit, & ita confirmata, vt eam ad obitum usq; absq; ulla uel[?] minima alicuius offensionis suspicione cōseruarint & auxerint.
units.tr: He lodged with Bullinger, his old friend, until his household followed him, that is, Julius with his wife and little son. From that time the two of them embraced each other so closely that, although their earlier bond had already been very strong, it was greatly increased by this closer intimacy and so firmly confirmed that they kept and strengthened it until death, without any suspicion of even the slightest offence.

units.la: Sunt autem hæ amicitiæ firmissimæ, quas virtutum & studio-rum similitudo coniungit: quæ cùm summa fuerit inter ambos, ac talis vt vterq; alterum non modò amaret verumetiam obser-uaret, non mirum est arctissimam quoq; eorum coniunctionem fuisse.
units.tr: Now the friendships that are the firmest are those joined by similarity of virtues and pursuits. Since this similarity was very great between the two of them, and such that each not only loved but also esteemed the other, it is no wonder that their union was also most intimate.

units.la: Quòd verò amarit concionatores & collegas cæteros, atq; fratrum quasi loco habuerit,quod item iuniores filiorum lo-co semper complexus fuerit, cùm omnibus notum sit,non necesse est vt in hac re explicanda tempus teram. Et qui hæc minus perspexerunt,quanta in eo fuerit suauitas in conciliandis sibi ho-minum animis vel hinc coniiciant, quòd eum non tantum colle-gæ in schola & ecclesiarum ministri,ac cæteri qui ipsum quotidie docentem audierunt, amarunt, sed etiam in senatu & in plebe optimus quisq;, cùm neq; docentem audire neq; loquentem intel-ligere possent,sic tamē eum coluerunt, vt vix alium è præcipuis in republica viris:id quod testata est omniū ordinum frequen-tia,quam heri in illius funere vidistis. Declarauit etiam suam in eum voluntatem amplissimus Senatus,quando eum vnanimi consensu honoris ergò ciuitate donauit. Quamuis enim lege la-ta cautum esset ob immensum ciuium numerum, ne quisquam eo anno & proximo in ciuitatem reciperetur, eam tamen in tan-to uiro seruare noluerunt, quòd recte existimarent, non legi sed potius urbi nostrae fieri iniuriam, si talis vir nobiscum quasi pe-regrinus & hospes maneret, & non inter ciues censeretur. Erat eo tempore Martyr quo Tigurum venit adhuc caelebs, sed ta-dem ab amicis persuasus, cum ipse singulari liberorum desiderio teneretur, eoq; magis quod ipse solus ex florente quondam Ver-miliorum familia superstes esset, uxorem altera ducere statuit, sexto anno post primae uxoris mortem. Erat in ecclesia Ita-lica Geneuae virgo Brixiensis honesto genere nata Catharina Merenda, quae illuc religionis nomine venerat, hanc Martyr optimorum virorum & totius Ecclesiae testimonio commenda-tam, uxorem sibi coniunxit. Suscepit ex hac Eliperium filiolū, & altero partu filiam Gerodoram, qui tamen ambo in prima infantia mortui sunt. Eandem reliquit grauidam, quae utinam uolente Dño filium posthumum pariat qui superstes aliquando patrem nobis eruditione & pietate referat. Quantum autem amarit & quanti fecerit hanc Rempublicam & Ecclesiam ex eo colligere potestis, quod cum sciret se uxorem relinquere gra-uidam, testamento cauit ut partus posthumus, si modo vitalis sit, nusquam alibi quàm apud nos educetur. Eandem eius vo-luntatem & amorem ex eo quoq; quod jam commemorabo conij-cere potestis. Altero postquam ad nos venerat anno, Geneuae mortem obijt vir clarissimus Maximilianus Celsus Marti-nenghi Comes, qui Italicae ecclesiae in ea urbe praefuerat. Sunt autem in illa ecclesia multi & praeclari viri, qui deserta Italia Geneuam tanquam in asylum & tutissimum portum piorum ho-minum se contulerunt, atq; inter hos multi sunt Lucenses vi-ri primarij ex ea republica, quorum pleriq; Martyris in Italia discipuli fuerunt, & ipso doctore ad agnitionem Christi perue-nerunt. Quamobrem cum alius in locum Maximiliani demor-tui. tui substituendus esset, summa omnium voluntate & consensu, ardentissimisq; studijs Martyr electus fuit, ac seniores Ecclesiae datis ad ipsum hac de re literis, eum non tantum rogabant verum etiam obtestabantur ut hanc vocationem ratam haberet: idem agebant Angli veteres illius amici, ex quibus multi praeclari viri tum Genevae exulabant religionis nomine: idem quoq; modestè ab eo petebat Ioannes Calvinus, non Genevensis tantum sed universae ecclesiae ornamentum. Dicebant esse in ea urbe & ecclesia optimam Italiae partem, plurimos item ipsius discipulos qui eius adventum expectent, plures etiam in eius adventum ad viam sese parare. Commemorabant electionis pulcherrimam formam, pulcherrimas inquam χειροτονίας[?] toties a Spiritu sancto approbatas, dispositissimas item suffragiorum distributiones, in quibus omnia summo ordine optimoq; consilio facta sint. His addebant tantum esse tamq; ardens totius ecclesiae desiderium, ut hunc ducem, pastorem, praeceptorem adipiscantur, ut nisi votis potiatur dolore eam debilitari quodammodo necesse sit. At Martyr etsi paratissimus erat suae gentis hominibus inservire, nihil tamen suo arbitrio statuendum esse existimavit, sed rem integram ad Senatum nostrum & ecclesiae ministros retulit: & quia illi vocationem hanc ratam non habebant: quod viderent se quidem Martyrem hoc tempore absq; singulari detrimento scholae & ecclesiae non posse dimittere, fratres aut Genevae in ecclesia Italica habere multos & bonos & doctos viros, quos optime in locum sanctissimae memoriae Maximiliani Celsi possint substituere: ipse quoq; huic eorum voluntati & iudicio suam voluntatem libenter accommodavit. Quin etiam cum postea annis aliquot interpositis, veteres amici oblatis amplissimis conditionibus ipsum in Angliam revocarent, & adderent, Reginam modo de eius voluntate certa fiat, paratam esse misso ad id legato ipsum in Angliam evocare, rursus ut ante ecclesiae & reipublicae nostrae moderatorum iudicio acquieuit. Quis hic non amplecteretur eius amorem erga nostram ecclesiam & rempublicam, reuerentiam erga magistratum, constantiam in retinendo semel suscepto munere: quis non videat animum ab ambitione & avari-tia alienissimum: cum alibi docere posset maiore hominum con-cursu, ampliori gloria, stipendio uberiore: his rebus non magis motus esset, quam si nihil omnino ad eum attinerent. Rursus vero quam promptus fuerit ad inserviendum aliis ecclesiis, quam nulla pericula metuerit, satis declarat profectio in Galliam quā anno superiori iussu & voluntate magistratus suscepit: de qua si pauca dixero quasi eandem in me audiendo beneuolentiā re-tinete, neq; enim diutius patientia vestra abutar. Cū ad xiij. Caledas Augusti episcopi ecclesiæ Gallicanæ à rege Poissiacum convenire iussi fuissent, & comitia quoque principum Galliæ in idem tempus fuissent indicta, nostris hominibus in Gallia spes facta est posse aliquod de religione colloquium instituì, è quo ma-gna ad ecclesiam utilitas redundaret. Quamobrem ab ecclesiis delecti sunt certi homines, qui in conventu omnium ordinum li-bertatem religionis promoverent, & doctores quoq; plurimi de-lecti, qui cum adversarijs disputare & conferre possent. Et quia Martyris singularis & excellens eruditio & incomparabilis disputandi facultas illis nota erant, hunc unum ex omnibus pere-grinis nominatim evocandum putarunt. Quamobrem à Chri-stianis ecclesiis, & ab illis principibus qui earum tutelā susceperant Tigurum missus est vir nobilis Cl. Bradella, ac unà cum illo venit etiam vir doctissimus Theodorus Beza, cuius in o-mnibus his actionibus primæ partes fuerunt: quæ-rebant hi quæ-nam Senatus, quæ ministrorum ecclesiæ, quæ ipsius Martyris voluntas esset, si aliquod colloquium institueretur, & ad id ipsè nominatim à Rege evocaretur: & cùm cognoscerent neminem pro sua parte tam sancto instituto defuturum, hic quidem Ge-neuam, alter verò rectà in Galliam redijt. Non ita multis in-terpositis septimanis, Beza ad colloquium evocatus per celeres equos illuc profectus est, & Bradella Tigurum redijt secum afferens literas à Regina matre, Rege Navarreno, & Condæo atq; atq; Admirallio principibus, quibus à Senatu Martyrem sibi mitti postulabant, & simul mittebant tabulas publicae securitatis seu salui conductus, ut nostri viderent nihil periculi subesse. Quare cum res videretur non negligeda, Senatus vocationi assensit, & Martyrem se itineri accingere iussit. Redibat forte eodem tempore in aulam vir clarissimus Matthaeus Cognetius regiae maiestatis apud Heluetios legatus, qui Martyrem in suum[?] comitatum recepit, & salvum Lutetiam Parisiorum deduxit. Inde ad aulam profectus à fratribus humanissimè exceptus est, & salutatis Serenissimo rege Nauarrae & illustrissimis principibus Condaeo & Admirallio ad illustrissimam Reginam Galliae vocatus est, quam postquam consueta reuerentia salutasset, & de suo aduentu verba fecisset, hortatus deinde est eam ad promouendam puram religionem. Docebat n. pia reformatione ecclesiae ipsam non solum regno Galliae consulturam esse, sed toti Europae, quod omnes in regnum Galliae oculos coniecissent. Imminere quidem & offerre se grauia pericula, sed non timendum esse, quod semper Deus adfuerit principibus huic rei studetibus, Asam, Iosaphatum, Ezechiam & Iosiam iuuisse, qui correxerunt populum cum idololatria prorsus corruptus esset. Constantium cum haberet collegas imo superiores Diocletianū & Maximianum, ausum esse Christum amplecti. Constantinū in grauissimis periculis pacem dediisse ecclesiae, qui collegam sortitus erat Licinium Christianis inimicum. Quod si Deus istos iuuit, eum non fore sui dissimilem, verum eundem qui prius fuerit. Addebat reges potissimum in hoc Deo seruire oportere, ut eorum opera pro illius non pro hominum voluntate colatur. Nunc uerò id unum maximè studendum ut religio & sacer cultus ad prima initia reuocetur, & superstitiones inductae remoueantur. Deum quidem potuisse absq; principum opera id facere, & aliquando fecisse, verum ordinaria via ita principes decreuisse illustrare. Quare illos decere non obliuisci se positos non minus prioris quàm posterioris tabulae custodes, ideoq; non licere eis curam diuini cultus prætermittere. Subijciebat præterea eos non esse audiendos qui affirmant ad principes hoc non attinere, cum in Deuteronomio longè aliter statuatur, & Paulus velit magi-stratum esse promotorem bonorum operum, inter quæ diuinus cultus primum locum tenet. Regina se veritatis studiosam es-se testabatur, atq; ideò etiam pro ipso misisse vt consilium daret quomodo possiet [?] miri concordia, ita vt absq; aduersariorum offen-sione pax habeatur, nunc enim tot esse discordias & seditiones in regno causa religionis, vt admodum turbetur. Ad id Mar-tyr libere respondit, etsi nihil boni sibi de aduersariorum volun-tate possit promittere, se tamen non negare benignè ac dulci-ter cum illis agendum esse, modò nihil de veritate imminuatur aut decidatur. Non mirum autem esse discordias aliquas ori-ri, quandoquidem Christus talia euentura prædixerit in Euan-gelij prædicatione, professus, sit se venisse vt gladium non pa-cem immitteret, ac ignem accendisse, neq; aliud velle nisi vt ar-deat. Neq; posse religionem puram ac veram instaurari ac re-tineri citra crucem: ideò illum aiebat oportere forti animo esse, ac syncerè istam prouinciam aggredi, & Deum iuxta sua pro-missa non defuturum, qui leniat mala & patientiam largiatur.
units.tr: That he loved the preachers and his other colleagues, and regarded them as brothers, and that he always embraced the younger men as if they were his sons, is known to everyone, so I need not spend time explaining it. Those who have not observed this closely may gauge from the following how much charm he had in winning people's affection. Not only his colleagues in the school and the ministers of the churches, and the others who heard him teach every day, loved him, but also the best men in the Senate and among the common people. Although they could neither hear him lecture nor understand him when he spoke, they honoured him as much as almost any other leading man in the commonwealth. The crowd of people of every rank who saw him buried yesterday bears witness to this. The most distinguished Senate also declared its goodwill towards him when, by unanimous consent, it granted him citizenship as a mark of honour. For although a law had been passed, because of the huge number of citizens, that no one should be admitted to the city in that year or the next, they were unwilling to keep it in the case of so great a man. They rightly judged that it would be an injury not to the law but rather to our city if such a man remained among us as a stranger and guest and was not counted among the citizens. When Martyr came to Zurich he was still unmarried, but at last, persuaded by his friends, and himself held by a strong longing for children, all the more because he alone survived from the once flourishing Vermigli family, he decided to take a wife, six years after the death of his first wife. In the Italian church at Geneva there was a maiden from Brescia, of honourable birth, Catherine Merenda, who had come there for the sake of religion. Martyr, having been recommended to him by the testimony of excellent men and of the whole Church, joined her to himself in marriage. By her he had a little son, Eliperius, and by a second childbirth a daughter, Gerodora, both of whom died in early infancy. He left her pregnant. May the Lord will that she bear a posthumous son who, surviving, may one day bring back to us his father's learning and piety. How greatly he loved and esteemed this commonwealth and Church you may gather from this: knowing that he was leaving his wife pregnant, he provided in his will that the posthumous child, if indeed it should be born alive, should be brought up nowhere but among us. You may also infer the same goodwill and love from what I am now going to mention. Two years after he had come to us, the most illustrious Maximilian Celsus, Count of Martinengo, who had led the Italian church in Geneva, died there. In that church there are many distinguished men who, having left Italy, betook themselves to Geneva as to a refuge and the safest harbour of godly people. Among them are many leading men from Lucca, most of whom had been Martyr's pupils in Italy and had come to the knowledge of Christ through him as their teacher. Therefore, when someone else had to be appointed in place of the late Maximilian, Martyr was chosen by the highest consent and the most eager wish of all. The elders of the Church wrote to him about this matter and not only asked him but also earnestly entreated him to hold this calling as settled. Likewise his old English friends, of whom many distinguished men were then in exile at Geneva for religion's sake, urged the same. John Calvin, the ornament not only of Geneva but of the whole Church, also asked him modestly for the same thing. They said that in that city and church was the best part of Italy, and many of his pupils who were waiting for his arrival, and more who were already preparing to set out on the road to meet him. They recalled the most beautiful form of election, the most beautiful elections [χειροτονίας], so often approved by the Holy Spirit, and likewise the most orderly distribution of votes, in which everything had been done in the best order and with the wisest counsel. To these things they added that the desire of the whole Church was so great and so ardent to obtain this leader, pastor and teacher, that unless he granted their prayers, the Church would necessarily be weakened by grief. But Martyr, although he was most ready to serve his own people, thought that nothing should be decided at his own discretion. Instead he referred the matter, still undecided, to our Senate and the ministers of the Church. They did not approve the calling, because they saw that at this time they could not let Martyr go without serious loss to the school and the Church, and because they had in Geneva, in the Italian church, many good and learned brothers who could be put in the place of the most holy memory of Maximilian Celsus. He himself also willingly accommodated his own wish to their will and judgment. Moreover, when some years later his old friends, offering the most generous terms, tried to call him back to England, and added that if the Queen would only be assured of his willingness, she was ready to summon him to England by sending a special envoy, he again yielded to the judgment of the rulers of our Church and commonwealth. Who would not embrace his love for our Church and commonwealth, his reverence for the magistrate, and his steadfastness in keeping the office once undertaken? Who would not see a mind most remote from ambition and greed? For he could have taught elsewhere before a larger crowd of people, with greater glory and a richer salary, yet these things moved him no more than if they had nothing at all to do with him. Again, how ready he was to serve other churches, and how little he feared any dangers, is sufficiently shown by his journey into France, which he undertook the previous year by the command and will of the magistrate. If you will keep the same goodwill towards me while I say a few words about it, I shall not abuse your patience for long. When the bishops of the French Church had been ordered by the King to meet at Poissy on the thirteenth of the Kalends of August, and the assembly of the princes of France had been summoned for the same time, our people in France began to hope that some discussion about religion might be arranged, from which great advantage would come to the Church. Therefore certain men were chosen by the churches who should promote liberty of religion in the assembly of all the estates, and also many teachers were chosen who could dispute and confer with the adversaries. And because Martyr's singular and excellent learning and incomparable skill in disputation were known to them, they thought that he alone of all the foreigners should be summoned by name. Therefore the noble Clarus Bradella was sent to Zurich by the Christian churches and by those princes who had taken them under their protection, and together with him came the most learned Theodore Beza, who had the leading role in all these proceedings. They asked what the wishes of the Senate, of the ministers of the Church, and of Martyr himself would be, if a colloquy were arranged and he were summoned by name by the King to take part in it. Since they knew that no one on their side would be lacking in so holy an undertaking, Beza returned at once to Geneva, while Bradella went straight to France. Not many weeks later, Beza, summoned to the colloquy, set out there with swift horses, and Bradella returned to Zurich bringing letters from the Queen Mother, the King of Navarre, and the princes Condé and the Admiral, in which they asked the Senate to send Martyr to them. At the same time they sent safe-conduct documents of public security, so that our people might see that there was no danger. Since the matter seemed not to be neglected, the Senate agreed to the calling and ordered Martyr to prepare for the journey. By chance at that same time the most illustrious Matthew Cognet, envoy of the royal majesty to the Swiss, was returning to the court. He took Martyr into his own company and safely led him to Paris. Going on from there to the court, he was most kindly received by the brothers, and after greeting the most serene King of Navarre and the most illustrious princes Condé and the Admiral, he was summoned to the most illustrious Queen of France. When he had greeted her with the customary reverence and had spoken about his coming, he then exhorted her to promote pure religion. For he taught that by a godly reformation of the Church she would look after not only the kingdom of France but the whole of Europe, since all eyes were turned on the kingdom of France. He admitted that serious dangers were threatening and presenting themselves, but said that they should not be feared, since God had always helped those princes who worked at this task: he had aided Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah, who corrected the people when they had been wholly corrupted by idolatry. He reminded her that Constantius, although he had colleagues, indeed superiors, Diocletian and Maximian, dared to embrace Christ. He said that Constantine, in the gravest dangers, gave peace to the Church, though his colleague by lot was Licinius, an enemy of the Christians. If God helped those men, He would not be unlike Himself but the same as before. He added that kings above all ought to serve God in this, so that God might be worshipped by their work according to His will and not according to the will of men. Now, he said, the one thing to be pursued most eagerly was that religion and the sacred worship should be recalled to their first beginnings, and that the superstitions introduced should be removed. God could indeed have done this without the work of princes, and at times He had done so, but by the ordinary way He had decided that princes should bring it to light. Therefore it became them not to forget that they were set up as guardians of the first table of the law no less than of the second, and so it was not lawful for them to neglect the care of divine worship. He further added that those should not be listened to who affirm that this does not concern princes, since Deuteronomy lays down quite the opposite, and Paul wishes the magistrate to be the promoter of good works, among which divine worship holds the first place. The Queen testified that she was a lover of truth, and that for this reason she had also sent for him, so that he might give counsel how concord could be restored, so that peace might be kept without offence to the adversaries, since there were now so many discords and seditions in the kingdom over religion that it was greatly disturbed. To this Martyr answered freely that although he could promise nothing good from the goodwill of the adversaries, he did not deny that they should be dealt with kindly and gently, provided nothing was diminished or given up from the truth. It is no wonder, he said, that some discords arise, since Christ foretold such things would happen in the preaching of the Gospel, declaring that He had come to send not peace but a sword, and had kindled fire, and wished nothing else than that it should burn. Nor, he said, could pure and true religion be restored and maintained without the cross. Therefore, he said, it was necessary to be of brave spirit and to undertake this task sincerely, and God, according to His promises, would not fail, who would soften evils and grant patience.

units.la: Præterea aliquoties interrogatus à Regina quodnam consilium haberet de rerum compositione, respondit, sibi non aliud occur-rere nisi vt liberè sineret Euangelicos ad sacros cœtus conueni-re, dando eis templa in quibus haberentur sacræ conciones. Nā si hoc efficeret, veritatem sese vltrò patefacturam, nec opus fo-re colloquijs aut disputationibus. Postremò cū rogaretur quid de Augustana confessione iudicaret, respondit, sibi videri nobis debere sufficere verbum Dei, quòd ibi omnia luculenter conti-neantur quæ ad salutem faciant. Neq.n. si ea confessio recipia-tur conciliationem secuturam cum Romanensibus, cum illam ut hæreticam proscripserint. In eandem sententiam Regi Nauar-reno & alijs magnis in aula viris respondit, qui eisdem re rebus ipsius sententiam quærebant. Secuta deinde est actio publica, ad quam Cardinales & Episcopi Martyrem non admittendum esse censebant. Regina tamen eum venire voluit. Habuit in hac actione orationem Cardinalis Lotharingus, quam etiam postea in publicum edidit, in hac multa de sua ecclesia dixit, ut quae haberet successionem continuatam, manuum impositionem & coleret Christum sine idololatria. Negavit Dei ecclesiam tantum modo ex electis constare, quod alioqui esset futura invisibilis, & homines de illa semper fore incertos. Praeterea subiecit concilia errare non posse, neq; doctrina, neq; moribus, sed multa immutare pro temporum varietate. Et ecclesiam ipsam affirmavit ante scripturas esse, atq; illarum interpretationem ab ecclesia petendam. Diuertit posthac ad rem sacramentariam, & de transubstantiatione atq; Missa nihil dixit, affirmavit autem corpus Christi praesens adesse, non quidem localiter nec circumscriptiue, sed caelesti modo & ut loquebatur, supersubstantialiter. Cū[?] peroraret, convertit se ad Reginam matrem & Regem, eosq; genibus flexis orauit ut in ea fide permanerent in qua nati & baptizati essent, atq; simul obtulit cum suis Episcopis omnia officia, obsequia, & obedientia. Interposito deinde aliquot diebus Be-zapro sua singulari eruditione Cardinalis Lotharingi orationē publicè graviter confutauit, Cardinalis verò se illi opposuit atq; petijt ut nostri aut confessioni Augustanae subscribant, aut breuem propositionem de Caena Domini à se allatam recipiant, nisi enim hac in re convenirent, se nolle ulterius agere & colloqui: quaerebat enim studiosè causas abrumpendi colloquij. Siluit in hac actione Martyr, quòd omnia Gallicè agerentur: verùm cùm denuò convenissent, admonitus à fratribus, permisso quoq; Reginae etiam ipse Italicâ lingua multis contra Lotharingum egit. Qui tamen congressum detrectare videbatur, & causabatur Martyrem Italicè locutum esse, quasi nō intellexisset, dicebatq; se malle agere cū homine suae linguae, attamen ad quaedam ab eo allata conatus est respondere. Quin & quidam Hispanus magister ordinis Iesuitarum, Italicè orationem contra nostros habuit, cui paucis Beza respondit. Martyr vero rursus de Coena ad-uersus Cardinalem disserere coepit, sed quia nox imminebat & praeterea actio turbulenta erat, ita vt nec ipse Cardinalis cla-moribus abstineret, eo die nihil ulterius actum est. Postea quam vero aduersarij frustra reluctantibus nostris, obtinuerunt, vt colloquium inciperetur ab articulo de Coena Domini, electi sunt ab vtraq; parte quinq; collocutores, aduersariorum quidem Va-lentinus & Sagensis Episcopi, Botillerus, Saligniacus, & De-pensius doctores: ex nostris autem Beza, Marloratus, Spina, Dominus de Sola & noster Martyr. Egerunt hi soli absq; ul-lis iudicibus, adhibitis tantum duobus notarijs: ac primum di-ligenter petebant, vt aliqua formula proponeretur, qua de praesentia corporis Christi in Eucharistia inter partes posset conue-niri, cumq; multa vltro citroq; fuissent allata, Martyr quoq; interrogatus breue chirographum suae sententiae proposuit, quae ta-men episcopis non satisfecit, quod nimis ieiunam esse dicerent, nostrarum vero partium collocutores Martyri adhaeserunt. Di-sceptatum deinde est inter eos de hac quaestione per aliquot dies, & tandem noua formula conscripta est, in qua posset vtraque pars conuenire de praesentia corporis Christi in Coena, atq; huic vtriusq; partis collocutores assenserunt & subscripserunt. Martyr vero cum videret ibi quaedam esse ambigua, testatus primum se non recedere a sensu prioris chirographi quod illis tradidisset, ipse vna cum Beza & reliquis nostrarum partium collocutoribus, posteriori formulae breuem declarationem adiecit, vt remota ambiguitate aduersarij viderent quis nostrorum sensus esset. Cardinales vero & Episcopi postea quam illis relatum est collocutores de hoc articulo convenisse, improbarunt ea quae a suis collocutoribus gesta erant, imo ipsos haereseos insimularunt, itaq; eorum opera colloquium ad aliquot dies suspensum est: iam enim cum sua voluntate, tum etiam instigatione legati Pontifi-cij decreuerant colloquium abrumpere. Interea vero Episcopi canones aliquot conscripserunt, & tandem 19. Octobris Cardinales Guisiaci & complures quoq; Episcopi ex aula discesserunt: è nostris etiam collocutoribus, cū nulla aut exigua spes esset colloquij restaurandi, plerique ad suas ecclesias redierunt. Edebantur interea decreta quibus nostri iussi sunt templa reddere, illis tamen libera facultas prædicandi concessa esset, & loca assignata in quibus conuenirent, certo tamen numero præscripto. Arma deinde utriq; parti ablata sunt, & edictum ne quis alteri religionis nomine conuitietur. Quamobrem cum Martyr videret se hic nihil amplius agere posse, præsertim cum Gallicæ linguæ exiguum usum haberet, missionem petere statuit, eoq; nomine Condensem[?] principem accessit, & ab ipso deinde ad Reginam ductus esset, apud quam verba faciens, primum inquit nos oportere Deo reddere, quæ sunt Dei & principibus quæ sunt eorum, his de causis se huc venisse, ut quoad Deum, religionem promoueret: deinde ut obsequeretur Regiæ eius Maiestati: quòd tamen eo libentius fecerit, quòd insignita sit præclarissimis virtutibus de quibus omnes honorificè loquantur, præterea quod regnum sit præstantissimum, & sibi ac illi sit communis patria: & maxime omnium ut magistratui Tigurino pareret, qui optimè animatus sit aduersus Regem & Reginam. Id aut non esse contemnendum, cum sit inter Heluetios non parua authoritatis & potentiæ. Deinde adijciebat se in negotio colloquij nihil intermisisse quod putaret ad re facere, egisse placidè ut iusserit. Quòd autem res non sit ulterius producta, per se non stetisse, non tamen defuturum fructum suo tempore, quamuis iam non habeatur. Nunc autem quando nihil agatur se petere missionem, quòd sit senex, iam autem instet hyems, quo tempore iter sit futurum incommodum ob pluuias, niues, & dies contractiores. Præterea quod audijsset se delatum eius maiestati, quasi huc venerit peregrinus, nec aliud spectarit quàm seditiones in regno excitare, quod his malis gauderet, rogabat ne facilè talia de se crederet, eò quòd sit homo ab ijs flagitijs prorsus alienus. Fuisse enim se Argentinæ, deinde in Anglia, ac rursus Argentinæ & denique in Helvetia, inde illam posse instrui, si fides sibi non haberetur, se semper quaesiuisse pacem & concordiam quantum per verbum Dei fieri posset. Ostendebat praeterea nihil fuisse quod eum ad hoc faciendum posset invitare: nam quoad regnum se illi a maioribus suis vehementer fuisse addictum: quoad Reginam multo minus, cum sit ex sua patria & tanquam lumen & splendor eius, unde se erga illam sic esse affectum, ut vitam pro eius dignitate ac salute libenter positurus sit, si res id exigat. Et inter cetera quae desideret inter prima esse, ut salua sit cum filijs eius & regno Galliae. Id cum ita sit, petebat ut se non in mala sed in bona gratia dimitteret. Ad haec Regina benigne & clementer illi respondit, gratias illi egit quod venisset, & missionem tutam ac securam promisit, idq; intra biduum. Rogabat praeterea si rursus opera eius peteretur ob hanc eandem causam, ne detrectaret subire iter denuo. Se quidem non ignorare magnum esse laborem, sed reputare illum & utilem & necessarium. Quoad aliorum criminationes, se quidem multa audire inquit, variis de rebus, sed reseruare semper sibi iudicium: ac testabatur se omnino bene de ipso existimare. Martyr adhaec illi ut par erat gratias agens, simul quoque pro afflictis ecclesiis rogabat, excusans quod contra regis voluntatem templa occupassent: nam cum audivissent regem velle ea restitui illi paruisse: addebat etiam si quid interdum committatur a rudibus & infirmioribus, id doctrinae non imputandum esse. Postquam a Regina dimissus fuisset, Regina quoq; Navarra atq; Rex humanissimè illi valedixerunt, idem fecerunt Condæus princeps atq; Admirallius: praeterea Regina mater & omnes iam nominati principes literis ad Senatum Tigurinum datis, illi quod Martyrem ad colloquium misisset, prout petiissent ab eo, gratias egerunt, & simul Martyrem meritis laudibus ornarunt. Adiunxerunt quoq; Condæus & Admirallius Martyri discedenti duos ex suis familijs nobiles & militares homines, qui eum incolumem Tigurum reduxerunt. Possem hoc loco Auditores recitare literas principum & doctorum quibus amplissimas laudes religionis, doctrina, fidei, & industriae in illum congesserunt, sed me & temporis & instituti mei ratio his immorari non patitur. Itaq; quoniam hactenus exposui quibus in locis docendo atq; disputando ecclesia Dei inseruierit, deinceps exponam quantum eidem scriptis suis contulerit. Primùm itaq; posteaquam Italiam deseruit, edidit patria lingua expositionem Symboli Apostolici, vt omnibus fidei sua rationem redderet. Deinde cum in Angliam venisset, & in explicatione vndecimi capitis prioris Epistolae ad Corinthios, multa disseruisset de Caena Domini, tandem sub finem capitis quaestionem hanc ex professo tractauit. Atq; primum refutauit eam coniunctionem qua panis & vinum vulgò dicuntur transsubstantiari in corpus & sanguinem Christi, quae videtur summa copulatio cum rebus sacramenti. Deinde excusssit aliorum sententiam quae statuit panem & vinum quoad suas integras & veras naturas in sacramento retineri, & ita retineri ut sibi adiunctum (vt loquuntur) naturaliter, corporaliter & realiter, verum corpus Christi & sanguinem habeant. Tertio loco eorum sententiam expendit qui dicunt ista minimè inter se coniungi alia ratione quàm sacramentali, id est per significationem & repraesentationem. Postremò indicauit quomodo ex opinionibus pertinentibus ad secundam & tertiam sententiam elicia-tur quod magis videatur ad pietatem facere in hoc sacramentali negotio. Tractationem hanc vna cum disputatione, quam eum publicè hac de controversia habuisse supra ostendimus, in Anglia primùm in lucem edidit. Eodemq; tempore commentaria in primam Pauli epistolam ad Corinthios, Tiguri apud nos excudi voluit, opus certè ob multarum abstrusarum & difficilium quaestionum perspicuam explicationem lectu dignissimum. Postquam verò ex Anglia Argentoratum redijt, & postea Tigurum vocatus est, nactus apud nos non tantum aliquid otij, sed etiam adeptus eam quam expetebat scribendi libertatem, multa quae ante vel conscripserat vel inchoauerat, recognouit, absoluit, & in publicum edidit. Ac primùm commentaria in epi-stolam D. Pauli ad Romanos, quam antea Oxonij publicè interpretatus fuerat, de quo libro hoc tantùm dicam, cum magna eruditione & diligentia hoc consecutum esse, ut omnes fateantur post tot doctissimos interpretes, veteres & recentiores qui in hac epistolam scripserunt, nihilominus librum hunc cum magno & peculiari fructu legi posse. Eodem tempore ab ipso edita est Defensio doctrinae veteris & Apostolicae de sacrosancto Eucharistiae sacramento aduersus Stephani Gardineri librum. Nam ille ante annos complures librum virulentum & pestiferum de Eucharistia sub nomine M. Antonij Costantij ediderat, in quo meris sophismatis & contortissimis fallacijs conatus est labefactare veram & orthodoxam doctrinam, quam à Christo & Apostolis atq; antiquissimis ecclesiae patribus acceptam hodie sequimur & profitemur. Atq; ad hunc librum conscribendum complurimi Papistarum suas operas contulerunt, & Gardinero omnia sua argumenta tradiderut, ut ille ex aceruo deligeret quicquid vellet: & de hoc libro triumphabant, & gloriabantur neminem esse qui cum hoc suo Goliatho auderet congredi. Quibus rebus commotus doctissimus iuxta ac sanctissimus vir D. Thomas Cranmerus Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, qui antea saepe cum Vintoniensi congressus, cum victoria & summa cum laude discesserat, hanc prouinciam in se suscepit. Verùm cùm in carcere arctissima custodia obseruaretur, & non modò librorum copia, sed ne charta quidem illi ad scribendum suppeteret, & postremò morte saeuissima quam in veræ fidei confessione constanter tulit sublatus esset, opus quod iam habebat præ manibus, conatus est inchoatum relinquere. Quamobrem multi ex Anglis pij & veræ religionis amantes viri, Martyrem saepè coram & per literas hortati sunt, ut illi in hac prouincia succederet, neq; pateretur contagione venenati huius libri simpliciorum animos infici, & Pontificios adeò impudenter & arroganter nostris insultare. Itaq; amicorum precibus & rei ipsius æquitate incitatus, tus, opus hoc aggressus est, & superatis variis ac multiplicibus impedimentis Tiguri absoluit, & typographis excudendum comisit. Defendit aut primum in hoc libro rationes nostrorum homi-num undecunq; a Gardinero collectas & confutatas. Deinde etiam regulas, quas ipse in sua Tractatione de Eucharistia ediderat, contra eiusdem calumnias tuetur. Tertio eas responsiones propugnat, quibus aduersariorum argumenta in hac disputatione dilui solent. Postremo asserit iustas verasq; interpretationes certorum locorum, quos ex Patribus Gardinerus cum suis pro se attulit. In uniuerso aut opere quicquid de tota Eucharistiae causa cum in sacris literis, tum in antiquorum Patrum Conciliorumq; monumentis proditum est, tam copiose & diligenter complexus est, & singula tam accurate & subtiliter excussit, ut hoc opus etiam non mediocriter doctis admirationi sit. Secuta deinde est hanc contra Gardinerum defensionem, alia Defensio contra Richardi Smythaei Angli, olim Theologiae professoris Oxoniensis, libros duos de Caelibatu sacerdotum, & votis monasticis. Nam cum Martyr Oxonij priorem epistolam ad Corinthios interpretaretur, & in 7. cap. ubi Apostolus de virginitate atq; matrimonio permulta scribit, de uotis quoq; copiose disputasset, Smythaeus cui ipse iussu regis ad profitendas sacras literas surrogatus fuerat, aderat assidue, & ea quae a Martyre dicebantur non tantum attente audiebat, sed etiam diligenter literis consignabat, ac deinde Louanium profectus, duos ineptos attamen venenatos libellos, de Caelibatu sacerdotum & votis monasticis, contra Martyrem edidit. Huic in commentarijs epistolae ad Corinth. Martyr non potuit respondere, nam urgentibus amicis & flagitantibus, eius libri editionem differre nō licebat, attamen responsionem hanc in septimi capitis fine pollicitus est, ac breui post otium nactus illi respondit: sed certis de causis graui-bus & magni momenti, demum post aliquot annos, cum Tiguri esset, hanc responsionem in publicum edidit. Refutat autem non tantum Smythaei rationes, sed omnia fere quae in hac causa dici possunt, diligenter & accuratè excusit, quod te-stari poterunt omnes qui hunc librū nō obiter evoluerint. Prae-terea Argentinæ postquam eò ex Anglia reversus fuisset, Judi-cum librum interpretatus est, & commentaria in eundem apud nos, ut nostis, edidit, in quibus quaestiones Theologicas nō ubiq; obvias quàm plurimas explicavit, & librū vere aureum, quem tamen multi propter difficultatem & obscuritatem singularem refugiebant, allato interpretationis lumine plurimum illustra-vit. Postremum cùm Joannes Brentius libellum edidisset de Personali unione duarum naturarum in Christo, in quo ille ad asserendam carnalem & corporalem atq; realem præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in sacra Cæna, novā & portentosam doctrinam de Ubiquitate corporis Christi defendendam suscepit, Martyr rogatus ab amicis dialogo edito libellum eius confutavit. Et quia agnoscebat Brentium aliis scriptis non omninò male de Ecclesia meritum esse, nomen eius apponere & eum nominatim infamare & traducere noluit, præsertim cum hoc nihil ad causam faceret, sed argumenta eius ne imperitis fucum facerent, copiosè diluit: deinde id quod caput causæ erat, Christi humanitatem non esse ubiq;, firmissimis sacræ scripturæ & vetustissimorum Patrum testimonis cōprobavit. Excitatus hoc scripto Brentius, edito libro vehementi & aculeato, Martyrem simul & Bullingerum uno impetu prosternere conatus est. Quem librum cum vidisset Martyr noster, homo alioqui naturā placidissimæ nonnihil tamen indignabatur, Brentium causam non bonam fide etiam adeò non bona agere, ut non dubitet & se & nostros omnes accusare quod impugnent gloriam & maiestatem Christi, negent Dei omnipotentiam, cùm tamen omnibus notum sit, ita ut ne Brentius quidem ignorare possit, his contraria nostros docere. Dolebat illi plurimum hominem alioqui magnum, & qui Ecclesiae posset esse utilis, tam pertinaciter tueri dogma, absurdum portentosum & plane novum, quod nullis evidentibus scripturarum testimonis, nulla Patrum ac veteris Ecclesiæ auctoritate nitatur, & quod neq; Papistæ, qui multa confinxerunt ad tuendam carnalem crassamq; præsentiam corporis Christi in Cœna sacra, vnquam aut fuerunt approbare. Nam, vti referebat, cùm in Galliam, quando colloquium habebatur, Brentiani quidam libelli allati fuissent, præcipui Pontificiorum Theologorum apertè dixêre, hoc Brentij dogma novum & inauditum & plane hæreticum esse. Quamobrem sese iam accinxerat vt criminationibus Brentianis, quæ multa & graues erant, atq; argumentis eius non ita multis, diligenter & accuratè respondere: verùm prob dolor inopinata morbi vi no-bis ereptus, quod statuerat, efficere non potuit. Quitamen casus vtcunq; ferri posset, quod & Bullingerus nostræ ecclesiæ pastor, qui cum illo respondendi laborem partitus fuerat, suo studio & labore, & præstanti præterea doctrina vtriusq; laborem fortiter sustinebit, & solus satis erit ad vtrunq; defendendum: & præterea argumenta Martyris, quæ ille plurima in suo dialogo protulit, stant adhuc firma, & hac impressione Brentiana non labefactari, nedum prosterni potuerunt. Illud potius dolendum est, non potuisse Martyrem absoluere alia & præstantiora opera, quæ magnam vtilitatem vniuersæ Ecclesiæ poterant afferre. Iam enim ab annis aliquot interpretatus est, vt nostis, duos Samuelis libros, & nunc Regum primo libro absoluto in secundo versabatur, atq; ea quidem quæ legit, etsi non omnia ab ipso recognita sunt, talia tamen sunt, vt cùm edita fuerint, quod breui futurum erit, volente Domino, vix quisquam extremam eius manum in his desiderare posset: ea autem quæ in secundo Regum libro desunt quis perficiet? quis hanc quasi Venerem Apelles manu inchoatam absoluet? Quis commentaria in Genesim, in Exodum, in Leuiticum, in Prophetas minores, in Ieremiæ lamentationes, ita recognoscet vt eam dignitatem, eum splendorem habeant ac si ab ipso emendata, recognita, & edita fuissent? Quid dicam de grauissimis maximarum rerum disputationibus, quid de commentarijs Aristoteleis, & aliis quæ ille inchoata & imperfecta reliquit. Antequam enim hæc non dico recognoscere posset, verumetiam pene antequam mandare posset quid de his vellet fieri, grauis & inopinati mor-bi vi oppressus & nobis ereptus est. Nam cum huius mensis quinta die ægrotare cæpisset, duodecima eiusdem ex hac vita migrauit. Fuit iã ante valetudine tenui & infirma cum ob affectam iam ætatem, tum quòd curæ & sollicitudines variæ & præsertim magni dolores quos ex afflicto statu Ecclesiæ Gallicæ accipiebat, vires eius sensim consumerent: quare cum eum inuasisset morbus epidemicus, quem multi vestrum experti sunt, facile naturam ante exhaustam superauit. Nos tamen quia hactenus morbus hic nemini lethalis fuerat, de Martyre quoque primis diebus nihil metuebamus. Spem etiam nostram ipse confirmauit, nam tertio & quarto die postquam eum morbus invaserat, rursus ad sua studia redijt, & statuit postera die, cum eius vices essent, publicè docere, quamuis ego repugnarem eumque monerem ut valetudini parceret, me enim eius vicè lecturum, neque dubitare auditores habita ratione valetudinis illius hoc facilè passuros: ille tamen contra sese satis firmum existimabat, & nisi quid aliud accideret, postridie docere velle inquit. Verùm ea ipsa nocte febris redijt, eumq; grauius quàm ante inuasit, catharri quoq; interea augebantur, & simul tussis illi permolesta erat, itaq; quamuis amici iuberent eum bene sperare de valetudine, & medici etiam aliquam spem facerent, ipse tamen mortem instare præsagiebat, ac hac de causa testamentum pridiè antequam obiret condidit, & vocato vicino suo viro ornatissimo D. Bernhardo Sprünglio quæstore, quem vxori grauidæ tutorem dederat, me id in eius præsentia recitare voluit, & ab eo petijt, ut operam daret quo Senatus illud sua auctoritate confirmaret. Nocte deinceps quæ eum diem consequuta est, satis bene quieuit, & morbus aliquantulum remisisse nobis videbatur, sed reuera uis naturæ a morbo superata illi non amplius reluctabatur. Interea verò quotidie amici eum inuiinuisebant, cum quibus ille antequam difficultas spirandi impediret, non minus iucunde variis de rebus colloquebatur, quam si nullo plane morbo infestaretur. Nam & de morbi vi & natura ex medicorum arte, in qua non indiligenter versatus fuerat, cum ipsis medicis qui amicitiae & officij causa quotidie illum inuisebant, differebat. Et quia plerisq; noctibus non insuauiter dormierat, beneficium hoc Dei amicis praedicabat, & ex Physicorum praeceptis commemorabat somni naturam, & efficaciam in toto corpore suauiter quasi irrigando. Saepe etiam de tussi quaerebatur, quae totum corpus, maximè tamen caput & pectus laederet, ac aliquoties testabatur, se quoad corpus quidem male habere, optimè autem quoad animum. Atque tum si coepisset uel fidei suae rationem exponere, uel commemorare quibusnam consolationibus animum suum erigeret, plane in hac re diuinus erat.
units.tr: <i>Moreover, when the Queen asked him several times what plan he had for settling the religious troubles, he replied that he could see no course other than to let the Evangelicals assemble freely for sacred meetings, giving them churches in which sacred sermons could be held. For if she did this, the truth would reveal itself of its own accord, and there would be no need for conferences or disputations. Finally, when he was asked what he thought of the Augsburg Confession, he replied that the Word of God ought to suffice for us, since everything that pertains to salvation is clearly set out there. For if that confession were accepted, there would be no reconciliation with the Romanists, since they had condemned it as heretical. He gave the same answer to the King of Navarre and to other great men at court, who were asking for his opinion on these same matters. Then a public session followed, to which the Cardinals and Bishops thought Martyr should not be admitted. The Queen, however, wished him to come. In this session the Cardinal of Lorraine gave an oration, which he afterwards published. In it he said much about his church, claiming that it had an unbroken succession, the laying on of hands, and that it worshipped Christ without idolatry. He denied that the Church of God consisted only of the elect, since otherwise it would be invisible and men would always be uncertain about it. He further added that councils could not err, either in doctrine or in morals, though they might change many things according to the variety of times. He affirmed that the Church itself existed before the Scriptures, and that their interpretation must be sought from the Church. He then turned to the matter of the sacrament, and said nothing about transubstantiation or the Mass, but affirmed that the body of Christ is present, not indeed locally or circumscriptively, but in a heavenly manner, and, as he put it, supersubstantially. When he had finished his speech, he turned to the Queen Mother and the King, and kneeling, begged them to persist in that faith in which they had been born and baptised, and at the same time he offered, with his Bishops, every service, duty and obedience. Some days later Beza, with his singular learning, publicly and gravely refuted the Cardinal of Lorraine's oration. The Cardinal, however, opposed him and asked that our men either subscribe to the Augsburg Confession, or accept a short proposition about the Lord's Supper that he had brought forward; for unless they agreed on this point, he would not be willing to act or confer any further. He was eagerly seeking reasons for breaking off the conference. Martyr kept silent in this session, because everything was conducted in French. But when they met again, urged by the brethren, and with the Queen's permission, he himself also spoke against Lorraine in the Italian language at length. Lorraine, however, seemed to refuse to engage with him, and complained that Martyr had spoken in Italian, as if he had not understood it; he said he preferred to deal with a man of his own language, yet he tried to answer some of the points Martyr had raised. Moreover, a certain Spanish master of the Jesuit order gave an oration against our men in Italian, and Beza answered him briefly. Martyr then began again to discuss the Lord's Supper against the Cardinal, but since night was coming on, and the session was disorderly, so that not even the Cardinal himself refrained from shouting, nothing further was done that day. Afterwards, when our men had struggled in vain, the opponents prevailed, and it was agreed that the conference should begin with the article on the Lord's Supper. Five speakers were chosen by each side: on the opponents' side the Bishops of Valence and Sées, and the doctors Boutillier, Saligniac and Despensse; on ours Beza, Marlorat, Spina, the Lord of La Sole, and our Martyr. These alone conducted the discussion, without any judges, with only two notaries present. First, they earnestly asked that some formula be put forward on which the parties could agree concerning the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist. When many things had been offered on both sides, Martyr too, being asked, put forward a short written statement of his opinion. This did not satisfy the Bishops, who said it was far too meagre; but the speakers on our side joined with Martyr. Then the question was debated among them for some days, and at last a new formula was drawn up, in which both parties could agree about the presence of Christ's body in the Supper; and the speakers on each side assented to it and subscribed it. But Martyr, seeing that some things in it were ambiguous, first declared that he did not depart from the sense of the earlier statement he had handed to them; and he himself, together with Beza and the other speakers on our side, added a short explanation to the later formula, so that, with the ambiguity removed, the opponents could see what our men's meaning was. However, when the Cardinals and Bishops were told that the speakers had agreed on this article, they disapproved of what their own speakers had done, and even accused them of heresy; and through their efforts the conference was suspended for some days, for the Papal legate had already resolved, both by his own will and by urging, to break off the conference. Meanwhile the Bishops drew up several canons, and at last, on 19 October, the Cardinals of Guise and several Bishops also left the court. Of our speakers too, since there was little or no hope of restoring the conference, most returned to their own churches. Meanwhile decrees were issued ordering our men to give back the churches, though they were granted the free right to preach, and places were assigned where they might assemble, but with a fixed number prescribed. Then arms were taken from both sides, and an edict was issued that no one should revile another in the name of religion. Therefore, since Martyr saw that he could accomplish nothing more here, especially as he had little use of the French language, he decided to ask for his dismissal, and for this purpose he approached the Prince of Condé, and was then led by him to the Queen. Speaking before her, he first said that we ought to render to God the things that are God's and to princes the things that are theirs; for these reasons he had come here, so that, as far as God was concerned, he might advance religion, and then that he might obey Her Royal Majesty; and he did this the more willingly because she was distinguished by the most outstanding virtues, of which everyone spoke with honour, and also because her kingdom was most excellent, and was a common homeland to him and to her; and above all he owed obedience to the Tigurine magistrate, who was very well disposed towards the King and Queen. This was not to be despised, since among the Helvetians it had no small authority and power. He then added that in the business of the conference he had omitted nothing that he thought bore on the matter; he had acted calmly, as he had been ordered. As for the fact that the affair had not been carried further, that was not his fault, yet the fruit would not fail at its proper time, although it was not now apparent. But now, since nothing was being done, he asked for his dismissal, because he was an old man, and winter was now coming on, when the journey would be troublesome because of rains, snows and shorter days. Moreover, he had heard that he had been reported to Her Majesty as having come here as a foreigner, with no purpose other than to stir up sedition in the kingdom, and as one who rejoiced in these evils; he asked that she should not readily believe such things about him, since he was a man utterly removed from such crimes. For he had been at Strasbourg, then in England, and again at Strasbourg, and finally in Helvetia, and from there he could be informed about him if he was not believed; he had always sought peace and concord as far as could be done through the Word of God. He showed, moreover, that there was nothing that could invite him to do such things: as for the kingdom, he had been strongly devoted to it by his ancestors; as for the Queen, even more so, since she was from his own country and was, as it were, its light and splendour; for which reason he felt such affection towards her that he would gladly lay down his life for her dignity and safety, should the situation require it. And among the other things he wished, the first was that she and her sons and the kingdom of France should be safe. Since this was so, he begged that she dismiss him not in ill favour but in good grace. To this the Queen replied kindly and graciously, thanked him for coming, and promised him a safe and secure dismissal, within two days. She further asked that if his services were again sought for the same cause, he should not refuse to undertake the journey again. She herself, she said, was not unaware that it was a great labour, but she considered it both useful and necessary. As for the accusations made by others, she said she heard many things about various matters, but always reserved her judgement; and she declared that she thought entirely well of him. Martyr, giving her the thanks that were fitting, at the same time also pleaded on behalf of the afflicted churches, excusing the fact that they had occupied the churches against the King's will: for when they had heard that the King wished them to be restored, they had obeyed; he added also that if anything was sometimes done amiss by the unskilled and weaker brethren, this was not to be imputed to the doctrine. After he had been dismissed by the Queen, the Queen of Navarre and the King bade him farewell most courteously; the Prince of Condé and the Admiral did the same. Moreover, the Queen Mother and all the princes already named, by letters sent to the Tigurine Senate, thanked it for having sent Martyr to the conference, as they had asked, and at the same time they honoured Martyr with deserved praise. The Prince of Condé and the Admiral also assigned to Martyr, as he left, two noble and military men from their households, who brought him back safe to Zurich. I could here recite to you, my hearers, letters of princes and scholars, in which they heaped the highest praises upon him for his piety, learning, faith and diligence; but the measure of time and of my purpose does not allow me to linger over these. And so, since I have so far set out in what places he served the Church of God by teaching and disputing, I shall now set out how much he contributed to it by his writings. First, therefore, after he left Italy, he published in his native language an exposition of the Apostles' Creed, so as to give an account of his faith to all. Then, when he had come to England, and in expounding the eleventh chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians had discussed at length the Lord's Supper, at the end of the chapter he treated this question professedly. And first he refuted that union by which bread and wine are commonly said to be transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ, which seems to be the closest possible joining with the things of the sacrament. Then he examined the opinion of others, who held that bread and wine remain in the sacrament in their whole and true natures, and so remain that they have, as it is said, naturally, corporally and really joined to them the true body and blood of Christ. Thirdly, he weighed the opinion of those who say that these things are joined to one another in no other way than sacramentally, that is, by signification and representation. Lastly, he showed how, from opinions pertaining to the second and third positions, what seems more conducive to piety in this sacramental matter may be drawn out. He first published this treatise in England, together with the disputation which, as we showed above, he had held publicly on this controversy. At the same time he wished his commentaries on the first Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians to be printed among us at Zurich, a work certainly most worth reading, because of its clear explanation of many abstruse and difficult questions. But after he returned from England to Strasbourg, and was afterwards called to Zurich, he found among us not only some leisure, but also obtained the freedom of writing that he desired; and he revised, completed and published many things that he had either written or begun before. And first, the commentaries on the Epistle of St Paul to the Romans, which he had earlier publicly expounded at Oxford. Of this book I will say only this: with great learning and diligence he achieved that everyone admits that, although so many most learned interpreters, ancient and recent, have written on this epistle, nevertheless this book can be read with great and singular profit. At the same time was published by him his Defence of the ancient and Apostolic doctrine concerning the most sacred sacrament of the Eucharist, against the book of Stephen Gardiner. For many years earlier Gardiner had published a virulent and pestilent book on the Eucharist under the name of Master Antonius Constantius, in which, by mere sophisms and most twisted fallacies, he tried to undermine the true and orthodox doctrine which we today follow and profess, as received from Christ, the Apostles and the most ancient Fathers of the Church. For the writing of this book very many Papists had contributed their labours, and had handed all their arguments to Gardiner, so that he might choose from the heap whatever he wished; and they triumphed over this book and boasted that there was no one who would dare to engage with this their Goliath. Moved by these things, the most learned and also most holy man, Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, who had earlier often contended with the Bishop of Winchester and had withdrawn with victory and the highest praise, took up this task. But when he was kept under the strictest guard in prison, and was not only without a supply of books, but not even paper for writing was available to him, and finally he was taken away by the most cruel death, which he bore steadfastly in confessing the true faith, he tried to leave unfinished the work he already had in hand. Therefore many pious men of England who loved the true religion urged Martyr, often in person and by letters, to succeed him in this task, and not to suffer the minds of the simpler folk to be infected by the contagion of this poisonous book, and the Papists to insult our men so shamelessly and arrogantly. Therefore, stirred by the prayers of his friends and by the justice of the matter itself, he undertook this work, and, overcoming various and manifold hindrances, completed it at Zurich, and entrusted it to the printers to be printed. In this book he first defended the arguments of our men, collected and refuted from every quarter by Gardiner. Then he also upheld the rules which he himself had set out in his Treatise on the Eucharist, against Gardiner's calumnies. Third, he defended those responses with which the arguments of the opponents are usually dissolved in this dispute. Lastly, he asserted the just and true interpretations of certain passages, which Gardiner and his men had brought forward from the Fathers in their own support. In the whole work, whatever has been handed down about the entire cause of the Eucharist, both in the Holy Scriptures and in the monuments of the ancient Fathers and Councils, he embraced so fully and diligently, and examined each point so accurately and subtly, that this work is a matter of no small admiration even to the learned. After this Defence against Gardiner there followed another Defence against the two books on the celibacy of priests and monastic vows by Richard Smyth, an Englishman, formerly professor of theology at Oxford. For when Martyr was expounding the first Epistle to the Corinthians at Oxford, and in the seventh chapter, where the Apostle writes very much about virginity and marriage, had also discussed vows at length, Smyth, whom the King had appointed to lecture in sacred letters in his place, was present continually, and not only listened attentively to what Martyr said, but also carefully wrote it down. Then, having gone to Louvain, he published two foolish yet venomous little books, on the celibacy of priests and monastic vows, against Martyr. Martyr could not reply to this in his commentaries on the Epistle to the Corinthians; for since his friends were urging and demanding it, he was not permitted to delay the publication of his book; yet he promised a reply at the end of the seventh chapter, and shortly afterwards, having leisure, he did reply. But for certain grave and weighty reasons he only published this reply in public after some years, when he was at Zurich. He refutes not only Smyth's arguments, but almost everything that can be said in this matter, examining it diligently and accurately; and all who have read this book not in passing will be able to testify to this. Moreover, at Strasbourg, after he had returned there from England, he expounded the Book of Judges, and published commentaries on it among us, as you know, in which he explained very many theological questions that are not everywhere encountered, and greatly illuminated with the light of interpretation a truly golden book, which many, however, shunned on account of its peculiar difficulty and obscurity. Last of all, when John Brenz had published a little book on the personal union of the two natures in Christ, in which, in order to assert the carnal, bodily and real presence of the body and blood of Christ in the holy Supper, he undertook to defend a new and monstrous doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's body, Martyr, asked by his friends, refuted that little book in a published dialogue. And because he acknowledged that Brenz had deserved well of the Church by other writings, he did not wish to name him, nor to infame and slander him by name, especially since this would contribute nothing to the cause; but he copiously refuted Brenz's arguments, so that they might not deceive the unskilled; then he proved, which was the head of the cause, that the humanity of Christ is not everywhere, by the most solid testimonies of Holy Scripture and of the most ancient Fathers. Roused by this writing, Brenz, with a vehement and biting book, tried to overthrow Martyr and Bullinger at a single blow. When our Martyr saw this book, he, a man otherwise of a most placid nature, was somewhat indignant that Brenz was defending a bad cause with such bad faith, that he did not hesitate to accuse both himself and all our men of attacking the glory and majesty of Christ and denying the omnipotence of God, although it is well known, so that even Brenz cannot be ignorant of it, that our men teach the contrary. He grieved greatly that a man otherwise great, and who might be useful to the Church, should so obstinately defend a dogma absurd, monstrous and altogether new, which rests on no clear testimonies of Scripture, no authority of the Fathers and the ancient Church, and which the Papists themselves, who have invented many things to defend the carnal and crass presence of Christ's body in the holy Supper, have never approved. For, as he reported, when some little books of Brenz's had been brought into France at the time of the conference, the chief Papist theologians openly said that this doctrine of Brenz was new, unheard of, and altogether heretical. For this reason he had already girded himself to answer diligently and accurately the accusations of Brenz, which were many and serious, and his arguments, which were not so many; but, to our sorrow, he was snatched from us by the unexpected violence of disease, and could not accomplish what he had resolved. Yet this misfortune, however it may be borne, can be made lighter: for Bullinger, the minister of our church, who had shared the labour of replying with him, will bear the burden bravely by his zeal and labour, and by his outstanding learning besides, and will be enough by himself to defend both sides; and moreover, Martyr's arguments, which he set out in great number in his dialogue, still stand firm, and could not be shaken, much less overthrown, by this Brenzian onslaught. It is rather to be lamented that Martyr could not complete other and more excellent works, which could have brought great usefulness to the whole Church. For he had for some years been expounding, as you know, the two Books of Samuel, and now, the first Book of Kings being finished, he was engaged on the second; and what he has read, although not all of it has been revised by him, is nevertheless such that, when published, as will shortly happen, God willing, scarcely anyone could desire his final hand in these pages. But what the second Book of Kings lacks, who will complete it? Who will finish this as if Apelles had begun it with his hand, like a Venus? Who will revise the commentaries on Genesis, on Exodus, on Leviticus, on the Minor Prophets, on the Lamentations of Jeremiah, so that they may have the dignity and splendour they would have had if they had been corrected, revised and published by him? What shall I say of his most weighty disputations on the greatest matters, or of his commentaries on Aristotle, and the other things which he left begun and unfinished? For before he could revise these, I do not say, but almost before he could give instructions as to what should be done with them, he was overcome by the violence of a grave and unexpected disease and snatched from us. For when he began to be ill on the fifth day of this month, he departed from this life on the twelfth of the same. He had already been for some time of frail and feeble health, partly because of his advancing age, partly because the various cares and anxieties, and especially the great sorrows which he received from the afflicted state of the French Church, were gradually wearing away his strength. Therefore, when the epidemic disease, which many of you have experienced, attacked him, it easily overcame a nature already exhausted. We, however, because until then this sickness had been fatal to no one, were not at all afraid for Martyr in the first days. He himself also strengthened our hope, for on the third and fourth day after the disease had seized him, he returned again to his studies, and resolved that on the next day, since it was his turn, he would lecture publicly; although I resisted and urged him to spare his health, for I would read in his place, and I did not doubt that the hearers, bearing his health in mind, would easily allow this. But he thought himself firm enough, and said that, unless something else happened, he would wish to lecture the following day. But that very night the fever returned and attacked him more severely than before; meanwhile his catarrh also increased, and at the same time a cough was very troublesome to him. And so, although his friends urged him to hope well for his health, and the doctors also gave some hope, he himself foresaw that death was at hand, and for this reason he made his will the day before he died; and calling his neighbour, the most distinguished man, Master Bernhard Sprüngli, Treasurer, whom he had made guardian to his pregnant wife, he wished me to read it in his presence, and asked him to take care that the Senate should confirm it by its authority. The night that followed that day he rested fairly well, and the disease seemed to us to have somewhat abated; but in truth the strength of nature, overcome by the disease, no longer resisted it. Meanwhile, however, his friends visited him every day, and with them, before the difficulty of breathing hindered him, he conversed on various matters no less cheerfully than if he had not been troubled by any disease at all. For he discussed both the power and nature of the disease, on the basis of medical science, in which he had been no small practitioner, with the doctors themselves, who out of friendship and duty visited him daily. And because on most nights he had slept not unpleasantly, he proclaimed this as a benefit of God to his friends, and from the precepts of the physicians he recalled the nature and efficacy of sleep, sweetly, as it were, irrigating the whole body. He also often complained of the cough, which harmed the whole body, but chiefly the head and chest; and several times he testified that he was ill in body, but very well in mind. And indeed, if at that time he began either to set out the grounds of his faith or to recall by what consolations he raised up his spirit, he was altogether divine in this matter.</i>

units.la: Pridie vero antequam moreretur, cum illi noctu adessemus amici aliquot, & inter hos Bullingerus praecipue, iacebat aliquandiu secum meditabundus, tum ad nos conuersus, voce satis clara testabatur se vitam & salutem in vno Christo agnoscere, qui solus a patre seruator humano generi datus sit, atque hanc suam sententiam rationibus & verbis scripturarum explicabat & confirmabat, addens postremo, Haec est fides mea, in hac ego moriar, eos autem qui secus docent & homines alio auocant Deus perdet. Atq; his dictis manum separatim singulis porrigens, Valete, inquit, fratres & amici charissimi.
units.tr: On the day before he died, several friends were with him at night, and among them Bullinger in particular. He lay for some time in thought, then turned to us and said in a fairly clear voice that he acknowledged his life and salvation in Christ alone, whom the Father has given as the only Saviour of mankind. He explained and confirmed this view with reasons and the words of Scripture, adding at the end: "This is my faith, and in this I will die. As for those who teach otherwise and draw men away to something else, God will destroy them." Having said this, he stretched out his hand to each of us separately and said: "Farewell, brethren and dearest friends."

units.la: Alio item die cum Bullingerus inter alia consolationis causa e Paulo dixisset, nostram politiam in caelo esse, agnosco inquit ille, sed non in caelo Brentij, quod nusquam est.
