Et huic quidem se libenter et ex animo ignoscere dicebat, optasse tamen si ita Deo visum fuisset, illi respondere, cum infirmiorum causa, tum vt salsissimas contra se calumnias refutaret.
units.tr: On another day, when Bullinger, among other things meant to console him, quoted Paul that our commonwealth is in heaven, he replied: "I acknowledge that, but not the heaven of Brentius, which is nowhere." He said that he willingly and from his heart forgave Brentius, but that he had wished, if it had been God's will, to answer him, both for the sake of the weak and to refute the most bitter calumnies against himself.

units.la: Et vt summatim dicam, cum toto morbi tempore erant eius sermones reliquae vitae anteactae similes, pleni nempe religione, fide, pietate, humanitate, tum maxime quo magis properabat dissolui & coniungi cum Christo, eò magis divinum quid, opus & energia scilicet sancti spiritus, in eo relucebat. Verumta-men eo die quo obijt ob vehementiam defluxionem magnum sentiebat difficultatem respirandi, & cum molestia loquebatur, quamvis voce uteretur submissa vix ut posset intelligi, itaque eo die non ita multa locutus est. Erat tamen hora forte diei decima cum ab eo discesserant medici, rediturì post meridiem, cum ille se è lecto tolli, & more solito indui iussit, ac aliquantulum pransus, sedens quiescebat: sic tamen ut in aliquem amicorum a-stantium caput reclinaret, quòd non posset id commodè ob uim mor-bi erigere: deinde uti erat vestitus in lectum reponi & quiesce-re voluit. Accesserunt interea eum medici, aderant illi fre-quentes amici, cum alij tum pastor & seniores Ecclesiæ Italicæ, cum quibus pauca locutus, rursus è lecto se tolli, & in eadem se-de reponi petiit. Discesserant iam ab eo plerique ex amicis, ut commodius quiesceret, medici quoque abierant, quorum aliqui noua quædam remedia quæ illi adhiberet[?] parabant: cùm ille ita sedens vestitus uti quotidie solebat, tenui voce Deo spiritu suo co-mendans animam agere cœpit: aderat adhuc illi Conradus Gef-nerus, & præter vxorem duo adolescentes illi familiares, à qui-bus statim Bullingerus & reliqui amici qui viciniores erant vocati sunt, his præsentibus extremum spiritum exhalavit, tan-ta quidem tranquillitate, ut non animam agere sed obdormi-scere videretur, & ut non mortuum sed viuentem adhuc eum nobis assidere, cernere nos arbitraremur. Oculos morienti con-pressit Bullingerus, eumque sepulchrali veste induit, & ami-cus homini amicissimo ultimum hoc pietatis officium magno in-terea & incredibili dolore perculsus præstitit.
units.tr: To sum up briefly: throughout the whole course of his illness his talk was like that of his earlier life, full of religion, faith, piety and kindness. Indeed, the nearer he hastened to be dissolved and joined with Christ, the more the divine element, namely the working and power of the Holy Spirit, shone forth in him. Yet on the day he died, because of the violence of the catarrh, he felt great difficulty in breathing, and he spoke with pain and in a voice so low that he could scarcely be understood, so that on that day he did not say much. Still, at about the tenth hour of the day, when the doctors had left him, intending to return after noon, he ordered himself to be lifted from the bed and dressed in the usual way. After eating a little, he sat resting, but leaned his head on one of the friends standing beside him, since because of the force of the disease he could not comfortably hold it up. Then, still dressed as he was, he wished to be laid back on the bed and to rest. Meanwhile the doctors came back to him, and many friends were present, both others and the minister and elders of the Italian congregation. After speaking a few words with them, he asked to be lifted from the bed again and placed back in the same chair. Most of the friends had by now withdrawn so that he could rest more comfortably, and the doctors had also gone, some of them preparing certain new remedies to apply to him. Then, as he sat fully dressed as he did every day, he began to breathe his last, commending his soul to God in a faint voice. Conrad Gessner was still with him, and besides his wife there were two young men of his household, and at once these men summoned Bullinger and the other friends who lived nearer. In their presence he breathed out his last, with such tranquillity that he seemed not to be dying but to be falling asleep, and we thought we saw him still living and sitting beside us, not dead. Bullinger closed his eyes and dressed him in burial clothes, and meanwhile, struck with great and incredible grief, he performed this last duty of piety as a friend for a most dear friend.

units.la: Atq; hic quidem, Auditores, exitus vitæ fuit Præceptoris nostri, viri omnium quos ego noverim optimi & sapientissimi atque iustissimi: verè enim hoc de illo dicere possum quod de Socrate suo Plato scriptum reliquit. Exposita est vobis vita eius: obitus etiam qualis fuerit audivistis: superest extremum illud quod forte à me expeexpectatis, ut dolorem quem ex morte eius percepistis verbis lenire coner: verum ego qui hoc possim, qui prae caeteris singulari moerore conficior? Sed hic illius virtus sumenda vobis est, qua ille polluit plurimum, & fortiter superanda aduersa omnia, & quod tempus efficeret, idipsum efficiat in vobis ratio bonis artibus informata, & quod summum est diuinis literis instructa, ut dolori & moerori modus aliquis statuatur. Et quoniam in vera firmaque fide ita pie & Christiane decessit e vita, ut nefas sit dubitare illum summas calamitates & miserias huius vitae, cum caelesti & sempiterna beatitudine & felicitate commutasse, nostrum est qui eum amamus magis laetari summo illius bono, quam ulla nostro commoueri incommodo: praesertim cum habeatis ingenij pietatis & doctrinae eius tam praeclara monimenta, ut eorum assidua lectione non modo dolorem lenire, verum ipsum quoque optima sui parte praesentem semper habere possitis. Atq; equidem si ex his quae saepe ex eo viuente audiuimus, quis eius post mortem sensus sit colligere possumus, nihil neque coram Deo sanctius, neque ipsi acceptius facere poteritis, quam si eam quam ab ipso didicistis doctrinam, puram & inuiolatam firmiter retineatis.
units.tr: Such, listeners, was the end of the life of our teacher, the best, wisest and most just man I have ever known. Indeed I can say of him what Plato left written about his Socrates. The course of his life has been set out for you, and you have heard how he died. There remains the last thing, which perhaps you expect from me: that I should try with words to soften the sorrow you have felt at his death. But who am I to do this, I who am worn down by a grief more singular than the rest? Rather, you must take up his virtue, by which he excelled above all, and bravely overcome all adversity. What time brings about, let reason do in you, reason formed by good arts and, above all, instructed in the divine letters, so that some measure may be set to grief and sorrow. And since he departed this life in true and firm faith, so piously and in a Christian way that it would be wrong to doubt that he exchanged the greatest calamities and miseries of this life for heavenly and eternal blessedness and happiness, it is for us who love him to rejoice more in his supreme good than to be troubled by any harm to ourselves. This is especially so since you have such clear memorials of his talent, piety and learning that by their constant reading you can not only soften your sorrow but also keep him ever present, in his best part. Indeed, if from what we often heard from him while he lived we can gather what his feeling would be after death, you can do nothing more holy before God, or more pleasing to him, than to hold firmly to the teaching you learned from him, pure and undefiled.

units.la: Vos vero Auditores, iuniores praesertim, quorum oculos perstringit nominis illius gloria, eisdem vestigijs illuc contendite, quo ipsum peruenisse admiramini. Vigilijs, laboribus, studio, diligentia, assiduitate eadem ornamenta doctrinae & eruditionis vobis comparate: coniungite studijs vestris religionem, pietatem, fidem, modestiam, temperantiam aliasque virtutes, quibus ille excelluit. Quas si ego non omnes oratione complexus sum, vos tamen qui eas nostis, animo illas complectimini: & ut praeclarum imitationis exemplar nunquam ab oculis animoque recedere patiamini. Quoniam vero clarorum & virtute praestantium virorum obitus, non solum ipsorum amissione, verum etiam omnis ratione Reipub. periculosus est: ut tale omen ab Ecclesia tua auertas te aeterne ac caelestis pater supplex precor. Respice quaeso pusillum tuum gregem & eum sicuti promisisti regito, & adversus lupos defendito: da illi non mercenarios sed fidos pastores, qui ad salubria pascua & fontes aquæ vivæ oves tuas ducant, & animam si opus sit pro illis ponant. Nobis quoq; ô Pater optime si non alterum Martyrem, quandoquidem id vix petere audemus, aliquem saltem dato doctorem, qui tuo spiritu afflatus quàm proximè ad incompa-rabilem eius doctrinam, & divinas atque immortales virtutes accedat. Quodque ego nunc precor, idipsum Auditores, vos & nunc in fine orationis huius, & posthac indesinen-ter ardentibus votis supplices à Deo Patre Do-mini nostri Jesu Christi petitote.
units.tr: But you, listeners, especially the younger among you, whose eyes are dazzled by the glory of his name, press on along the same path by which you admire that he reached the goal. By watchings, labours, study, diligence and constant application, acquire for yourselves those same adornments of learning and erudition. Join to your studies religion, piety, faith, modesty, temperance and the other virtues in which he excelled. If I have not embraced all of these in my speech, you who know them should embrace them in your mind, and never allow this splendid pattern of imitation to depart from your eyes and your heart. But since the death of famous men eminent in virtue is dangerous to the commonwealth not only through the loss of the men themselves but in every way, I humbly pray you, eternal and heavenly Father, to turn such an omen away from your Church. Look kindly, I beg you, upon your little flock, and guard it, as you have promised, and defend it against the wolves. Give it not hired men but faithful ministers, who may lead your sheep to wholesome pastures and to the fountains of living water, and who will lay down their lives for them if need be. And to us also, O best Father, if not another martyr, since we hardly dare to ask for that, at least give a teacher who, inspired by your Spirit, may come as near as possible to his incomparable teaching and his divine and immortal virtues. What I now pray for, listeners, you too should now, at the end of this speech, and hereafter without ceasing, ask of God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ with fervent prayers.

units.la: SIQVIS unus ex omnibus reuerende Pater, controuersiam quæ est inter summos Theologos de Christi seruatoris nostri præsentia in sacra Cœna, diligenter & exacte cognouit atq; tractauit, huic ego Petrũ Martyre fuisse existimo. Nam primum in ea tempora incidit, quan-do multis iam libris editis tota hæc causa diligenter excusa & quasi uentilata fuit. Deinde tanta diligentia & industria in hac causa uer-satus est, ut omnia omnium hac de re scripta quæcunque habere potuit, diligentissimè legerit. Attulit præterea ad causæ cognitionem singularem eruditionem & excellens ingenij acumen, memo-riam uero incredibilem & propemodum infinitam, itaque prom-ptissimè semper & acutissimè singulas rationes perspicere & pon-derare consueuerat, & ea quæ semel cognouerat nunquam ex ani-mo & memoria sua effluere patiebatur. Accesit his omnibus as-sidua & pene quotidiana docendi atque disputandi consuetudo. Nam & Argentorati & postea etiam in Anglia, sæpe multumq; de hac causa familiariter cum D. Martino Bucero Theologo longè acutissimo contulit. Præterea cum in Anglia uestra, tum etiam nuper in Gallia, de hac ipsa con-trouersia cum præcipuis Romana-rum partium Theologis disputauit: Quæ cum ita sint, nemo puto negabit eius scriptis in hoc genere plurimum tribuendum esse. Ex quibus cum alia maioris operis scripta iam olim euulgata sint, hæc par-ua opuscula quasi appendicula maiorum operum, nunc primum in lucem prodeunt. Cum enim multis desit tempus & ocium evoluendi prolixiora uolumina, & illis etiam qui ocio abundant, utile sit breuem aliquam summam habere certorum capitum, ad quæ omnia argumenta, quæ alioqui certo numero comprehendi non possunt, reducant, existimaui hæc scripta quæ & totam con-trouersiam sacramentariam perspicuè & breuiter explicant, & argumentorum omnium fontes & certa capita indicant, studiosis hominibus grata & accepta fore. Quamuis autem à Martyre non in hunc finem scripta sint ut in publicum edantur, sunt tamen nihilonihilominus talia quæ multum iuuare possint etiam mediocriter eruditorum studia, etsi enim forte non ita polita sunt ut illa quæ ipse edidit, facile tamen apparet hæc ex eadem officina profecta esse. Mitto autem illa ad te reuerende Pater, non quod studia tua his scriptis iuuari posse existimem, cum tantam habeas huius con-trouersiæ peritiam, quatam uix in paucis quibusdam reperias: sed ut habeas à me hæc quasi [illegible, ~5 letters] quædam Martyris nostri, quæ tibi leniant dolorem, uel potius mœrorem, quem opinione omnium maiorem te ex optimi atque amicissimi hominis obitu accepisse non dubito.
units.tr: Reverend Father, of all men who have carefully and exactly studied and handled the controversy among the leading theologians about the presence of our Saviour Christ in the holy Supper, I think Peter Martyr is the one to whom it belongs. For he came upon those times when this whole cause had already been thoroughly discussed and, as it were, winnowed in many books that had been published. Then he dealt with this cause with such great diligence and industry that he read most diligently everything that anyone had written on the subject and could obtain. Moreover, he brought to the understanding of the cause a singular learning and an excellent sharpness of wit, and a memory that was incredible and almost boundless. So he was always accustomed to perceive and weigh each argument very readily and very sharply, and he never allowed what he had once understood to slip out of his mind and memory. To all this was added a constant and almost daily habit of teaching and disputing. For both at Strasbourg and afterwards also in England, he often and at length discussed this cause in familiar conversation with Doctor Martin Bucer, a theologian by far the keenest. Besides, both in your England and lately also in France, he disputed about this same controversy with the chief theologians of the Roman party. Since these things are so, I think no one will deny that his writings in this kind deserve very great weight. Of these, while other writings of greater work were published long ago, these small pamphlets, as it were an appendix to the greater works, now first come to light. For while many lack the time and leisure to unroll longer volumes, and even those who abound in leisure find it useful to have a brief summary of certain heads to which they may refer all arguments, which otherwise cannot be contained in a fixed number, I judged that these writings, which explain the whole sacramentarian controversy clearly and briefly and point out the sources of all arguments and the fixed heads, would be welcome and acceptable to studious men. Although Martyr did not write them for this purpose, that they should be published, nonetheless they are of such a kind that they can greatly help even the studies of moderately learned men. For although perhaps they are not as polished as those things he himself published, it is nevertheless easy to see that they came forth from the same workshop. I send these to you, Reverend Father, not because I think your studies can be aided by these writings, since you have such a knowledge of this controversy as one would scarcely find in a few men, but so that you may have from me these [illegible, about five letters] of our Martyr, which may soothe your pain, or rather your grief, which I do not doubt you have received from the death of so good and most friendly a man, greater than anyone's opinion.

units.la: Solent alij amicorum quos amiserunt uestes, arma, annulos, pocula atque ipsa etiam mortuorum ossa conseruare: nonnulli desiderium suum solantur aureis, aut argenteis, aut etiam pictis amicorum imaginibus, ego uero si modo recte animum tuum perspexi, arbitror te inprimis affici ingenij reliquijs & effigie animi, quam scripta authoris multo uerius & exactius exprimunt, quam ulla pictorum aut sculptorum ars. Addidi præterea his de Eucha-ristia scriptis Carmina aliquot, quæ V. CL. Conradus Gesnerus, Vuolfgangus Musculus, Rodolphus Gualtherus, & reliqui quorum nomina carminibus addita sunt, homines tibi noti & tui amantes in obitum Martyris conscripserunt. Existimo enim te si quid ocij habueris a studijs atque occupationibus grauissimis, quibus perpetuo distineris, hæc quoque non illibenter lecturum.
units.tr: Others are accustomed to keep the garments, weapons, rings, cups, and even the very bones of friends they have lost; some console their longing with golden, silver, or even painted images of their friends. But I, if I have rightly perceived your mind, think that you are especially moved by the remains of his genius and the likeness of his mind, which the writings of the author express far more truly and exactly than any art of painters or sculptors. Besides, I have added to these writings on the Eucharist some poems, which Conrad Gesner, the most learned man, Wolfgang Musculus, Rudolf Gwalther, and the rest whose names are added to the poems, men known to you and fond of you, wrote on the death of the Martyr. For I think that if you have any leisure from your studies and most weighty occupations, by which you are constantly kept busy, you will read these also not unwillingly.

units.la: Præsertim cum in iuuentute tua Musas poeticas studiose & feliciter coloueris, id quod ingenij tui præclara monimenta testantur. Cupio autem hac quasi publica testificatione declarare meam in te ob-seruantiam, qua te non tantum ob eruditionem singularem, & amplissimam dignitatem colo & reuereor, sed etiam ob amorem et beneuolentiam summam qua me hactenus complexus es.
units.tr: Especially since in your youth you cultivated the poetic Muses diligently and successfully, as the splendid monuments of your genius bear witness. I wish, moreover, to declare by this, as it were, public testimony my regard for you, by which I honour and revere you not only for your singular learning and most distinguished dignity, but also for the great love and goodwill with which you have embraced me until now.

units.la: Te autem reuerende Pater rogo ut hoc meę in te uoluntatis testimonium, impar, fateor, magnitudini amoris & meritorum in me tuorum, non asperneris, hæc enim scripta etsi exigua sunt, sunt tamen scripta ab hominibus tibi amicissimis, & mittuntur tibi ab homine tui amantissimo atque studiosissimo, qui te omnibus rebus ornatum esse & florere ex animo cupit. Deus te incolumem quam diutissime Ecclesiæ suæ conseruet.
units.tr: And you, Reverend Father, I ask that you not spurn this testimony of my good will towards you, unequal, I confess, to the greatness of the love and of the kindnesses you have shown me; for these writings, although they are slight, were written by men most friendly to you, and they are sent to you by a man most devoted and eager to serve you, who wishes from his heart that you may be adorned with every blessing and flourish. May God keep you safe for his Church for as long as possible.

units.la: Datum Ti-guri pridie nonas Ianuarij.
units.tr: Given at Zurich, the day before the Nones of January.

units.la: EPITOME IN DEFENSIO-NEM D. PETRI MARTYRIS aduersus Steph. Gardinerum, ab ipso Martyre concinnata.
units.tr: EPITOME of the Defence of Master Peter Martyr against Stephen Gardiner, put together by the Martyr himself.

units.la: RES Eucharistica quatenus eam nobis Dominus tradidit, cum facilis tum simplex esset cognitu. Haec si diuinarum literarum arbitrio sensuque tractaretur, haberetúrque humanae rationi naturae Christi, atque sacramenti receptae definitionis: in ea vel intelligenda aut tractanda, nihil plane laboraretur. Sed contentione atq; aduersariorum contigit importunitate, ut iam caeco labyrintho quodam impeditior euaserit, parumq; absit quin altercãdo veritatem amiserimus. Illi enim ut sententiae orthodoxae & perspicuae non concedant, imò prae illa quibuscunque modis prodigiosa inventa sua tueantur, omne genus fuci, cavillationum, atq; impostura adhibuerunt. Proinde cum à me hisce diebus captionum & sophismatum quibus utuntur, cõfertissimis aciebus sedulò occurreretur, & ea qua potui diligentia responderetur: volumen propemodū immensum creuit. Veritus ergo ne pij homines lectione admo-dum prolixa nimis fatigati, redeant item incerti, atq; anteasue-rint, quàm ad meum librum euoluendum accederent: (Nam rationibus utrinq; auditis eisq; subinde recentibus ac nouis, fie-ri non posset, quin succedentia praeteritorum memoriam obscu-rent, aut tantum non obliterent) statui quandam Epitome vel Resolutione, quam Graeci ἀνάλυσιν vocant, rem ipsam sub oculos totam ponere, ut lecturi mea, quiq; ea vel nunc legunt vel iam perlegerunt, in promptu & ad manus habeant certa quaedam capita non minus dilucida quàm breuia, ad quae disputa-tionis iam editae cum argumenta tum responsa facile referre queant. Id vero ni fallor eius disceptationis lectoribus non minus adiumento erit quàm nautis, dum per altum mare huc & illuc iactantur incerti, cynosurae aspectus. Quod itaque à me bono amicoq; fit animo, velim omnes bonos & pios in bonam partem accipere. Methodumq; à me sic excogitatam quàm attentissimè considerare, ac deinde ex verbo Dei de illa sententiam candidè ferre. Sed pluribus nolo praefari, cùm in Epitome consectanda sit breuitas quàm maximè.
units.tr: The Eucharistic matter, as the Lord delivered it to us, was easy and simple to understand. If it were handled according to the judgement and sense of the divine Scriptures, and if it were measured by human reason, by the nature of Christ, and by the accepted definition of a sacrament, then there would be no real difficulty either in understanding it or in treating it. But through the contention and the importunity of our opponents it has come about that the matter has become more entangled, as if in some blind labyrinth, and we have come close to losing the truth through wrangling. For they, so that they will not grant the orthodox and plain opinion, but rather defend their own monstrous inventions by whatever means they can, have used every kind of deceit, quibbling and trickery. Therefore, since in recent days I have been diligently meeting, with my most closely arranged battle lines, the captious arguments and sophisms they use, and have answered them with all the care I could, the book has grown to an almost immense size. I fear, then, that godly people, wearied by such a very long reading, may return uncertain, or may have forgotten what went before before they come to read my book. For when arguments have been heard on both sides, and those arguments are constantly fresh and new, it cannot but happen that what follows dims the memory of what came earlier, or nearly wipes it out. I have therefore resolved to set the whole matter before the eyes in a certain Epitome or Resolution (which the Greeks call analysis), so that my readers, and those who now read or have already read through the work, may have at hand certain headings, no less clear than brief, to which they can easily refer both the arguments and the replies of the disputation already published. This will, I think, be no less a help to the readers of that dispute than the sight of the Cynosure is to sailors who are tossed hither and thither, uncertain, over the deep sea. Whatever I do here, I do in a friendly and good spirit, and I wish all good and godly people to take it in good part, and to consider attentively the method I have devised, and then to pass a fair judgement on its view from the word of God. But I do not wish to say more by way of preface, since brevity is to be aimed at as far as possible in an Epitome.

units.la: VERBA Coenae accipienda esse Tropice.
units.tr: THAT the words of the Supper are to be taken tropically.

units.la: Primùm quidem in Sacramento Eucharistiae panem & vinum, quae diuinae literae, Patres ac sensus ibi verè adesse testantur: Corporis & sanguinis Domini signa esse affirmamus, non vtiq; prophana & vulgaria, sed quemadmodum in caeteris mysterijs assignari consueuerunt. Aduersarij nostri è diuerso corpus & sanguinem Christi proprie & verè illa esse praedicant. Rogamus, qui sciant? Quoniam, inquiunt, Christus dixit, Hoc est corpus meum. At nos dictum seruatoris nostri ea loquendi formula seu tropi genere, interpretamur, quo in sacramentis praesertim, signarerum ipsarum quae significantur vocabulis appellari solent. Nostrae huic sententiae illi refragantur, aiuntq; Christi verba non tropica sed propria omninò & simplicia esse.
units.tr: First of all, we affirm that in the Sacrament of the Eucharist the bread and the wine, which the divine writings, the Fathers and the sense itself testify are truly present there, are signs of the body and blood of the Lord. They are not, of course, profane and common things, but are such as are customarily assigned in the other mysteries. Our opponents, on the contrary, declare that these are properly and truly the body and blood of Christ. We ask them, how do they know this? Because, they say, Christ said, "This is my body." But we interpret the saying of our Saviour in that form of speech, or kind of trope, by which, especially in sacraments, the signs are commonly named by the words of the things that are signified. Our opponents oppose this view of ours, and say that the words of Christ are not tropical but wholly proper and plain.

units.la: A nobis obijcitur nullam esse certam rationem ex Euan-gelica historia, quae verba illa simpliciter intelligenda conuincat. Nam cùm Coena Domini à Matthaeo, Marco, Luca & Paulo explicatur, ibi permulti deprehenduntur tropi. Calix dicitur nouum Testamentum: nec ipsum tamen poculum nec is qui in eo continetur liquor est re ipsa testamentum.
units.tr: We are challenged that there is no sure reason from the Gospel history which proves that those words must be understood simply. For when the Lord's Supper is described by Matthew, Mark, Luke and Paul, very many tropes are found there. The cup is called the New Testament; yet neither the cup itself nor the liquid contained in it is, in actual fact, the testament.

units.la: Indigne sumentes affirmantur iudicium sibiipsis edere, ac bibere, at proprie iudicium nec edi nec bibi potest.
units.tr: Those who eat and drink unworthily are said to eat and drink judgement to themselves; but judgement can properly be neither eaten nor drunk.

units.la: Est verò longè alienum à corpore Domini vt verè comeda-tur, quia nephas est ipsum omninò frangi, dentibus commoli atq; dissolui.
units.tr: Moreover, it is far removed from the body of the Lord that it should be truly eaten, because it is an abomination that it should be broken at all, ground with the teeth and dissolved.

units.la: Dixit seruator noster, cùm eidem mensae accubuisset, vehementer se desiderasse illud pascha una cum discipulis manducare. Nemo vero ignorat non ipsum פסח[?] id est Domini transitum, sed agnum, qui ut eius symbolum adhibebatur in ea solennitate comedi solitum fuisse.
units.tr: Our Saviour, when he had reclined at the same table, said that he had greatly desired to eat that Passover with his disciples. But no one is unaware that the Passover [פסח], that is, the passing over of the Lord, was not itself eaten in that solemnity, but the lamb, which was used as its symbol, was customarily eaten.

units.la: Quoties, inquit in epistola ad Corinth. priore, biberitis hoc poculum, &c. Num poculum? an non potius quod in eo infusum est haurimus? Paulus itaq; tropo quàm usitatissimo sic est loquutus. Quamobrem in Cœna Domini referenda, cùm spiritus sancti scribæ, permultis orationibus tropicis fuerint usi, & id de quo agimus, nempè, Hoc est corpus meum, figurato sermone ab eis fuisse dictum quid prohibet?
units.tr: "As often," he says in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, "as you drink this cup, etc." Does he mean the cup? Or rather do we not drink what is poured into it? Paul therefore spoke with a most common trope. Why, then, when the writings of the Holy Spirit have used very many tropical expressions in relating the Lord's Supper, should it be forbidden that the matter we are discussing, namely "This is my body," was spoken by them in a figurative manner?

units.la: Mitto alias permultas divinarum literarum sententias quas ab omnibus pie sentientibus per tropos constat exponi. Etenim si velim eas commemorare, jam non Epitome sed justus liber esset conscribendus. Cum itaq; nostram hanc sententiam sic interpretamur, nihil vel novum vel a sanctis scripturis alienum comminiscimur.
units.tr: I pass over the many other sayings of the divine writings which it is agreed are explained tropically by all who think piously. For if I were to recall them, the work would no longer be an Epitome but a large book would have to be written. Since, then, we interpret our view in this way, we invent nothing either new or foreign to the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Quod verba quæ apud Paulum & Lucam de calice scribuntur Tropicè sint enunciata, ut jam docuimus, neminem inficias ire merito posse, quis attentus lector non videat. Unde quæ scripserunt Matthæus & Marcus de eadem re tropicè accipienda erunt, nisi quis neget priora ex posterioribus esse exponenda, scripsisse vero Paulum & Lucam post Matthæum & Marcum nemo ambigit.
units.tr: That the words which Paul and Luke write about the cup are uttered tropically, as we have already shown, no attentive reader can fail to see, and no one can rightly deny it. Hence what Matthew and Mark wrote about the same matter must also be taken tropically, unless someone denies that the earlier passages must be explained by the later; and no one doubts that Paul and Luke wrote after Matthew and Mark.

units.la: Atqui quod Matthæus & Marcus de sanguine tradunt ut simpliciter dictu, intelligi non potest. Ita scribunt illi, Τοῦτό ἐςὶ τὸ αἷμά μου[?], jam vero quid pronomen τοῦτο[?] aliud referre potest quam poculum? Siquidem illud Christus & in manibus accepisse & apostolis dedisse commemoratur, nec Lucas & Paulus aliud asserunt, cùm dixisse Christum tradunt, Hic calix novum Testamentum est, &c. Poculum autem quis audet dicere sanguinem esse? Expendantur ergo verba Matthæi & Marci ex una parte, ex altera Lucæ & Pauli recte, & negetur Tropus, si possus.[?]
units.tr: Yet what Matthew and Mark hand down about the blood cannot be understood as spoken plainly. They write thus: "This is my blood" [Τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου]. Now what can the pronoun "this" [τοῦτο] refer to other than the cup? For it is recorded that Christ both took the cup into his hands and gave it to the apostles; nor do Luke and Paul assert anything else, since they relate that Christ said, "This cup is the New Testament," etc. But who would dare to say that the cup is blood? Let the words of Matthew and Mark, on the one hand, and those of Luke and Paul, on the other, be weighed rightly, and let the trope be denied, if it can be.

units.la: Ipsi aduersarij etsi prӕoptant inseruire potius opinioni suӕ quàm veritati, verba Domini tamen absq; Troporum adminiculo interpretari non possunt. Ostendendo quippè Sacramento Eucharistiӕ, non licet ipsis de eo toto pronunciare, Hoc est corpus meum: pudeat ergo eos nos eius criminis reprehendere, cuius ipsi accusari iure & merito possunt.
units.tr: The opponents themselves, although they prefer to serve their own opinion rather than the truth, nevertheless cannot interpret the words of the Lord without the aid of tropes. For when they point to the sacrament of the Eucharist, they are not permitted to say of the whole of it, "This is my body." Let them therefore be ashamed to reproach us with that charge, of which they themselves can rightly and justly be accused.

units.la: Ipsa porrò sacramenti definitio, quod sacrӕ rei sit signum, & gratiӕ quӕ non videtur, visibilis forma, nostram sententiam maximè propugnat, efficitur enim ex ea publicè recepta definitione, ea quӕ in Eucharistia videntur corporis & sanguinis Domini signa esse, nisi velimus ipsam Eucharistiam ex albo sacramentorum expungere.
units.tr: Moreover, the very definition of a sacrament, that it is a sign of a sacred thing and a visible form of an invisible grace, strongly supports our view. For it follows from that publicly accepted definition that those things which are seen in the Eucharist are signs of the body and blood of the Lord, unless we wish to strike the Eucharist itself from the list of sacraments.

units.la: Nec enim aliter exponi queunt formulӕ dicendi, quibus diuina scriptura vtitur, cùm de parte sacramenti aspectabili, rem ipsam quӕ significatur pronuntiat. Circumcisio enim quì fœdus Domini vocaretur nisi eam signum ipsius esse dixerimus? Paulus huius sententiӕ est author, qui circumcisionem σφραγῖδα id est sigillum vel signum iustitiӕ per fidem adeptӕ appellat. Baptismus quoq; regenerationis lauacrum dicitur: Et agnus in veteri Testamento, sicuti antea demonstrauimus פסח vocabatur.
units.tr: For the formulas of speech which the divine Scripture uses, when it pronounces the thing signified of the visible part of a sacrament, cannot be explained in any other way. For how would circumcision be called the covenant of the Lord, unless we say that it is a sign of it? Paul is the author of this view, who calls circumcision a seal [σφραγῖδα], that is, a sign or seal of righteousness obtained through faith. Baptism too is called the washing of regeneration. And the lamb in the Old Testament, as we showed before, was called the Passover [פסח].

units.la: Accedant & patres qui non semel diuersis verbis tradunt, Christum sui corporis signum dedisse, figuram dedisse, Corpus suum repræsentasse, Typum & ἀντίτυπα esse illa quӕ à nobis videntur corporis & sanguinis Domini. Cyprianus, Cyrillus, Augustinus, Theodoretus, & Gelasius quam apertissimè docent ista signa vocabulo rerum significatarum nuncupari. Cùm ergo diuinӕ literӕ in hoc sacramento tradendo tropos admittat, eos ipsa natura sacramentorum exigat, Patresq; manifestissime recipiant, nos quod vtamur tropica interpretatione in verbis Domini exponendis accusabimur?
units.tr: Let the Fathers also be brought in, who more than once, in various words, teach that Christ gave the sign of his body, gave a figure, represented his body, and that those things which are seen by us are types and antitypes [ἀντίτυπα] of the body and blood of the Lord. Cyprian, Cyril, Augustine, Theodoret and Gelasius teach most plainly that these signs are named by the name of the things they signify. Since, then, the divine writings admit tropes in handing down this sacrament, since the very nature of sacraments demands them, and since the Fathers most clearly accept them, shall we be accused for using a tropical interpretation in expounding the words of the Lord?

units.la: Allatӕ iam rationes tantum apud nonnullos valuerunt (quӕ est vis veritatis) aduersariorum, vt ea quӕ in hoc sacramento sensibus obvia fiunt, nimirum panem & vinum, signa corporis & sanguinis Christi esse fateantur, hac tamen lege, ut significatas res in sese praesentes habeant. Sed hoc a vero longe alienissimum esse permultis rationibus ostenditur.
units.tr: Although the arguments of our opponents have carried some weight with certain people (such is the power of truth), so that they admit that the things which appear to the senses in this sacrament, namely bread and wine, are signs of the body and blood of Christ, yet only on this condition: that the things signified are present in themselves. But that this is very far from the truth is shown by very many arguments.

units.la: VERBORVM Christi tropus non exigit corporis & sanguinis eius realem & substantialem praesentiam.
units.tr: That the trope of Christ's words does not require a real and substantial presence of his body and blood.

units.la: Primum scripturae divinae tradunt Christum quo ad humanam naturam hinc abisse, eius in caelum ascensionem, ut in articulo fidei continetur statuunt. Asserunt Christum dixisse nos eum non semper nobiscum habituros, verum oportere caelum usq; ad extremum diem illum continere, ut inde tandem ad iudicandum veniat.
units.tr: First, the Scriptures of God teach that Christ, as regards his human nature, departed hence; they affirm his ascension into heaven, as is contained in the article of faith. They assert that Christ said we would not always have him with us, but that it was necessary for heaven to contain him until the last day, so that from there he would at length come to judge.

units.la: Deinde non convenit humano corpori, ut sit eodem tempore in multis locis, nec etiam concedi potest[?] ut praesens sit in mundo citra locum, pugnant enim haec omnino cum definitione humani corporis. Nisi velimus ergo verum Christo adimere corpus, cavendum ne illud in multis locis vel diffusum vel praesens simul esse affirmemus.
units.tr: Next, it does not belong to a human body to be in many places at the same time, nor can it be granted that it is present in the world without place, for these things wholly conflict with the definition of a human body. Unless we wish to take from Christ a true body, we must therefore take care not to affirm that it is diffused in many places or present in several at once.

units.la: Ne id quidem Angelorum, ut ita dicam, essentia, quae mole corporis privatur, habet, ut eodem tempore simul diversis in locis esse possit.
units.tr: Nor does even the essence of angels, so to speak, which is deprived of the bulk of a body, have the ability to be in diverse places at the same time.

units.la: Quin & ipsa Dei natura si esset corporea, haudquaquam evitare posset, quin & partitionem & definitionem admitteret: haec porro cum ita sint, quemadmodum plenissime attestantur Patres, omnino efficitur, ut Christi corpus iis adiunctis atque proprietatibus sit obnoxium.
units.tr: Indeed, even if the nature of God were corporeal, it could by no means avoid admitting both division and definition. Since these things are so, as the Fathers fully attest, it follows entirely that Christ's body is subject to these adjuncts and properties.

units.la: Nec ipsa postulat sacramentorum natura, ut res significatas vel sibi cohaerentes habeant, vel eas in seipsis contineant. An in circumcisione divinum foedus claudebatur? Sane praeterierat, & cum patribus initum fuerat antequam Abrahamo praeciperetur circumcisio: & si quid eius foederis extabat, id totum in mente diuina & fidelium animis retinebatur. In carne vero non ipsum, sed eius signum a Deo mandatum gestabatur. Agnus item Paschalis, transitum Domini quo ad rem in se ipso non claudebat. Quis etiam diceret carnem & sanguinem Domini vel in aqua deserti, vel in manna clausa fuisse, & in aqua baptismi spiritu & gratiam inuisibiliter delitescere? Quod si caete-ris sacramentis non tribuitur, & quidem ex eorum natura, ut res praesentes habeant vel sibi cohaerentes, vel in seipsis clausas, nec de Eucharistia aliter statuere debemus, si nobis eius ratio & proprietas cum caeteris sacramentis constare debet, maxime vero cum de ea praesentia verbum Dei nihil huiusmodi tradi-derit.
units.tr: Nor does the nature of the sacraments itself require that the things signified either cohere with them or be contained within them. Was the divine covenant enclosed in circumcision? Certainly it had passed by, and had been made with the fathers before circumcision was commanded to Abraham; and if any of that covenant remained, it was all retained in the divine mind and in the hearts of believers. In the flesh, however, not the thing itself but its sign was borne, as commanded by God. Likewise the Paschal lamb did not contain the Lord's passing over as far as the thing itself is concerned. Who would also say that the flesh and blood of the Lord were enclosed either in the water of the desert or in the manna, or that in the water of baptism the Spirit and grace lie hidden invisibly? But if this is not attributed to the other sacraments, and indeed not by their nature, namely that they have the things present, either cohering with them or enclosed within them, neither should we decide otherwise about the Eucharist, if its account and property must agree with the other sacraments; especially since the Word of God has delivered nothing of this kind about that presence.

units.la: Praeterea cum Paulus priore ad Corinth. scribat, veteres nobiscum eundem cibum spiritualem comedisse, & eundem spiritualem potum nobiscum bibisse, Carne vero & sanguinem Christi haud quaquam praesentia habuerint, cum nondum extarent, isti vero in Eucharistia praesentia haec statuant, sequitur plane non esse nobis eadem sacramenta cum veteribus contra Pauli sententiam. Symbolis minime conveniunt: Manna enim illi & aquam, nos vero panem & vinum habemus. Rebus etiam significatis sunt diversa, quia illi res significatas absentes, utpote futuras, fide percipiebant, hi vero res cum symbolis praesentes se percipere dicunt. Nullum porro maius discrimen in his sacramentis excogitari potest, quam cum signis tum rebus significatis dissidere. Quin ergo potius cum Paulo dicamus, rebus significatis veterum sacramenta cum nostris eadem esse, quanquam signa sint diversa, & eodem modo nempe fide & spiritu a nobis & illis percipi: illi enim carnem & sanguinem Christi ut pro nobis danda erat, fide percipiebant, nos vero ut iam data, fide & spiritu completimur.
units.tr: Moreover, since Paul writes in his first letter to the Corinthians that the ancients ate with us the same spiritual food and drank with us the same spiritual drink, yet they did not have the flesh and blood of Christ present, since these did not yet exist, while our opponents maintain that these are present in the Eucharist, it plainly follows that we do not have the same sacraments as the ancients, contrary to Paul's judgment. They do not agree in the signs: for they had manna and water, but we have bread and wine. They also differ in the things signified, because they perceived the things signified by faith while absent, as things future, whereas these men say they perceive the things present along with the signs. Indeed, no greater difference can be imagined in these sacraments than to disagree both in the signs and in the things signified. Why, then, should we not rather say with Paul that the sacraments of the ancients are the same as ours in the things signified, although the signs are different, and that both they and we receive them in the same way, namely by faith and the Spirit? For they received the flesh and blood of Christ by faith as it was to be given for us, while we are fed by faith and Spirit as it has already been given.

units.la: Evitari quoq; non posset quin tam impij quàm pij carnem & sanguinem Domini comederent & biberent, si adversariorum admitteretur opinio:id quod aperte refellit Christus author sacramentorum in Euangelio Ioan. cap. 6. ubi carnem & sanguinem suũ fide edi & bibi ait. Fide ergo cum destituantur impij & à Christo alieni, quam communionem quaso habeant cum carne & sanguine Christi? symbola sane tantum ore percipere valent, & ad ipsorum quidem condemnationem, siquidem neq; Christus in eis neq; in Christo ipsi manent.
units.tr: It could not be avoided that the impious as well as the pious would eat and drink the flesh and blood of the Lord, if the opinion of our adversaries were admitted: a thing which Christ, the author of the sacraments, plainly refutes in the Gospel of John, chapter 6, where he says that his flesh and blood are eaten and drunk by faith. Since therefore the impious and those alien from Christ are destitute of faith, what communion, I ask, do they have with the flesh and blood of Christ? They are indeed able to receive only the symbols with the mouth, and that to their own condemnation, since Christ does not dwell in them, nor they in Christ.

units.la: Rogandi sunt etiam isti qui statuunt in hoc sacramento Domini sanguinem praesentem adesse: qua ratione quoue colore sacrificium, ut vocant, suum ausint incruentum appellare? Profecto si Domini sanguine ut Chrysostomus hyperbolicè scripsit, è latere Domini fluentem in suo calice volunt excipi, enitantur quantum volunt sciunt & possunt, quia cruentum potum hauriant nunquam efficient.
units.tr: Those who hold that the blood of the Lord is present in this sacrament must also be asked: by what reasoning, or with what colour, do they dare to call their so-called sacrifice unbloody? Truly, if they wish to catch in their chalice the blood of the Lord flowing from the side of the Lord, as Chrysostom wrote hyperbolically, let them strive as much as they like, and as much as they know and can, they will never manage to drink bloody drink.

units.la: Est verò & illa pugnantium natura, ut de eodem subiecto nunquam simul, hoc est eodem tempore affirmari possint. Quaobrem Christi corpus cum sursum tum deorsum, visibile ac invisibile, unum & multa, mortale simul & immortale, fractu & integrum simul esse non potest. Hanc rationem nobis non finximus, sed hausimus à Christo, ab Angelis, Apostolis, Patribus, & ipsa natura. Contestantur enim hi omnes haec nequaquam simul esse posse. Porro longum esset referre quot in locis & scriptis suis patres, hanc Domini secundum carnem absentiam asseuerent.
units.tr: Moreover, it is the nature of contradictories that they can never be affirmed of the same subject at the same time, that is, at one and the same moment. Therefore the body of Christ cannot be both above and below, visible and invisible, one and many, mortal and immortal at once, broken and whole at once. We did not invent this reasoning, but drew it from Christ, from the angels, the apostles, the Fathers, and nature itself. For all these testify that these cannot be simultaneous. Indeed, it would take too long to recount in how many places and writings the Fathers affirm this absence of the Lord according to the flesh.

units.la: Quasi verò etiam hæc ab istis iactata & propugnata praesentia carnis & sanguinis Domini in Eucharistia dū ipsa peragitur, vel maiorem vel praestantiorem, vel ullam aliam nobis adferre possit utilitatem, quam non ex perceptione spirituali, quae uti sæpè diximus, fide ac mente peragitur, assequamur.
units.tr: As if this presence of the flesh and blood of the Lord in the Eucharist, which they have thrust forward and defended while the rite itself is performed, could bring us any greater or more excellent benefit, or any other benefit at all, than we obtain from spiritual perception, which, as we have often said, is carried out by faith and mind.

units.la: Illud postremò quaerimus ab aduersarijs nostris: An corpus Domini absq; sanguine in pane & sanguinem in vino absq; corpore statuant. Hoc si dicant Christi naturam humanam per duas mysterij partes distrahunt, quod citra impietatem committi non potest, cum sanguis & corpus in natura humana Christi, coniunctione perpetua sint unita, sin verò dixerint ea simul esse, at suas ac suas nescio quas concomitantias finxerint, id saltem effu-gere non poterunt, quin corpus Christi congeminent, totum videlicet sub pane totumq; sub vino, vel quemadmodum volunt sub eorum accidentibus constituentes.
units.tr: Finally, we ask our adversaries this: do they hold the body of the Lord to be in the bread without blood, and the blood to be in the wine without body? If they say this, they divide the human nature of Christ into two parts of the mystery, which cannot be done without impiety, since blood and body in the human nature of Christ are united by a perpetual bond. But if they say they are together, then, having devised I know not what concomitances of their own, they will at least be unable to escape multiplying the body of Christ, namely wholly under the bread and wholly under the wine, or establishing it, as they wish, under their accidents.

units.la: Accedit postremò, verbis Christi minus quàm sit in partibus sacramenti de illis pronunciari, cùm de pane solum corpus & de vino tantùmmodo sanguinem prædicent.
units.tr: Finally, it is added that the words of Christ are spoken less fully about the parts of the sacrament than they should be, since they declare the body only of the bread and the blood only of the wine.

units.la: Hæc præcipua & summa sunt capita quæ in libro meæ de-fensionis contra Gardinerum continentur, quoad nostræ par-tis argumenta & confirmationes attinet. Nunc verò id reli-quum est, ut nonnulla dicta seu certas quasdam sententias candido lectori proponam, ex quibus non tantùm argumenta nostra propemodum omnia deducuntur, verumetiam rationes adversariorum facilè dissolui possunt, atque tota hæc disceptatio tum dilucida tum facilis euadit.
units.tr: These are the chief and principal heads contained in the book of my defence against Gardiner, as far as the arguments and confirmations of our side are concerned. What remains now is that I set before the candid reader certain sayings or fixed opinions, from which almost all our arguments are derived, and by which the reasonings of the adversaries can easily be dissolved, and this whole dispute becomes both clear and easy.

units.la: Christus in sacra Cœna panem ipsum corpus suum, & vi-num sanguinem suum appellauit. Qui fit ut verba eius, Hoc est corpus meum, simpliciter & absq; Tropo accipi nequeant, siquidem nec panis & vinum proprie & verè corpus & sanguis Christi esse possunt.
units.tr: In the holy Supper Christ called the bread his body and the wine his blood. Hence it comes about that his words, "This is my body," cannot be taken simply and without a trope, since neither bread nor wine can properly and truly be the body and blood of Christ.

units.la: Hæc verba, Hoc est corpus meum, &, Hic est sanguis meus, tropicæ sunt dicendi formulæ, quibus Dominus ea quæ signifi-cantur, de symbolis externis pronunciauit.
units.tr: These words, "This is my body" and "This is my blood," are figurative forms of speech, by which the Lord pronounced of the external symbols the things that are signified.

units.la: Edere carnem seu corpus Christi, & bibere eius sanguinem, est credere, hæc pro nobis in precium redemptionis fuisse data, & istis quà pro nobis in cruce oblata fuerunt coniungi.
units.tr: To eat the flesh or body of Christ, and to drink his blood, is to believe that these things were given for us as the price of redemption, and to be joined to those things which were offered for us on the cross.

units.la: Christi natura humana ab ascensu in cœlum usq; ad extre-mum eius aduentum, quo mundum iudicabit, nusquam alibi est quàm in cœlis.
units.tr: The human nature of Christ, from his ascension into heaven until his final coming, when he will judge the world, is nowhere else than in heaven.

units.la: In eucharistiæ fideli sumptione corpori & sanguini Christi nō tantum aio [?] seu mente per fidem copulamur, sed spiritus, gratiæ ac virtutis dni nostri participes euadimus, nō sanè vi operis, sed ex ipsius bonitate, ac fideli promissione, cui fidelè assensum communi-cando præbemus.
units.tr: In the faithful reception of the Eucharist we are joined by faith not only in soul or mind to the body and blood of Christ, but we become partakers of the Spirit, grace and power of our Lord; not indeed by the force of the work, but from his goodness and faithful promise, to which we give faithful assent by believing.

units.la: Impij homines ipsam Christi carnem & sanguinem haud-quaquam comedunt & bibunt, nisi quatenus externa signa, panem inquam & vinum, quæ suo quodam modo sunt & dicuntur corpus & sanguis Christi, usurpant.
units.tr: Impious men do not at all eat and drink the very flesh and blood of Christ, except insofar as they take the external signs, I mean bread and wine, which in a certain manner are and are called the body and blood of Christ.

units.la: Christo non minus in Baptismo iungimur quàm in Eucha-ristia, quare par utrobiq; illius præsentia & perceptio nimirum spiritualis ponenda est.
units.tr: We are joined to Christ no less in Baptism than in the Eucharist; wherefore his presence and reception must be held to be equally spiritual in both.

units.la: Patres in veteri Testamento corpus & sanguinem Christi, quod ad rem ipsam attinet, non secus ac nos edebant & bibebant.
units.tr: The Fathers under the Old Testament ate and drank the body and blood of Christ, so far as the thing itself is concerned, no differently than we do.

units.la: In sacra Cæna fideles corpus & sanguinem Domini verè sumunt, at spiritualiter, hoc est fide quo ad mentem atq; animũ.
units.tr: In the holy Supper the faithful truly take the body and blood of the Lord, but spiritually, that is, by faith in mind and soul.

units.la: Corpora nostra corpore ac sanguine Christi suo quodam modo aluntur, & ad æternam vitam instaurantur.
units.tr: Our bodies are nourished in a certain way by the body and blood of Christ, and are restored to eternal life.

units.la: Nos ipsi fideli participatione Cænæ Domini quodam genere spiritualis mutationis, in corpus Christi alimur & propemodum transelementamur.
units.tr: By the faithful participation in the Lord's Supper we ourselves are fed into the body of Christ, and are almost transelemented, by a certain kind of spiritual change.

units.la: Per incarnationem filij Dei, carne & sanguine cum eo communicamus, quandoquidem natura nostra verè ab eo assumpta creditur. Et vicissim dum communicando fide amplestimur corpus eius & sanguinem, quæ pro nobis in mortem data sunt, eorum spiritualiter efficimur participes.
units.tr: Through the incarnation of the Son of God we communicate with him in flesh and blood, since our nature is believed to have been truly assumed by him. And conversely, while by faith in communion we embrace his body and blood, which were given for us unto death, we are made spiritually partakers of them.

units.la: Sermo diuinarum literarum, vel auditus, vel lectus quatenus à nobis fide recipitur, corpus Christi est & panis, quo animi nostri nutriuntur.
units.tr: The word of the divine writings, whether heard or read, insofar as it is received by us in faith, is the body of Christ and the bread by which our souls are nourished.

units.la: Cœtus credentium est corpus Christi, cuius ipse caput & nos membra cum sumus, tum dicimur.
units.tr: The assembly of believers is the body of Christ, of which he is the head and we are said to be the members, when we are so.

units.la: Pauperes & oppressi pro Christi nomine sunt eius corpus. Hinc illa vox Paulo, Quid me persequeris?
units.tr: The poor and the oppressed for the name of Christ are his body. Hence that word to Paul: Why are you persecuting me?

units.la: Miracula interdum edita circa Eucharistiæ symbola, neq; transsubstantiationem elementorum eius, neq; præsentiam corporis realem & substantialem, vt ita dixerim, probant.
units.tr: Miracles sometimes performed around the symbols of the Eucharist prove neither the transubstantiation of its elements nor a real and substantial presence of the body, if I may so put it.

units.la: Corpus Christi spiritualiter adesse communicantibus non significat invisibiliter quidem, sed tamen proprie adesse, ut Pa-pistæ dicunt. Sed quod fidei nostræ ac spiritui præsens fiat, non secus atq; mors illius, quam vere credimus, & bona futuræ vitæ quæ spe certissima expectamus, quarum rerum præsentia tantum ad fidem & spiritum nostrum referri potest.
units.tr: That the body of Christ is spiritually present to those who communicate does not mean that it is present invisibly indeed, but nonetheless properly, as the Papists say. Rather, it is made present to our faith and spirit, just as his death, which we truly believe, and the good things of the future life, which we await with most certain hope, are; and the presence of these things can be referred only to our faith and spirit.

units.la: Aduersarij qui de sua consecratione panis & vini tam mul-ta loquuntur, an precibus an verbis ea perficiatur expedire non possunt.
units.tr: Our opponents, who speak so much about the consecration of bread and wine by themselves, cannot explain whether it is effected by prayers or by words.

units.la: In Eucharistia nullum aliud sacrificium admittimus quàm gratiarum actionis, precum & nostri ipsorum oblationis, hæc vero non tantum à ministro, sed etiam à plebe communicante offerri.
units.tr: In the Eucharist we admit no other sacrifice than that of thanksgiving, prayers and the offering of ourselves; and these are offered not only by the minister but also by the communicating people.

units.la: Sacrificium item ibi esse damus, quatenus veri sacrificij commemoratio ibi fit. Et sacramenta, id est, externa symbola, quæ proponuntur, eiusdem veri sacrificij signa sunt, & illud communicantibus ex instituto Domini referunt.
units.tr: We likewise grant that there is a sacrifice there, insofar as a commemoration of the true sacrifice is made there. And the sacraments, that is, the external symbols which are set forth, are signs of that same true sacrifice, and by the Lord's institution they refer it to those who communicate.

units.la: Quas iam commemoraui sententias prudens & candidus lector mei libri, in eo deprehendet non tantum fuisse tractatas, imò etiam multis cum scripturæ, tum patrum testimonijs confirmatas. Quare si ei cordi fuerit totam istam controuersiam, ceu in tabella quadã ob oculos habere, perspicuè ac dilucidè quodammodo pictam, sententias hasce cumprimis, deinde rationes quas in hac Epitome attuli, cogitatione attenta frequen-tiâ, repetitione faciat sibi quàm familiarissimas.
units.tr: The opinions which I have now recalled, the prudent and candid reader of my book will find in it not only treated, but also confirmed by many testimonies both of Scripture and of the Fathers. Therefore, if it be his care to keep this whole controversy before his eyes, as it were in a certain table, painted in some manner clearly and plainly, let him make these opinions above all, and then the arguments which I have brought forward in this Epitome, by attentive thought, frequent repetition, and reiteration, his most familiar possession.

units.la: Nam & inde ut spero, proficiet, nec eum opera collocata, unquam pœnitebit.
units.tr: For from this, as I hope, he will profit, and the work once undertaken will never cause him regret.

units.la: CONFESSIO SEV SENTENTIA D. PETRI MARTYRIS VERMILII de Coena Domini, exhibita amplissimo Senatui Argentinensi, cum[?] uocaretur Tigurum, Anno M.D.LVI.
units.tr: THE CONFESSION, OR OPINION, OF MASTER PETER MARTYR VERMIGLI on the Lord's Supper, presented to the most distinguished Senate of Strasbourg when he was called to Zurich, in the year 1556.

units.la: SERVATOR noster Iesus Christus duabus naturis constat in vna eademq; persona seu hypostasi coniunctis, nec his quidem vel cofusis aut permixtis, sed proprietatibus & conditionibus vtriusq; saluis & integris. Ideoq; Christi diuinitati quae infinita est, & nullis mensuris aut terminis circumscribitur, vt sit vbique, citra controuersiam conceditur. Humanitati vero ex ipsius natura & veritate, ita circumscriptio, termini & fines debentur, vt nec vbiq; neq; absq; certo aliquo loco esse possit: non sane imbecillitate diuinae potentiae, sed naturae humanae perpetua immutabilitate conditione. Sicut enim fieri non potest, vt vel numerus ternarius sit senarius, vel vt res heri gesta sit infecta, sic non est possibile, vt, quod est humanum corpus, non sit humanum corpus, cuius definitio necessario magnitudinem, partes distinctas, & membra comprehendit. Quamobrem quicunq; illud fundunt, & tam late patere volunt, quam diuinum verbum, & ob id, vel vbique, vel in multis locis esse, id quod est humanum corpus, non esse humanum corpus affirmant, & quod est creatum, id dicunt nō esse creatu-ram. Quia nulli creaturae conuenit, cum sit finita, eodem tempore in multis locis esse. Christum vero, quo ad naturam humanam Ecclesia creaturam esse ex verbo Dei nunquam dubitauit. Christus igitur, qua homo est, mundum reliquit, a nobis corpore praesens non habetur: cum eo enim ascendit in coelum, quod eum continere seu accipere oportet, vsq; ad tempora restitutionis omnium, vt Petrus in Actis apostolicis cap. 3. docuit.
units.tr: Our Saviour Jesus Christ consists of two natures joined together in one and the same person or hypostasis, yet not confused or mixed, but with the properties and conditions of each kept safe and whole. Therefore it is granted without controversy that the divinity of Christ, which is infinite and bounded by no measures or limits, is everywhere. But humanity, by its own nature and truth, is owed circumscription, limits and boundaries, so that it cannot be everywhere, nor without some definite place. This is not from any weakness of the divine power, but from the perpetual and unchangeable condition of human nature. For just as the number three cannot be six, or what happened yesterday cannot be undone, so it is not possible that what is a human body should not be a human body; its definition necessarily includes magnitude, distinct parts and members. Wherefore those who stretch the human nature of Christ so widely as they wish the divine Word to extend, and on that account affirm that what is a human body is either everywhere or in many places, and say that what is created is not a creature, since no creature, being finite, can be in many places at the same time. But the Church has never doubted, from the word of God, that Christ as to his human nature is a creature. Christ therefore, as man, has left the world, and is not had present with us in body; for he ascended into heaven with that body, which must contain or receive him until the times of the restoration of all things, as Peter taught in the third chapter of the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: Sacramentum Eucharistiae sic institutum a Christo seruatore seruatore nostro fateor, ut verbis eius adhibitis, quæ communionem veram fidelium cum eo pollicentur, & symbolis interpositis panis & vini, quæ spiritus sanctus, dum sacra Cœna peragitur, quò ad fideles, efficacia instrumenta sunt, fides in nobis excitetur, qua vere, non ficte animo apprehendamus, & corpus & sanguinem eius, ut pro nobis in mortem & crucem tradita sunt, in remissionem peccatorum. Quæ sanè perceptio, licet rerum absentium sit & animo fiat, non tamen ipsi animo tantum prodest, verum & ad corpus sumentium redundat, ita ut vi quadam sanctificationis, coniunctionisq; spiritualis capax fiat beatæ resurrectionis, & æternæ vitæ. Quare neq; in symbolis, neq; in ipsis communicantibus, realem aut substantialem, corporalemve corporis Christi præsentiam admitto, neq; possum agnoscere, cùm tamen communionem & participationem, corporis & sanguinis eius, communicantibus dari spiritualem, non dubitem, sed affirmem, quæ nihilominus & ante sacramenti manducationem habeatur, fidei vero exercitio in comedendo mysterio crescat. Quia nisi ante sumptionem Eucharistiæ carni & sanguini Christi communicaremus, ab eo essemus alieni, fide careremus, & indignè ad mensam spiritualis eius conuiuij adiremus.
units.tr: The sacrament of the Eucharist, as instituted by Christ our Saviour, I confess, is so to be used that, with his words, which promise the true communion of the faithful with him, and with the bread and wine as the signs placed in between, which the Holy Spirit, while the holy Supper is celebrated, makes effective instruments for the faithful, faith is stirred up in us, by which we truly and not feignedly lay hold, in our minds, on his body and blood, as they were delivered for us to death and the cross, for the forgiveness of sins. This reception, although it concerns things absent and is done in the mind, does not benefit the mind alone, but also flows back into the body of those who receive, so that by a certain power of sanctification and spiritual union it becomes capable of the blessed resurrection and eternal life. Therefore I admit neither a real, substantial, nor corporal presence of Christ's body in the signs or in the communicants themselves, nor can I acknowledge one. Yet I do not doubt but affirm that a spiritual communion and participation in his body and blood is given to the communicants, which nonetheless is had even before the eating of the sacrament, and grows through the exercise of faith in eating the mystery. For unless we communicated in the flesh and blood of Christ before the reception of the Eucharist, we would be aliens from him, we would lack faith, and we would approach his spiritual table unworthily.

units.la: Qui fide vera in Christum sunt destituti, quamuis ad symbola percipienda, panem inquam & vinum, accedunt, tamen corporis eius & sanguinis minimè participes fiunt, nisi quatenus illa signa corporis & sanguinis Domini appellatione donantur. Ea.n. connexio est inter signa sacra & res, quæ significantur, ut diuinæ literæ nomina eorum facilè permutent. Nam & caro Christi panis dicitur, ut Ioannis 6. apparet, & panis in sacra Cœna corpus Christi vocatur. Ita etiam Dominus & Iudæi se aiebant comedere Pascha, cum ipsum agnum ederent, quo Pascha, id est transitus, denotabatur. Possem itaq; dare, impios corpus Domini sumere, quia signa eius accipiunt. Et quemadmodum in deserto murmuratores manna edebant, & aquam de petra bibebant, qui tamen cum expectato Christo nullam cõmunionem[?] habebant: sic è diuerso sancti & pij Hebræi, dum vnà cum illis ederent & biberent, spiritualis cibi & potus nobiscum erant participes. Et ne dubitemus, quis ille cibus potusve fuerit, quem communem nobiscum habuerunt, Paulus 1. ad Corin. 10. cap. id explicat, dicens: Bibebant de spirituali consequente eos petra: petra autem erat Christus. Proinde impij, qui eo destituuntur instrumento, quo corpus & sanguis Domini sumuntur, nimirum fide, idcirco non res ipsas quæ significantur, verum symbola tantum earum accipiunt. Qui verò fide sunt instructi, ut corporis ore signa edunt & bibunt, ita fide atq; ore mentis corpus & sanguinem Christi verè apprehendunt.
units.tr: Those who are destitute of true faith in Christ, although they approach to receive the signs, namely bread and wine, nevertheless do not become partakers of his body and blood, except insofar as those signs are given the name of the body and blood of the Lord. For there is such a connection between the holy signs and the things signified that the divine writings readily exchange their names. For the flesh of Christ is called bread, as appears in John chapter 6, and in the holy Supper the bread is called the body of Christ. So too the Lord and the Jews said they were eating the Passover when they ate the lamb itself, by which the Passover, that is the passing over, was signified. I could therefore say that the impious receive the body of the Lord, because they receive its signs. And just as in the desert the murmurers ate manna and drank water from the rock, yet had no communion with the expected Christ, so on the other hand the holy and pious Hebrews, while they ate and drank together with those others, were partakers with us of spiritual food and drink. And lest we doubt what that food or drink was, which they had in common with us, Paul in 1 Corinthians chapter 10 explains it, saying: "They drank of the spiritual rock that followed them; now the rock was Christ." Accordingly the impious, who lack that instrument by which the body and blood of the Lord are received, namely faith, therefore receive not the things themselves that are signified, but only their signs. But those who are furnished with faith, as they eat and drink the signs with the mouth of the body, so with the mouth of the mind, by faith, they truly lay hold on the body and blood of Christ.

units.la: Verba illa, Hoc est corpus meum, à Domino omninò tropicè dicta sunt. Cùm.n. panem in manus acceperit, illumq; ostenderit discumbentibus Apostolis, de eo, si panis esse non desinat, quod suum corpus fuerit, affirmare non potuit. Quis.n. proprio sermone panem dicat esse humanum corpus? profectò, nemo, qui sapiat. Sunt enim eæ formæ naturæq; omninò distinctæ ac separatæ, ita ut vna esse altera minimè queat. Quamobrem cùm sit adhibendus tropus, is deligatur oportet qui sacramentis magis conueniat. Sacramentorum autem definitio recepta est, ut sint sacrarum rerum signa. Proinde sicut victima Hebræorum pascha dicebatur, quod pascha, id est transitum significaret, & Circumcisio Dei fœdus, quod illius esset signum, neq; petra, de qua veteres bibebant, alia ratione dicta sit Christus: ita panis Eucharistiæ appellatur corpus Domini, quod illud significet, non sanè vulgari, scenica, vel theatrali significatione, sed efficaci: quadoquidem spiritus sanctus eo instrumento utitur ad fidem in nobis excitandam, qua corporis Domini communionem promissam apprehendamus. Darem etiam, panem ipsum corpus Christi suo quodam modo esse, ac dici, nempè, quod eius sit sacramentum. Nam & scripturæ & patres de Sacramentis nō raro ita loquuntur. Illi autem, qui contrariam sententiam defendunt, & ipsi forte in verbis allatis tropum concedent, imò necessitate coacti locutionem illam sic explicant, Hoc est corpus meum, id est, cum hoc, nimirum pane, datur corpus meum. Quam ego quoq; interpretationem recipere non grauarer, si dari corpus Christi absq; substantiali vel corporali praesentia intelligerent. Quod quia nolunt admittere, ideo ad ambiguitatem cauendam, illo tropi genere abstineo, & communi ac recepto Significationis, quo & patres antiquitus vtebantur, sum contentus.
units.tr: The words "This is my body" were said by the Lord wholly tropically. For when he had taken the bread in his hands and shown it to the reclining apostles, he could not affirm of it that it was his body, if it did not cease to be bread. For who in his right mind would say in plain speech that bread is a human body? Surely no one. For those forms and natures are wholly distinct and separate, so that the one cannot be the other. Therefore, since a trope must be employed, one ought to choose the one that better suits the sacraments. Now the accepted definition of sacraments is that they are signs of holy things. Accordingly, just as the Hebrews' victim was called the Passover because it signified the Passover, that is the passing over, and circumcision was called God's covenant because it was the sign of it, and the rock from which the ancients drank was called Christ for no other reason, so the bread of the Eucharist is called the body of the Lord because it signifies it, not in some common, theatrical or stage sense, but in an effective sense, since the Holy Spirit uses that instrument to stir up faith in us, by which we may lay hold on the promised communion of the Lord's body. I would even grant that the bread itself is, and is called, the body of Christ in a certain way, namely because it is the sacrament of it. For both the Scriptures and the Fathers often speak of sacraments in this way. But those who defend the opposite opinion, and perhaps themselves concede a trope in the words quoted, but compelled by necessity, explain that mode of speaking as follows: "This is my body," that is, "with this, namely the bread, my body is given." I too would not hesitate to accept that interpretation, if they understood the body of Christ to be given without a substantial or corporal presence. Since they are unwilling to admit this, therefore, to guard against ambiguity, I abstain from that kind of trope, and am content with the common and accepted kind of signification, which the Fathers also used of old.

units.la: In eo controuersiae nostrae status est, quod à multis non existimatur, corpus Christi vere posse communicari, nisi realiter & corporaliter, vt ita loquar, praesens fuerit. Verùm ij meo iudicio vim fidei non satis perceptam habent. Non enim animad-uertunt, per eam praesentia nobis fieri, quae alioqui longissimè distant. Veteres quoq;, quotquot pij erant, vt Paulus attestatur, eundem cibum potumq; spiritualem nobiscum perceperunt, id est, corpus & sanguinem Domini, vt ad Corinthios dicitur. Neq; spirituali veraeq; communioni harum rerum obstabat magna temporum distantia, in qua Christo iam nato haec esse coeperunt. Fide quippe illis praesentia reddebantur. Quid igitur impedient modò locorum spatia, quae inter caelum, vbi Christus degit, & nos intercedunt, quò minus corpore illius ac sanguine verè fruamur, & eis viuificemur? Nihil plane, si fides adsit, quanostri animi verbo Dei & sacramentis adiuti subuehantur in caelum, ibiq; spirituali cibo & potu corporis atq; sanguinis Christi reficiantur, & ad vitam aeternam instaurentur. Dumq; Caelum subinde nomino, metaphora nulla vtor, sed reuera ipsos caelestes orbes intelligo, in quos Christus cùm à nobis ascendit, receptus est, vt sancta scriptura perhibet.
units.tr: The state of our controversy is this: many do not think that the body of Christ can truly be communicated unless he is present really and corporally, if I may so speak. But in my judgment those men do not have a sufficiently grasped power of faith. For they do not notice that through faith a presence is made for us of things which otherwise are very far apart. The ancients too, as many as were pious, as Paul bears witness, received the same spiritual food and drink with us, that is, the body and blood of the Lord, as is said to the Corinthians. Nor did the great distance of time, in which these things began to be before Christ was born, hinder the spiritual and true communion of these things. For by faith they were made present to them. What then now hinders the spaces of place, which lie between heaven, where Christ dwells, and us, from our truly enjoying his body and blood, and being quickened by them? Nothing at all, if faith is present, so that our minds, aided by the word of God and the sacraments, are lifted up into heaven, and there are refreshed with the spiritual food and drink of the body and blood of Christ, and are restored to eternal life. And when I name heaven here and there, I use no metaphor, but truly mean the heavenly orbs themselves, into which Christ, when he ascended from us, was received, as holy Scripture declares.

units.la: Quisq; fidelium, cùm sit Christi membrum, vbicunq; fuerit, habet illum pro capite, & ei verè atq; arctissimè coniungitur, ita vt inde vitam atq; spiritu hauriat, quae sic à diuinitate fluunt, vt per carnem & sanguinem Domini tradita in mortem, ad nos deriuentur. Nil enim Deus caelestium donorum communicat mortalibus, nisi per vnum mediatorem Dei & hominum, hominem[?] Iesum Christum, ut Paulus ad Timotheum ait. Qui fit ut ossa nostra, & carnes nostræ, qua cœlestem regenerationem, & æternam vitam participant, sint ex carnibus eius, & ex ossibus eius, ut Ephesios idem apostolus docuit. Nisi enim ab illis penderent, et spiritualiter illis cohærerent, neq; regenerationem, neq; vitam æternam, neq; spiritum per illa ex Deo ad se traherent. Unde quamuis inter nos & Christi corpus magna locorum spatia interponantur, ab eo tamè pendemus, & illi mirabiliter adiungimur: cumq; spiritualis, arcana & diuina sit ista coniunctio, substantialis & corporalis præsentia corporis & sanguinis eius non requiritur, nosq; illam idcirco non ponimus, quia veritati humanæ naturæ Domini repugnat, & à scripturæ testimonijs clarè discrepat.
units.tr: Every believer, since he is a member of Christ, wherever he may be, has him as his head, and is joined to him truly and most closely, so that he draws life and spirit from him. These flow from the Godhead and are delivered to us through the flesh and blood of the Lord, which were given up to death. For God communicates no heavenly gifts to mortals except through the one mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, as Paul says to Timothy. Hence our bones and our flesh, which share in heavenly regeneration and eternal life, are "of his flesh and of his bones," as the same apostle taught the Ephesians. For unless they depended on him and clung to him spiritually, they would draw neither regeneration, nor eternal life, nor the Spirit from God through him. Therefore, although great distances of place lie between us and the body of Christ, we nonetheless depend on him, and are wonderfully joined to him. And since this conjunction is spiritual, hidden and divine, the substantial and corporeal presence of his body and blood is not required, and we do not affirm it, because it contradicts the truth of the Lord's human nature and clearly disagrees with the testimonies of Scripture.

units.la: In rebus humanis, cum vir in longinquam regionem ob aliquos occurrentes casus proficiscitur, uxore ad tempus domi relicta, non desinit propterea cum illa, ut scripturæ loquuntur, una esse caro. Manet igitur salua eorum vera, propria & legitima coniunctio, licet unus ab altero longissimè absit. Quanto magis Christus, qui Ecclesiæ, ut Apostolus ait, vir est, omnibus suis membris coniunctus manet, licet in cœlum abierit, & corporaliter discesserit?
units.tr: In human affairs, when a husband sets out for a distant region because of some pressing circumstances, leaving his wife at home for a time, he does not on that account cease to be one flesh with her, as the Scriptures put it. Their true, proper and lawful union therefore remains intact, even though the one is far away from the other. How much more does Christ, who is the husband of the Church, as the Apostle says, remain joined to all his members, even though he has gone up into heaven and departed from us bodily?

units.la: Ad istam igitur unionem, quam cum Domino, id est, corpore, sanguine atq; ossibus eius habemus, nō est opus contactu physico, neq; locis coniunctis, continuis aut contiguis, Spiritus tantum & fides adhibenda sunt, quibus toti Christo sponso & seruatori nostro quàm arctissimè copulamur. Qui autem negant veram istam coniunctionem cum carne Christi fieri, & haberi absq; substantiali corporalive ipsius præsentia, videtur potentiæ Dei parum tribuere, cum interea nos perpetuo moneant ad illam respiciendam, quando iudicamus, corpus Christi non posse neq; u-biq;[?], neque multis in locis esse simul. Eo ipsi remedio quod alijs porrigunt, utantur, & illam Dei potentiam concedant, quâ ve-ritas, & nostra pia sententia requirit. Eaq; data nihil detrahetur de humanitate Domini, salua manebit sacramenti natura, & oraculis diuinarum literarum unà consentiemus.
units.tr: For this union, then, which we have with the Lord, that is, with his body, blood and bones, there is no need of physical contact, or of places joined, continuous or contiguous. Only the Spirit and faith are required, by which we are joined as closely as possible to the whole Christ, our bridegroom and saviour. But those who deny that this true communion with the flesh of Christ takes place, and is had apart from his substantial and bodily presence, seem to attribute too little to the power of God, although they constantly warn us to look to that power when we judge that the body of Christ cannot be everywhere, nor in many places at once. Let them use the remedy they offer to others, and concede that power of God which both the truth and our pious view require. Once that is granted, nothing is taken away from the humanity of the Lord, the nature of the sacrament will remain safe, and we shall agree together with the oracles of the divine letters.

units.la: In confessione Augustana, quātum ipse video, nihil est hac de re, quod cum sententia iam exposita non possit conuenire.
