Sed quia ἐν τῷ ῥητῷ καὶ διανοίᾳ, ut manifeste apparet, minimè inter nos conuenimus, ideo quod ex verbo Dei credo atq; intelligo, explicare volui, ne ulli postea verba sibi data esse iuste conqueri possint. Et haec complexus sum paucissimis, de quibus docendo, disputando & scribendo non possum diutius tacere, salua & integra conscientia.
units.tr: In the Augsburg Confession, so far as I can see, there is nothing on this matter that cannot agree with the view already set out. But since we clearly do not agree with one another "in the word and in the meaning" [ἐν τῷ ῥητῷ καὶ διανοίᾳ], I have wished to explain what I believe and understand from the word of God, so that no one can afterwards justly complain that he has been deceived. I have summed these things up very briefly, and on these matters I cannot remain silent any longer in teaching, disputing and writing, while keeping my conscience sound and whole.

units.la: Ideo oro, ut de illa substantiali corporali[?] præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in Cœna, & de cæteris, quæ iam commemoraui, mihi liberum sit, clarè ac dilucidè, quemadmodum sentio, tractare dicto & scripto, cum opportunum fuerit.
units.tr: I therefore beg that I may be free to treat, clearly and plainly, as I think, by word and in writing, when the occasion arises, that substantial and corporeal presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper, and the other matters I have already mentioned.

units.la: Quod si non videatur concedendum, bona gratia & venia vestrarum amplissimarum dominationum, peto, ut missus fiam.
units.tr: But if this should not seem fitting to grant, I ask, by your gracious favour and pardon, most distinguished lords, that I be dismissed.

units.la: SENTENTIA D. PETRI MARTYRIS VERMILII DE PRAESENTIA Corporis Christi in Eucharistia, proposita ab ipso in colloquio Poisiaci habito.
units.tr: THE OPINION OF D. PETER MARTYR VERMILIUS CONCERNING THE PRESENCE OF THE BODY OF CHRIST IN THE EUCHARIST, set forth by him at the colloquy held at Poissy.

units.la: REVERENDI Antistites, ac doctissimi viri cum videretur initus propemodum consensus de corporis Christi præsentia in usu Cœnæ, vobis heri sum professus quæ mea de illo dogmate fides ac sententia esset, quàm ut tum verbis expressi, sic in præsentia de scripto recitare statui, quò certiorem ac magis perspicuam illam vobis faciam. Sentio itaq; corpus Christi reale atq; substantiale tantum in cœlis esse, fideles tamen communicando verum eius corpus, & verum sanguinem quæ pro nobis tradita sunt in crucem, spiri-tualiter & per fidem verè percipere. Quare in pane & vino Cœnæ transubstantionem & consubstantiationem minimè pro-bo. Deinde affirmo nostræ coniunctioni cum corpore ac sangui-ne Christi locorum distantiam non obstare, quoniam Cœna Domini res est cœlestis, & licet ore corporis accipiamus in terris panem & vinum, sacramenta corporis & sanguinis Domini, fide tamen, & ope spiritus sancti animi nostri, quorum impri-mis est hic spiritualis & diuinus cibus, ad cœlum euectli [?], præ-senti corpore ac sanguine Christi fruuntur. Et ideo affero non opus esse statuere corpus Christi verè substantialiter & corpo-raliter adesse vel nobis, vel symbolis præsentia non locali. Res adhæc significatas aio non aliter coniungi symbolis externis, quàm sacramentaliter, quòd ab eis non prophanè ac leuiter, sed ex instituto Domini efficaciter significentur. Hæc est sum-ma fidei meæ quam in hoc dogmate sequor, & idcirco allatas formulas consensus ea ratione admitto, qua referuntur, vel ac-commodari possunt ad sensum iam explicatum: contra quem si quis illas vel rapiat, vel interpretetur, ab eo me pro-fiteor dissidere. Cumque in his formulis fiat mentio substantiæ corpo-ris Christi, per illud nomen, seu vocabulum, nil aliud intelligo, quàm verum Christi corpus. Non enim fides nostra in rem fi-ctam, aut phantasma dirigitur, sed in corpus humanum verum & naturale, quod verbum Dei ex beata virgine assumpsit, & in crucem pro nobis dedit. Unde non est, quod ex ea voce credamur existimare, præsentiam eius realem alibi, quàm in cœlis esse.
units.tr: Reverend prelates and most learned gentlemen, since an agreement on the presence of the body of Christ in the use of the Supper seemed to be almost reached, I declared yesterday what my faith and opinion on that doctrine were. Since I had only expressed them in words then, I have resolved now to read them to you from a written text, so that I may make my position clearer and more plain to you. I hold, therefore, that the body of Christ is real and substantial, and that it is in heaven alone; yet the faithful, by communicating, truly perceive, spiritually and by faith, his true body and true blood, which were given for us and delivered to the cross. For this reason I by no means approve of transubstantiation or consubstantiation in the bread and wine of the Supper. Next I affirm that the distance of places does not stand in the way of our union with the body and blood of Christ, since the Lord's Supper is a heavenly thing. Although we receive bread and wine on earth with our mouth, as the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, nevertheless by faith and by the power of the Holy Spirit our souls, whose first and chief food is this spiritual and divine food, are raised up to heaven and enjoy the present body and blood of Christ. Therefore I maintain that there is no need to hold that the body of Christ is truly, substantially and bodily present to us or to the symbols, with a presence that is not local. I say that the things signified are joined to the external symbols in no other way than sacramentally, in that they are signified by them not carelessly and lightly, but effectually, by the appointment of the Lord. This is the sum of the faith that I follow in this doctrine. Accordingly, I admit the formulas of agreement that have been produced, in the sense in which they are stated, or in which they can be adapted to the sense already explained. If anyone either twists those formulas or interprets them against this sense, I declare that I dissent from him. And when mention is made in these formulas of the substance of the body of Christ, by that name or word I understand nothing other than the true body of Christ. For our faith is not directed to a fictitious thing or a phantasm, but to the true and natural human body, which the Word of God assumed from the blessed Virgin and gave up on the cross for us. Hence there is no reason for anyone to think, from that expression, that his real presence is anywhere other than in heaven.

units.la: Ego Petrus Martyr Vermilius Florentinus hæc manu mea scripsi, & ore proprio sum protestatus coram Reuerendis Dominis collocutoribus.
units.tr: I, Peter Martyr Vermilius of Florence, wrote these things with my own hand, and declared them with my own mouth before the Reverend Lords my fellow colloquists.

units.la: EPISTOLA D. P. MARTY-RIS DE CAUSA EUCHARISTIAE ad amicum quendam, virum magni nominis.
units.tr: THE EPISTLE OF D. P. MARTYR ON THE CAUSE OF THE EUCHARIST, to a certain friend, a man of great name.

units.la: S. D.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: DE regraui, & hominum certaminibus iam prope-modum obcaecata, paucis & dilucide scribere, tu ipse vir clarissime, qui es dicendi Magister optimus, & scribendi peritissimus, apprime nosti quam sit arduu & factu perdifficile. Ideo mirari non desino quae causa fuerit, cur id a me, qui & dicendo & scribendo fere nihil possum, tuis proximis literis petere non sis veritus. Quia tamen rogasti, & ego pro mea in te obseruantia recepi me facturum, per primum, eumq; fidum tabellarium, fidem meam decreui liberare. Quod etiam eo alacrius faciam, quod me sentio ad eum non scribere, qui sit controuersiae ignarus: nam ut video, in Eucharistiae cau-sa iam totus habitas, tantum abest ut in ea hospes dici possis. Cum itaq; de te sic existimem, ita summa capita perstringam, ut ea potius notasse, quam explicare voluisse demonstrem. Tu bo-ni consules, ac si voluntatem tuam minus expleuero, non animum meum in te propensissimum, verum te ipsum qui rogaueris, accusabis.
units.tr: Although the matter has been nearly buried under the controversies and quarrels of men, you, most distinguished man, who are an excellent master of speech and most skilled in writing, know very well how hard and how difficult it is to write briefly and clearly on it. So I cannot stop wondering why you did not hesitate to ask this of me in your last letter, when I can do almost nothing either in speaking or writing. Nevertheless, since you asked, and since I promised out of my regard for you, I have decided to keep my word through the first trustworthy courier. I will do this all the more willingly because I am writing to someone who is not ignorant of the controversy; for, as I see, you already live entirely in the question of the Eucharist, and you could hardly be called a newcomer to it. Therefore, thinking of you as I do, I will touch only the main heads, so as to show that I meant to note them rather than to explain them. You will kindly accept this, and if I do not fully satisfy your wish, you will blame not my very great goodwill toward you but yourself, for having asked.

units.la: Panis & vini μετουσίαν missam facio: quod aduersarij nō minus quàm nos ab ea se profiteantur abhorrere. Nec etiam la-borandum puto, an oratio Domini, qua panem esse corpus suum, & vinum sanguinem suum, dixit, proprijs an figuratis ac ξομ-ναῖς[?] accenseri debeat.
units.tr: I set aside the transubstantiation of bread and wine, which our opponents profess to abhor no less than we do. Nor do I think we need to labour over whether the Lord's words, in which he said that the bread is his body and the wine his blood, should be counted among the proper sayings or the figurative [τροπικαῖς] ones.

units.la: Siquidem illi contra quos disputamus, ad sanitatem vtcunq; reuersi, tropū[?] in ea oratione iam se agnosce-re confitentur: sed ita confitentur, ut corpus & sanguine domi-ni vere, proprie, ac reipsa pani & vino copulet, atq; τῇ μετουσίᾳ Papæ, σωματοσίαν[?] duarum naturam supponant, statuantq; carnem & sanguinem Christi non tantùm in cœlis esse, verumetiam in pane ac vino sacræ Cœnæ adesse præsentia. Nec verentur Domini corpus, quamuis humanum sit, affirmare simul eodemq; tempore in multis locis esse. Imò progrediuntur eò, ut illud æque ac naturam diuinam pronuntient esse ybiq;. Deinde præsentiam illi corpori tribuunt, quæ locum minimè occupet. Ego verò Christi naturā humanam semper certo quodam loco fuisse compre-hensam dico, quem ita occuparit, ut eodem tempore alibi non fue-rit. Euangelica historia illum tradit aliquando fuisse in Ga-lilæa, nonnunquam Hierosolymis, interdum in domo Simonis, & alias in Bethania. Vnde constat ab ea certum aliquem locum datum esse corpori Christi. Simul autem alibi non fuisse aperte demonstrat, cum Christum dixisse perhibeat, Lazarum fuisse mortuum, & se gaudere quòd ibi non fuerit: Quibus vtiq; ver-bis ita se ostendit in illo fuisse itinere, ut alibi non fuerit. Ange-lus quoq; dixit mulieribus, cum Dñi corpus in sepulchro quære-rent, Surrexit, Non est hic: quo declarauit, ita è sepulchro dis-cessisse, ut ibi corpore non amplius adesset. Et Petrus Act. 3. de illo enuntiauit: Quem oportet quidem cœlum accipere vsque in tempora instaurationis omnium, &c. Si futurus est in cœlis quoad naturam humanam, ut Apostolus dixit, vsq; ad extremum diem, quid eius carnem & sanguinem in terris quærimus? At de Apostolo quid loquor? Ipse Christus discipulis aiebat se re-linquere mundum, & ab illis discedere. Atq; monuit fore, ut perpetuò secum pauperes, non autem illum essent habituri. Pro-inde sic imbutus & instructus diuinis oraculis, humanam Christi naturam in cœlis ab inferiori mundo sepositam vsq; ad mundi finem agere credo, eamq; tunc ad orbem iudicandum inde rur-sus esse venturam, ut ab angelis moniti sunt Apostoli, & nos ar-ticulo nostræ fidei profitemur. Hoc est, ut summatim dicam, quod sentio de loco & præsentia corporis & sanguinis Domini.
units.tr: For those against whom we dispute, though they have somewhat returned to sound sense, now confess that there is a trope in that saying; but they confess it in such a way that they join the body and blood of the Lord truly, properly and really to the bread and wine, and by the transubstantiation of the Papists they assume a double nature, and hold that the flesh and blood of Christ are not only in heaven but also present in the bread and wine of the holy Supper. Nor do they shrink from affirming that the body of the Lord, though it is human, is at the same time in many places. Indeed they go so far as to declare that it is everywhere, just as the divine nature is. Further, they attribute to that body a presence that does not occupy any place. But I say that the human nature of Christ has always been contained in a certain definite place, which it so occupied that at the same time it was not elsewhere. The gospel history tells us that at one time he was in Galilee, at another in Jerusalem, sometimes in the house of Simon, and at other times in Bethany. From this it is clear that a certain definite place was given to the body of Christ. At the same time it plainly shows that he was not elsewhere, since it reports that Christ said that Lazarus had died, and that he rejoiced that he had not been there. By these words he showed that he was on that journey in such a way that he was not elsewhere. The angel also said to the women, when they were seeking the body of the Lord in the sepulchre, "He is risen, he is not here"; by which he declared that he had left the sepulchre in such a way that his body was no longer there. And Peter, Acts 3, spoke of him: "Whom indeed heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things," etc. If he is to be in heaven as regards his human nature until the last day, as the Apostle said, why do we seek his flesh and blood on earth? But why do I speak of the Apostle? Christ himself told his disciples that he was leaving the world and departing from them. And he warned that the poor would always be with them, but he himself would not. Therefore, taught and instructed by the divine oracles in this way, I believe that the human nature of Christ is kept in heaven, set apart from the lower world, until the end of the world; and that from there it will come again to judge the world, as the apostles were told by angels, and as we profess in the article of our faith. This, to sum up, is what I think about the place and presence of the body and blood of the Lord.

units.la: Qui autē è diuerso cælum ybiquarium sibi formant & singunt, quasi eius materia sit mollis instar cerae, ac figmenta eorum sequatur facillime, quocunque illam ducere uisum fuerit: quin dni corpus uel in pluribus locis simul, uel, quod multo audacius est, ubique adesse praedicat: qui etiam illud pani & uino sacrae Coenae copulant, ubiubi gentium habeatur: qui deniq; ibi absq; loco & inuisibiliter adesse praesens decernunt: eos oēs precor, obsecro & obtestor, ut haec sua praeclara & mirabilia commenta, ne portenta dixerim, in diuinis literis tandem aliquando conscripta demonstret: quod si fecerint, ingenuè uicisse confitebimur. Sed quia, ut certò scio, praestare non poterunt, illos porrò sedulò moneo, ut ex capite suo noua dogmata nouosq; articulos fidei cudere desinant, & nobis ea obtrudere credenda, quae domi eorum nata sint, non aut in agro scripturarum diuinarum creuerint. Non me latet eos in hac tota ratione id nobis exprobrare, quòd nō Theologos, uerum naturales Philosophos agamus. Etenim fatentur, quae dicimus, ex decretis naturae, cum uera esse tum necessaria: uerum ea mysteria, quae diuina & caelestia cum sint, naturam multis modis uincunt, eius regulis & decretis non oportere subijci. Sed cum in eis ampliectendis & consyderandis ratio nostra offenditur, diuinam potestatem, quae immensa est, nos tum debere intueri. Caeterum haec diluere nō est difficile. Primùm, quo sanctarum scripturarum testimonia sequimur, ut illa recesuimus, eo nos minimè Philosophiam, sed uerbum Dei sequi testamur. Deinde, si naturam audimus, ubi sermonibus Dei non repugnat, nihil facimus Chri-stiana Theologia indignum. Habet siquidem natura Deū authorem ac uindicem, & idcirco eius regulae ac decreta non ex ea, uerum ex ipso Deo proficiscuntur, ideoq; conuellenda & refige-da non sunt, quoad nō offendatur, uerbū diuinis literis proditum eis repugnare. Hanc naturae uocē maximus optimusq; Theologus Augustinus in epist. ad Dardanū audiuit, cum inquit, Spa-tia locorū tolle à corporibus, & nusquā erunt: & quia nusquam erunt, nec erunt. Idq; nō pronuntiauit, de natura uel corporibus Physicis agens, uerum scribens ex professo de Anima & corpore Dñi. Eandem naturæ vocem & Cyrillus audivit, qui scripsit in suis Dialogis de Trinitate, Ipsam Dei naturā, si partibus esset, ut quidā sentiebant, omninò fore quanta, nec nō in loco, neq; posse circumscriptione euitare. In nostra itaq; sententia tuenda, verbū imprimis Dei amplectimur, audimus naturæ vocē, dū suo authori nō adversatur, & unà cū patribus rectè sentientibus facimus. Ut aut ad potentiā Dei confugiamus, in hac propositā cōtrouer-sia opus nō habemus. Cōmonefacimus attamen pios, diuinā om-nipotentiam, quā unà cū omnibus fidelibus credimus, nō esse ci-tra omnem exceptionē admittendam. Nam & Paulus excipit, Deū non posse negare seipsum. Excipitur itē passim, à Deo fieri non posse, ut quæ facta sunt infecta reddantur. In scholis etiam Theologicis definitū est, ea Deum nō posse facere, quæ, ut loquū-tur, contradictionem implicant: quod cum vitio rerū fiat, nō Dei ulla infirmitate, de summa illius potentia nihil minuitur. Atte-ndum præterea nō paucos hæreticos isto suffugio esse usos, cum illorū prava et insana dogmata refellerentur à sanctis patribus, nō solum ut absurda, verumetiā ut impossibilia. Respondebat.n. ut se tuerentur, Omnia Deo esse possibilia. Neq; manus illis da-re propterea cogimur, quòd Christus de pane dixerit: Hoc est corpus meum, & de vino, Hic est sanguis meus: quia cum & no-stra & illorum eius orationis interpretatio extet, locus ambi-guus redditur: quamuis nobis expositio nostra est certissima. Argumentum vero quod ab ambiguo deducatur, omnes no-runt quàm sit retusum atque imbecille.
units.tr: Those, on the other hand, who fashion and form for themselves a heaven that is everywhere, as if its matter were soft like wax and followed their figments most easily, wherever they wished to lead it; who preach that the Lord's body is present in many places at once, or, what is far more bold, is everywhere; who also join it to the bread and wine of the holy Supper wherever they are found among the nations; and who finally decree that it is present there without place and invisibly: all these, I beg, entreat and call upon, to show their famous and wonderful inventions, not to say monstrosities, written down at last somewhere in the divine letters; and if they do so, we will confess that they have won fairly. But since, as I know for certain, they will not be able to do this, I further earnestly warn them to stop forging new doctrines and new articles of faith out of their own head, and to stop thrusting on us as things to be believed those things that were born in their own homes and have not grown in the field of the divine Scriptures. I am not unaware that in this whole argument they reproach us with being not theologians but natural philosophers. For they admit that what we say follows from the decrees of nature, and is both true and necessary; but they say that those mysteries, being divine and heavenly, surpass nature in many ways and ought not to be subjected to its rules and decrees; and that when our reason is offended in embracing and considering them, we must rather look to the divine power, which is immense. However, it is not hard to refute this. First, by following the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, we declare that in doing so we are not following philosophy at all, but the Word of God. Second, if we listen to nature where it does not conflict with the words of God, we do nothing unworthy of Christian theology. For nature has God as its author and defender, and therefore its rules and decrees come not from itself but from God himself, and so they should not be overthrown or rejected, unless it is shown that the word revealed in the divine letters contradicts them. The greatest and best theologian, Augustine, heard this voice of nature in his letter to Dardanus, when he said: "Take away the spaces of places from bodies, and they will be nowhere; and because they will be nowhere, they will not be at all." He did not say this while discussing nature or physical bodies, but while writing expressly about the soul and the body of the Lord. Cyril too heard the same voice of nature, who wrote in his Dialogues on the Trinity that the very nature of God, if it had parts, as some thought, would necessarily be of a certain size, and also in a place, and could not avoid circumscription. In defending our view, then, we first embrace the Word of God; we listen to the voice of nature so long as it does not oppose its Author; and in this we agree with the Fathers who thought rightly. As for taking refuge in the power of God, we have no need of it in this controversy. Nevertheless we remind the godly that the divine omnipotence, which we believe together with all the faithful, is not to be admitted without any exception. For Paul too makes an exception: God cannot deny himself. Elsewhere it is also excepted that God cannot make what has been done undone. In the theological schools it has been defined that God cannot do those things which, as they say, involve a contradiction; and since this comes from the nature of things and not from any weakness in God, nothing is taken away from his supreme power. Moreover, it should be noted that not a few heretics have used this refuge when their perverse and insane doctrines were refuted by the holy Fathers, not only as absurd but also as impossible. For they replied, in order to defend themselves, that all things are possible with God. Nor are we forced to give way to them because Christ said of the bread, "This is my body," and of the wine, "This is my blood," since both our interpretation and theirs of that saying exist, and so the passage is rendered ambiguous, although our exposition is most certain to us. But everyone knows how feeble and weak is the argument that is drawn from an ambiguous passage.

units.la: Quid igitur? dices. An cœnā Dñi absq; illius corpore ac san-guine habere docebis? Quomodo præterea hæc aut manducari aut bibi, si præsentia reipsa non adsunt, probabis? Porrò scriptura utrūq; testatur, nos in sacra cœna carne ac sanguine Christi ve-sci ac potari. Ut de eo antea dicā, de quo interrogor posterius, cor-pus et sanguine dñi Spiritualiter edi ac bibi affirmo, id est animi ore, qui spiritu & fide sit imbutus. Dum n. in sacra cœna mente agitamus dñi mortē, ac syncera fide ista redimendorū nostrū causa in crucem fuisse impensa fideliter credimus, ea magno nostro bono edimus & bibimus. Nam sunt animis nostris instar optimi cibi & saluberrimi potus, eamq; fidem excitat Deus in suis per spiritu sancto, duobus adhibitis externis instrumentis, verbo inquam, & panis ac vini elementis. Qui ergo credunt & fide amplectuntur, Dñi carnē & sanguinē fuisse nostrae salutis causa in morte tradita, ea spiritualiter comedunt & spiritualiter bibunt. Proinde fatemur ad esum & potationem Physica & propria, exigi esculentae ac poculentae rei praesentia: alioqui res absentes nec edi neq; bibi posse. Vicissim aut negamus e spirituali esu & potu elici seu concludi, ea quae ἀλληγορικῶς dicuntur edi & bibi, corporaliter ac proprie adesse praesentia. Fide aut constare carnis Christi manducatione, ipse apud Ioan. 6. cap. luculentissime testatus est. Quare is Euangelista, cum rem tota ibi a se iudicaret affatim explicatam, in historia postremae Coenae, quomodo externa signa panis & vini adiecta fuerint, minime commemorauit. Adhaec idem ex eo colligitur, quod ad verum & proprium Christi corpus, vera propriaq; manducatio accommodari non potest, cum iam dilacerari cominui & moli nequeat. Ore quidē corporis & panis & vinum proprie comeduntur ac bibitur, quae suo modo caro & sanguis Christi dicuntur, quod sint earum rerum externa signa: ideo vtcunq; ore dici possumus edere ac bibere corpus & sanguinem Dñi. Unde Cyprianus & Augustinus, cum de harum rerum quae significantur esu agerent, nimirum spirituali, prudenter dixerunt, Quid paras dente & ventrem? Crede & manducasti. Non itaq; opus est corpus & sanguinem Dñi e coelis in terras demitti, vel adhuc in mundo versari, vt nostrae Coenae se admisceant, sed nostras mentes verbo Dei, & signis externis comonefactas, oportet ad coelum per fidem subuehi, quo sacro isto cibo vescantur atq; alantur. Hinc etiam consequitur, illos qui fide prorsus desituuntur, corpus & sanguinem Christi minime percipere, quod ea (vt dixi) fide tantum & spiritu comedantur & bibantur. Symbola quidem externa ij comedunt & bibunt, res autem significatas minime attingunt: sicuti qui obcaecati sunt, lucem & colorem, quæ oculis capiuntur, minimè possunt recipere.
units.tr: But what then, you will say? Will you teach that the Lord's Supper can be had without his body and blood? And how will you prove that these are eaten or drunk if they are not really present? Yet Scripture testifies to both, that in the holy Supper we eat and drink the flesh and blood of Christ. To answer first the question I am asked last: I affirm that the body and blood of the Lord are eaten and drunk spiritually, that is, by the mouth of the soul, which is imbued with the Spirit and with faith. When in the holy Supper we bring to mind the Lord's death, and faithfully believe with sincere faith that it was undertaken for the redemption of us, we eat and drink those things to our great good. For they are to our souls like the best food and the most wholesome drink. God stirs up this faith in his people through the Holy Spirit, using two external instruments, namely the word and the elements of bread and wine. Those, therefore, who believe and embrace by faith that the flesh and blood of the Lord were given up in death for the cause of our salvation, eat and drink them spiritually. Accordingly, we confess that for eating and drinking in the physical and proper sense the presence of the food and drink itself is required; otherwise absent things could be neither eaten nor drunk. Conversely, we deny that from a spiritual eating and drinking it follows or is concluded that those things which are said [ἀλληγορικῶς] to be eaten and drunk are present bodily and properly. That the eating of Christ's flesh consists in faith, he himself has most clearly testified in John 6. Hence that evangelist, since he had there fully explained the whole matter himself, did not at all mention, in the account of the last Supper, how the external signs of bread and wine were added. Moreover, the same is gathered from this, that a true and proper eating cannot be applied to the true and proper body of Christ, since it can no longer be torn, ground down or chewed. Indeed, with the mouth the body, bread and wine are properly eaten and drunk, and these are in their own way called the flesh and blood of Christ, because they are the external signs of those things; therefore in some way we can rightly say that we eat and drink the body and blood of the Lord with the mouth. Hence Cyprian and Augustine, when they spoke of the eating of those things which are signified, namely the spiritual eating, wisely said: Why do you prepare teeth and belly? Believe, and you have eaten. There is therefore no need for the body and blood of the Lord to be sent down from heaven to earth, or to remain still in the world, so as to mingle themselves with our Supper; rather our minds, reminded by the word of God and by the external signs, must be carried up to heaven by faith, where they may feed on and be nourished by that holy food. From this it also follows that those who utterly lack faith do not at all receive the body and blood of Christ, since these are eaten and drunk (as I have said) by faith and the Spirit alone. Such people indeed eat and drink the external symbols, but they do not touch the things signified, just as those who are blinded cannot receive light and colour, which are perceived by the eyes.

units.la: Cùm postea rogor, an in ecclesia Cœnam sine corpore ac sanguine Christi haberi existimem, Respondeo. Si de ea præsentia loquamur, quam corporalem, realem atq; substantialem vocant, corpus & sanguinem Christi abesse confiteor: neq; si adessent, plus utilitatis, commodi & emolumenti nobis afferrent, quam inde hauriamus dum in cœlis manent procul à nobis disiuncta. Deinde caro & sanguis Christi nobis præsentia sunt spiritu, gratia, meritis, & aliis admirabilibus fructibus, quæ diuinitus per ea in nos deriuantur: quemadmodum Sol dicitur nobis adesse præsens per lucem, radios, & bonos influxus quos inde percipimus. Neq; corpus & sanguis Dñi sic animis nostris præsentia sunt, spiritualiter & per fidem, ut vires & facultates suas saluberrimas ibi tantum contineant, sinantque corpora fidelium ipsarum prorsus expertia. Non ita res habet. Sed quia credendo corpus & sanguinem Domini pretia esse nostræ salutis, iustificamur & regeneramur, vel in ipsa cum iustificatione tum regeneratione augemur & confirmamur. Iustificatio autem & regeneratio principia sunt nostræ felicis immortalitatis. Inde fit, ut Cœnam Domini fideliter percipiendo non modò animi pascantur & re-creentur, sed item corpora etiam atque etiam beatæ Resurre-ctionis capacia reddantur, &c.
units.tr: When afterwards I am asked whether I think the Supper is held in the Church without the body and blood of Christ, I answer: If we speak of that presence which they call corporal, real and substantial, I confess that the body and blood of Christ are absent; nor, even if they were present, would they bring us more usefulness, benefit and advantage than we now draw from them while they remain in heaven, removed far from us. Next, the flesh and blood of Christ are present to us by the Spirit, by grace, by merits, and by other wonderful fruits which are derived to us from them by divine power; just as the sun is said to be present to us through its light, its rays and the good influences which we receive from it. Nor are the body and blood of the Lord so present to our souls, spiritually and through faith, that they contain their most wholesome powers and faculties only there, and allow the bodies of the faithful to be wholly without them. That is not how the matter stands. Rather, since by believing that the body and blood of the Lord are the price of our salvation, we are justified and regenerated, or are increased and confirmed both in justification itself and in regeneration. Justification and regeneration, moreover, are the beginnings of our happy immortality. Hence it comes about that by receiving the Lord's Supper faithfully, not only are our souls fed and refreshed, but our bodies too are made more and more capable of the blessed resurrection, etc.

units.la: Hic est[?] meæ fidei sensus de sacra Domini Cœna, quem tibi vir præstantissime, fortasse minus enucleatè, propter orationis ieiunitatem, quàm fideliter expòsui. Sed te confido missis verbis impolitis atq; incultis, rebus ipsis & sententijs amico animo hæsurum. Vale, ac me tui amantissimum, ut facis, ama, & pro fructu meæ vocationis ora. D. Bullingerus cæteriq; amici plurimam tibi salutem adscribi voluerunt. 24. Maij 1562. Tiguri.
units.tr: This is the sense of my faith concerning the holy Supper of the Lord, which I have set out for you, most excellent sir, perhaps less clearly because of the poverty of my style, but faithfully. Yet I trust that you, as a friend, will hold to the things and the meanings themselves, with the rough and unpolished words set aside. Farewell, and love me, as you do, as one who loves you most dearly; and pray for the fruit of my calling. Bullinger and my other friends wish the most hearty greetings to be added for you. 24 May 1562. Zurich.

units.la: Tuus quantus est
units.tr: Yours, as much as I am

units.la: Petrus Martyr.
units.tr: Peter Martyr.

units.la: CARMINA DOCTO-RUM ALIQUOT VIRORUM IN OBITUM D. PETRI MARTY-RIS Vermilij conscripta.
units.tr: CARMINA DOCTORUM ALIQUOT VIRORUM IN OBITUM D. PETRI MARTYRIS VERMILII CONSCRIPTA. (Verses by several learned men on the death of Dr Peter Martyr Vermilius.)

units.la: ΕΙΣ ΠΕΤΡΟΝ ΜΑΡΤΥΡΑ ΒΕΡΜΙΛΙΟΝ Θεολόγον τὸν πάνυ Ἐξόδιον.
units.tr: To Peter Martyr Vermilius, the most divine theologian, on his departure.

units.la: Οὐκ ἐτὸς, ἀλλ' ἐπόν γε φερώνυμον ἄνομα Πέτρῳ[?] Μαρτυρεῖς, ὀξ ἱεροῦ ὕδατος ἀρχηγόνου Εἴχες· ἐπεί σοι τοῦτο πεφορμένον[?] εἴη[?] οἴω, Θέσκελον ἀμφότερον, κρεῖττον ἰδ' ἀνδρομέου.
units.tr: Your name Martyr, bearing the name of Peter, is no accident. You had it from the sacred water that gave you birth. I think that this was prophetic for you, both the name and the fate, more than human.

units.la: Μαρτυρείη γάρ σοι Χειρὸς[?] ἐξ παντὸς ἐτύχθη Ὁ σκοπὸς ἠδὲ τέλος ῥῆσις ἠδὲ βίου.
units.tr: For your life and your death were both shaped by the witness you bore, which was your aim and your end.

units.la: Ἐν ταύτῃ Πέτρου ἡ ἴκνην[?], μέχρι γηραιῷ ἰδοῦ Καὶ φυλέων αἱ ἴδου, ἀσταθέως ἐβίως.
units.tr: In this witness Peter's course was set; he lived unsteadily to old age, and his days were spent in it.

units.la: Τῶτό Οἱ Εὐρώπη πᾶσ' οἶδεν ἡ εὐρυόδεια, Αὐσονία Θρῶτον, σοὶ γεγονυῖα πάτρα.
units.tr: All Europe knows this, the wide-ruling continent, and Ausonia, your first homeland.

units.la: Εἶτα ἡ Τέυτονίς αἶα, πολυκλειτὴς τε Βρεταννῶν, Καὶ τελος Ἑλβετίων ἐθνος ἀρνὶ φίλον.
units.tr: Then the Teutonic land, famed among the Britons, and the Helvetian nation, dear to the Lamb.

units.la: Ὢν ἐν θεοφιλῇ πόλει πέντ' ἠλίοισι Ἐξηγησάμενος τὰς ἱερὰς σελίδας, Κυρίου ἐκ ἡμετέρης ἔτει ἀλφα ἐπὶ ξιακοσφ[?], Οἰκοδομεῖν Θεῖαν γλιχόμενος διδαχήν,
units.tr: Being in the God-loving city for five years, expounding the holy pages, in the year of our Lord 1556, eager to build up divine teaching,

units.la: Ἡλυθες εἰς Κέλτας, βασιλεὺς δ' ἐκάλεσε Ναβάρρων Καὶ βασιλὶς Κελτῇ χήρα ἑοῦσα τότε.
units.tr: you came to the French. The king of Navarre summoned you, and the queen, who was then a widow of the French.

units.la: Νοσήσας ἡ πάλιν εἰς ἑλβετικὸν τὸ Τίγουρον, Κυρίῳ ἀδμαίνων πνεῦμ' ἀνέηκας ἐὸν, Οὐ πλήθους μὴ νόσον ἐπιπλομένου ἐνιαυτῷ.
units.tr: Having fallen ill again, you returned to Zurich in Switzerland, and breathed out your spirit to the Lord, not from a plague of many diseases that came upon you in the year.

units.la: Σῶμα μὲν οὖ ξυδον μηξὶς ἐκ κατέχει.
units.tr: Your body, however, is held by the earth, and the mound of the grave covers it.

units.la: Νῆς δ' ὑπερουρανίῃ ἐν παξίδι, μυελάστασι[?] Σωῶ πολλὰς ἁγίων[?], ζῇ βίον ἀθάνατον.
units.tr: But in the heavenly paradise above the sky you live an immortal life with the many saints.

units.la: Κονεᾶδος Γεσνῆεος[?], ὁ ζῶντά τε φιλήσας αὐτὸν καὶ ἀγασάμενος ὅττι πλεῖσον[?], καὶ τῇ εὐσεβεστάτῃ αὐτὲ ἐξόδῳ ὥδαγ- νόμῳ ἐμελέτα[?].
units.tr: Conrad Gesner, who loved him while he lived, and admired him greatly, and who wrote a song on his most pious departure.

units.la: ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΑΥΤΟΝ Ἐπιτάφιον, τῷ αὐτῷ.
units.tr: On the same man's epitaph, by the same author.

units.la: Ἐν τῷδε Πέτρῳ Μάρτυρ ἔγκειται τάφῳ Θείων διδάσκαλῶν λόγων[?], οὗ καὶ ἀπὸ γλώττης νέκταρ ἐκβλύζον ῥέεν[?], ἔτει ἀπὸ χρισονίας[?], ὃ, δίσσον αὐτῷ εἴση ἀριθμῷ ἕνομα[?], ῥῶ μὴ ἀφελῶν, δὶς ξία ἢ θεοδρίς[?].
units.tr: In this tomb lies Peter Martyr, teacher of divine words, from whose tongue nectar flowed. In the year of the Christian era, the number of which you can read, take away one letter and add twice twenty and a half-century.

units.la: Idem Latine.
units.tr: The same in Latin.

units.la: Hoc tumulo Πέτρος, tum re, tum nomine, Μάρτυρ Conditus est, Christi testis amorq; sui. Annum si libeat Domini cognoscere, μὴ ῥῶ Abijce de Græcis, bis tria & adde, notis.
units.tr: Here lies Peter, Martyr in deed and in name, a witness of Christ and dear to his own. If you wish to know the year of the Lord, take the Greek letter away, and add bis tria, twice three, to the marks.

units.la: In tumulum incomparabilis viri, D. Petri Martyris Vermilij, Florentini, RODOLPHVS GVALTHERVS Tigurinus.
units.tr: On the tomb of the incomparable man, Dr Peter Martyr Vermilius of Florence, by Rudolph Gwalther of Zurich.

units.la: Martyra me diues genuit Florentia, sed me, Ampla licet, totum claudere non potuit. Mox etenim summum duce te super aethera scandens, CHRISTE, tui didici iussa colenda patris.
units.tr: Rich Florence bore me as a Martyr, but though she is great, she could not contain all of me. For soon, O Christ, rising above the heavens under you as leader, I learned the commands of your Father that are to be honoured.

units.la: Nec didici tantum, diuo sed numine ductus Illorum toto testis in orbe fui.
units.tr: I did not only learn them, but, led by the divine will, I became a witness of them throughout the whole world.

units.la: Martyra me vidit, qua qua patet, Itala tellus, Quae tota est studijs irradiata meis.
units.tr: The Italian land, as far as it stretches, saw me as a Martyr, a land wholly lit up by my studies.

units.la: Martyra me fortis vidit Germania, quae me Eiectum patrio fouit amica solo.
units.tr: Germany, strong in faith, saw me as a Martyr, and, a friend, cherished me when I was cast out of my native soil.

units.la: Martyra me vidit generosa Britannia & huius Immemor haud vnquam nominis esse potest.
units.tr: Noble Britain saw me as a Martyr, and can never be forgetful of this name.

units.la: Martyra non ficto vidit me Gallia vultu, Gallia martyrijs nobilitata suis.
units.tr: France saw me as a Martyr with an unfeigned face, France made noble by her own martyrdoms.

units.la: Sed procul Italia ne tarda in fine senecta Languerem, Heluetios iussit adire Deus.
units.tr: But God ordered me to go to the Swiss, lest I should languish, far from Italy, in a slow old age at the end.

units.la: Nobile vicinas Tigurum qua respicit Alpes, Et CHRISTI toto spargit in orbe sonum.
units.tr: Noble Zurich, which looks towards the Alps that stand nearby, spreads the sound of Christ through the whole world.

units.la: Hoc quoque constantem Christi me Martyra vidit, Et studij seruat pignora grata mei.
units.tr: Here too Christ's Martyr saw me, steadfast, and keeps the welcome pledges of my study.

units.la: Hoc me confectum studijs multoq; labore Fouit, & optato nunc tegit ossa sinu.
units.tr: Here, worn out by my studies and much labour, she cherished me, and now in her chosen bosom she covers my bones.

units.la: O mihi, o cunctis Tigurum dilectius oris, O vrbs prae patria semper amata, Vale.
units.tr: O Zurich, dearer to me than any shore, O city always loved above my fatherland, farewell.

units.la: Ossa tuis lachrymis Tigurum tu nostra rigasti, Dum mea mens summi gaudet in arce poli.
units.tr: You, Zurich, have watered our bones with your tears, while my mind rejoices in the height of the highest heaven.

units.la: Nec tamen ossa modo, nostri monumenta, reseruas: Ingenij sed habes & monumenta, libros.
units.tr: Yet you keep not only my bones, the monuments of me, but also the monuments of my genius, my books.

units.la: Vtq; hi perpetua vulgati luce fruentur, Perpetuus Christi sic ego Martyr ero.
units.tr: And as these are enjoyed, published, in perpetual light, so shall I, Christ's Martyr, be perpetual.

units.la: ALIVD eiusdem.
units.tr: Another by the same.

units.la: Definite à lachrymis, quia non sum morte peremptus, Parte sed en viuo nunc meliore mei. Vt cœlo fruerer, terris iactatus & alto Pro Christi subij mille pericla fide.
units.tr: Be done with tears, for I have not been destroyed by death; behold, the better part of me now lives. That I might enjoy heaven, I was tossed on land and sea, and for Christ's sake I bore a thousand dangers with faith.

units.la: Nunc igitur cœlum invenì sedesq; beatas, Moxq; suam inveniet Brentius Utopiam.
units.tr: Now then I have found heaven and blessed seats, and soon Brenz too will find his own Utopia.

units.la: VVOLFGANGI MUSCULI Decastichum.
units.tr: Decastich of Wolfgang Musculus.

units.la: Gratulor ipse tibi cūm mundum conspicor istum Martyr, quod saluum te Deus eripuit. Rursum ubi doctrinæ Christi considero sortem, Ad gemitum & luctum me tua fata vocant. Quidquid id est, pro te sit semper gloria Christo, Namq; ut sis Martyr & Petrus ipse dedit. Ut Martyr de Christo es testificatus aperte, Et probat esse Petrum te tua firma fides. Ingressus sedem cœli es non ἀτοπικῶς[?], sed Sanctorum quæ sit commoda spiritibus.
units.tr: I myself congratulate you, Martyr, when I look upon this world, that God has snatched you away safe. Again, when I consider the lot of Christ's teaching, your fate calls me to groaning and mourning. Whatever it is, let glory always be to Christ for you, for he made you both Martyr and Peter. As you were a Martyr who bore clear witness of Christ, your firm faith proves you to be Peter. You have entered the seat of heaven, not in an absurd way, but as is fitting for the spirits of the saints.

units.la: RODOLPHI COLLINI SENIORIS.
units.tr: Of Rudolph Collinus the elder.

units.la: Ergo ego chare senex nobis te propter ademptum Cogor in æterna vivere tristitia? Ergo ego vicinus frustra tibi factus, ut acri Pro lætis studijs carpar amaritie? Vidi ego complures doctos, vaga flumina mittunt Qua sua Ticinus, Sequana, Danubius, Vidi ego, sed nullum, te præter, (parcite docti) Quem vere potui dicere doctiloquum. Tu mihi solus eras, in summo limine vitæ, (Nam binis annis te fueram senior) Cuius honorandæ voces oracla fuere, Certa pij & docti pectoris indicia. Nunc quibus orbato mihi spes hæc unica restat, Mox simul in cœlis me fore, te socio. Illic cum Domino JESV licet esse beatis Semper, & aeterna vivere laetitia.
units.tr: Dear old man, am I then forced to live in eternal sadness because you have been taken from us? Have I, your neighbour, been made in vain, so that I am torn with bitter grief instead of joyful studies? I have seen many learned men, whom the wandering rivers of the Ticino, the Seine and the Danube carry along; I have seen them, but none, except you (pardon me, learned men), whom I could truly call eloquent in learning. You alone were mine, at the threshold of life, for I was older than you by two years. Your honoured words were oracles, sure signs of a devout and learned heart. Now, bereft of you, I have this one hope left, that soon I shall be with you in heaven. There, with the Lord Jesus, the blessed may live always, and live in eternal joy.

units.la: JOANNIS KESLERI Sangallensis.
units.tr: JOHANNES KESSLER of St. Gall.

units.la: Petro illi nomen, firmo quia robore Christum Edocuit, stabilis qui solet esse petra. Testis erat vivus, sed nunc monumenta loquuntur Religio verae quid pietatis habet. Urna viri cineres tenet haec, colit aetheris ἄσυ[?] Spiritus, illustris vivet in orbe labor.
units.tr: His name was Peter, because with firm strength he taught Christ, who is wont to be a steadfast rock. While he lived he was a witness, but now his monuments speak to what true piety holds. This urn holds the man's ashes; his spirit dwells in the heights of heaven [ἄσυ[?]], and his distinguished labour will live on in the world.

units.la: JOANNIS HALLERI.
units.tr: JOHANNES HALLER.

units.la: Quàm bene Nasonis cecinit doctissima Musa Conveniunt fatis nomina saepe suis. Sic ego dum Martyr dicor me Christus Jesus Aeterni verbi Martyra constituit. Italus audivit, Gallus, Germanus & Anglus, Martyrium sanctum quod tibi Christe dedi. Illud & absolvi Tigurina doctor in urbe, Hic mea membra jacent, spiritus astra tenet.
units.tr: How well the most learned Muse of Naso sang that names often agree with their fates! So, while I am called a martyr, Christ Jesus has appointed me a martyr of the eternal Word. Italians heard it, and French, Germans and English, the holy martyrdom that I gave to you, Christ. I also finished this as a teacher in the city of Zurich. Here my limbs lie; my spirit holds the stars.

units.la: VVOLFGANGI HAL-leri Διαλογισμός.
units.tr: WOLFGANG HALLER's Dialogue.

units.la: Μαρτυρόφιλῳ & Martyri.
units.tr: To Martyrophilus and to Martyr.

units.la: Cur moreris Martyr? cur nos ô chare relinquis? Cur filum resecat pallida Parca tibi? Quis subito morbus te nobis eripit, aut quae Tempore tam celeri vis inimica rapit? Profueras multum, sed quid nunc proderis orbi, In gelidam felix corpore versus humum?
units.tr: Why do you die, Martyr? Why, dear friend, do you leave us? Why does the pale Parca cut your thread? What sudden disease snatches you from us, or what hostile force seizes you in so swift a time? You were of great use, but what use are you now to the world, happy man, turned into cold earth in your body?

units.la: Quos etiam fœtus iam post tua fata relinquis, Utilis ut semper tu quibus esse queas?
units.tr: Whom, even children, do you leave behind now after your death, you who could always be useful to them?

units.la: Quove etiam vadis? quæ nunc tibi mansio, sors te Libera quæ curis carne iacente manet?
units.tr: Where are you going? What dwelling now awaits you, what free release from cares remains for you, with your flesh lying here?

units.la: Tu quoq; quo medio luctus solabere nostros? Et quid commendas, dum pie Martyr abis?
units.tr: And you, by what means will you comfort our grief? And what do you commend as you depart, dear Martyr?

units.la: MARTYR Μαρτυρφίλῳ[?].
units.tr: MARTYR to Martyrophilus.

units.la: Quod breuibus mœrens, ac dulcis amice rogabas, Dicam, quò tester spemq; fidemq; meam.
units.tr: Since you ask, grieving and dear friend, in few words, I will tell you, so that you may bear witness to my hope and faith.

units.la: Morte mihi vitam conscindi conijcis atra, Sed ne fallaris, cautius ista tene.
units.tr: You suppose that my life is cut off by black death; but do not be deceived, hold these things more cautiously.

units.la: Non morior, soluor. cum Christo viuere lucrum Est mihi, qui vita me meliore beat.
units.tr: I do not die; I am released. To live with Christ is gain for me, who blesses me with a better life.

units.la: Nec vos ac nunquam rediturus porrò relinquo, Sed certò in mundi fine redire volo.
units.tr: Nor do I leave you for ever, never to return; rather I surely wish to return at the end of the world.

units.la: Cum rediens Christus, renouata carne, fideles Corporibus claris ad sua regna vehet.
units.tr: When Christ returns, he will carry the faithful, with flesh renewed, in bright bodies, to his kingdom.

units.la: Nec resecat filum fatalis parca repente, Sed fixa à Domino meta salutis adest.
units.tr: The fatal Parca does not suddenly cut the thread; rather the goal of salvation fixed by the Lord is at hand.

units.la: Hic etenim solus mortis vitæq; magister, Consilio æterno tempora nostra regit.
units.tr: For he alone is the master of death and of life, and by his eternal counsel he rules our times.

units.la: Non adeò propere fatalibus exuor annis, Dissolui dudum sæpius ante petens.
units.tr: I am not stripped of my mortal years so hastily; I have long sought, and often before now, to be dissolved.

units.la: Bis sex nam lustris, ac binis insuper annis Vixi: Sat multum temporis illud erat.
units.tr: For I have lived six lustra and two years more; that was time enough.

units.la: Nec subito morbus me vobis abstulit acer, Perpetuus morbus cum siet iste mihi.
units.tr: Nor has a sharp disease taken me from you suddenly, since that was a constant sickness for me.

units.la: Quo nunquàm carui, pia mens confecta dolore, Pro grege dispersò, maxime Christe, tuo,
units.tr: Which I never lacked: a pious mind worn down with grief for your scattered flock, greatest Christ,

units.la: Quem tibi (proh) laniat rabies vesana luporum, Atq; impostorum dogmata falsa premunt.
units.tr: which, alas, the mad rage of wolves tears to pieces, and the false doctrines of impostors press upon.

units.la: Pro quibus ad Dominum diuina voce vocandis, Sum natus dudum, debile corpus ego.
units.tr: For these, to be called to the Lord by a divine voice, I was born long ago; I am a weak body.

units.la: Namq; per exilia atque enses, per tela, per ignes, Per mare, per terras, actus ab hoste fui. Perq; venenatas, infando crimine, mensas Insidiatorum, saepe petitus eram. Nec minus immodici talem fecere labores, Quos nunc cum fructu maximus orbis habet. Debilis accessit, morbus per se ipsa, senectus. Quid me igitur mirum claudere fata fuit? Sic voluit Dominus, nam vitae terminus hic est, Quem Deus aeterno fixerat ipse mihi. Profueram fateor, dum me prodesse volebat, Frugi qui dederat pluribus esse simul. Non tamen hoc laudat laruatae Curia Romae, Nec qui sectarum dogmata falsa tenent. At valeant, aut (quod magis his optemus amici) Emendent subito turpia facta sua, Doctrinam falsam, sceleratam deniq; vitam, Ne meritis tandem praemia digna ferant. Sed nunc me dempto nostrorum signa laborum, Nostri quos mundo Spiritus ipse libri Insignes foetus peperit, cunctisq; reliquit, Qui de doctrina, spe[?] fideq; mea Testari possint, semper superesse legiq; Debent, quo prosint: quod precor ipse Deum. Huc vos qui cupitis me porro audire relego, Utilis his semper, dum manet orbis, ero. Quo vadam rogitas? sit quae mihi mansio, forsq; In qua defunctus gaudia multa petam? In coelum vado, loca, lucida, clara, beata, Spiritibus sanctis commoda, certa, bona. Christus ubi noster, mediator, stigma salutis, Perpetuum nostri pignus amoris habet. Rex, Dominus, domitor, vindex, protector & vltor, Ad dextram summi confidet vsq; patris.
units.tr: For through exiles and swords, through weapons, through fire, over sea and land, I was driven by the enemy. Through poisoned tables, by an unspeakable crime, I was often sought by the plots of my enemies. Not less have my immoderate labours made me what I am, and the greatest world now enjoys their fruit. Weakness came upon me, sickness of itself, and old age. Why, then, is it strange that fate closed my life? So the Lord willed, for this is the end of my life, which God himself fixed for me in eternity. I was of use, I confess, while he wished me to be useful, who gave me to be fruitful to many at once. Yet the court of masked Rome does not praise this, nor do those who hold the false doctrines of the sects. But let them be well, or (what we friends would wish more for them) let them quickly amend their shameful deeds, their false doctrine and, finally, their wicked life, lest at last they bear the rewards their deserts merit. But now, with my labours dismissed, the signs of our labours, which the Spirit himself has brought forth in our distinguished books, remain for all, and must always remain and be read, so that they may profit; this I pray God himself for. To you who wish to hear me further I send you back; while the world lasts, I shall be useful to these. Where am I going, you ask? What dwelling may be mine, and what place where, once dead, I may seek many joys? I go to heaven, to places bright, clear and blessed, fitting for holy spirits, secure and good. There Christ our mediator, the mark of salvation, holds the perpetual pledge of our love. King, Lord, conqueror, avenger, protector and punisher, he sits at the right hand of the highest Father for ever.

units.la: In solio ac regno, cum vero corpore verè Verus homo, æternus nec minus ipse Deus: Corpore nequaquam vero diffusus ubique, Dogmatis Utopij finxit ut ille pater. Et sic in cœlis, in certa sede beatus, Ipsa re video fallere dogma novum. Hic etenim in cœlis cœlestia gaudia prensa[?] Quæ Deus æterno præparat ipse suis. His fruar in Domino, donec compleverit annos Mundus, quos Dominus fixerat ipse suos. Corpore tunc etiam, purgata carne, resumpto Æternum gaudens perpete pace fruar, Interea precibus luctus dispellite vestros, Atque Dei verbo credite, speq; bona Dum Dominus dederit superesse & vivere, quævis Sufferte, & fortem vos quoque ferte meam. Sic expectando Dominum implorate subinde, O Iesu venias paxq; salusq; citò. Hæc tibi sufficiant, claudendo lumina namq; Vitam depono, spiritus astra petit.
units.tr: On the throne and in the kingdom, with a true body, truly man, and no less eternally God; not diffused everywhere with a true body, as that ubiquitarian father devised his dogma. And so, blessed in heaven in a sure seat, I see with my own eyes that the new dogma is false. For here in heaven I hold the heavenly joys that God himself prepares for his own. I shall enjoy these in the Lord until the world has completed the years that the Lord himself fixed for his own. Then, with my flesh purified and my body taken up again, I shall rejoice eternally and enjoy an everlasting peace. Meanwhile, dispel your grief with prayers, believe the word of God and hold to good hope; and while the Lord grants you to remain and live, endure whatever comes, and bear my strength as your own too. So, always awaiting the Lord, implore him: O Jesus, come, and quickly bring peace and salvation. These things will suffice for you; closing my eyes, I lay down my life, and my spirit seeks the stars.

units.la: BLASII MARCUARDI.
units.tr: BLASIUS MARCUARDUS.

units.la: Extincto nuper Tigurina Academia claro Martyre, lugubri talia voce refert. Sæpe mihi luctus mors invida causa fuisti, Mersisti teneras sæpius imbre genas. Sæpe suos fleuit Respub. nostra parentes, Hostili quondam qui cecidere nece. At vix ulla fuit tam iusti causa doloris Atque mihi, quæ sim Martyre nuda meo. Martyre nuda meo, sacrum qui mystica vatum & Ardua discussit tot monumenta patrum.
units.tr: When the famous martyr of the Zurich Academy was lately taken from us, he spoke in these mournful words: "Often, Death, you have been a cause of grief to me, envious as you are, and often you have drenched my tender cheeks with rain. Often has our commonwealth wept for its parents, who once fell by hostile slaughter. But there was never any cause of grief so just as the one that now strips me, bereft of my martyr. Bereft of my martyr, who unlocked the sacred and lofty monuments of the Fathers, and the mysteries of the prophets."

units.la: Christiq[?], infestos vt murus aheneus hostes, Voce sacri late fudit Euangelij. Testis erit Latium, & florens Germania testis, Anglia testis erit, Gallia testis erit.
units.tr: As a brazen wall against hostile enemies of Christ, he poured forth far and wide the voice of the holy Gospel. Latium will be a witness, and flourishing Germany will be a witness; England will be a witness, and France will be a witness.

units.la: Sed iuuat immodicos nil quidquam fundere fletus, Fata velut cunctis non subeunda forent. Maiores laudem factis peperere perennem, Hic peperit scriptis nomina digna suis.
units.tr: But it is no use to pour out immoderate tears, as if these fates were not to be undergone by all. Our ancestors won lasting praise by their deeds; he won names worthy of his writings.

units.la: Illi Christigenam testati sanguine mentem, Ipse tibi Martyr dogmate martyr erit. Vna dies nequijt Heroas tollere cunctos, Non omnes doctos abstulit vna dies.
units.tr: He bore witness to the Christian mind with his blood; you, martyr, will be a martyr to them by your teaching. One day could not remove all the heroes; one day did not carry off all the learned men.

units.la: IOANNIS CONRADI Fabricij.
units.tr: IOANNES CONRADUS FABRICIUS.

units.la: Martyra mors Petrum nostris subduxit ocellis Clausit & exiguo membra sepulta loco. Quo se grex ouium tanto pastore perempto Vertet, & unde sibi pabula nota petet? Quis doctos vltra simili sermone docebit? An cuiquam est[?] tantis mens cumulata bonis? Non dubitanda loquor, percellimur omine tanto, Et vereor mœstas urbis adesse dies. Summe Deus pastorq; gregis submitte labori Pastores, templi commiserere tui.
units.tr: Martyr's death has withdrawn Peter from our eyes and has shut away his body, buried in a small place. Where will the flock of sheep turn, now that so great a shepherd has been destroyed, and whence will it seek its familiar pasture? Who will teach the learned any further with such eloquence? Or is there anyone whose mind is heaped with such great gifts? I speak without doubt: we are struck down by so great an omen, and I fear that the sorrowful days of the city are at hand. Highest God and shepherd of the flock, submit to labour your ministers; have pity on your temple.

units.la: EPIGRAMMATA IN EVNDEM.
units.tr: EPIGRAMS ON THE SAME MAN.

units.la: In D. Petri Martyris Vermilij Florentini imaginem, Ioannis Parkhursti Angli Tetrastichon.
units.tr: On the portrait of Dr. Peter Martyr Vermigli of Florence, a tetrastich by John Parkhurst, Englishman.

units.la: Florida quem genuit Florentia, Martyris ista Effigiem Petri picta tabella refert. Doctrinam, ingenium, dotes animiq; stupendas, Non posset Cicero pingere pro meritis.
units.tr: Flourishing Florence bore him, and this painted panel shows the likeness of Martyr Peter. His learning, his talent, and his astonishing gifts of mind, Cicero could not paint worthily.

units.la: RODOLPHVS Gualtherus in nuptias D. PETRI MARTYRIS Vermilij & Catharinæ Merendæ.
units.tr: Rudolph Gualther, on the marriage of Dr. Peter Martyr Vermigli and Catharine Merenda.

units.la: Quòd Christum vita semper testaris & ore, Martyris haud frustra nobile nomen habes. At Catharina simul sociali fœdere iuncta, Indicat à Christo præmia parta tibi. Ille suos proprio mundatos sanguine testes Et sponsæ & proprij corporis instar habet. Accipite hæc igitur saluantis symbola Christi, Et læti optato viuite coniugio. Hic precor optata faciat vos prole parentes, Quæ matrem referat, patris & ingenium.
units.tr: Because you always bear witness to Christ in your life and your speech, you have the noble name of Martyr, and not in vain. Catharine, joined to you at once in a companionable covenant, shows the rewards won for you by Christ. He holds his own, cleansed by their own blood, as witnesses and as the likeness of his bride and of his own body. Accept, then, these tokens of Christ the Saviour, and live joyfully in the marriage you desired. Here I pray that you become parents of the offspring you wish for, who may reflect the mother's and the father's nature.

units.la: Regula Zuinglia Gualtheri uxor cum pro Eliperio Vermilio D. Petri Martyris F. fidem suam in baptismo obstringeret.
units.tr: Regula Zwingli, wife of Gualther, when she pledged her faith in baptism for Eliperius, son of Dr. Peter Martyr.

units.la: Parue puer, docti spes exoptata parentis, Exiguum magni pignus amoris habe[?].
units.tr: Little boy, longed-for hope of a learned parent, hold this small pledge of a great love.

units.la: Hoc te Gualtheri donauit Regula, corpus Cùm sacra baptismi tingeret vndatuum. Viue puer, tantiq; tene vestigia patris, Altera Vermiliæ spesq; decusq; domus. Sancta Spei coniuncta Fides tibi cuncta secundent, Flagret & æthereo pectus Amore Dei. Vnica mortalis sit CHRISTVS regula vitæ, Ancora qui pariter certa salutis erit.
units.tr: Regula Gualther gave you this, when she dipped your body in the sacred waters of baptism. Live, boy, and follow the footsteps of your great father, the second hope and glory of the house of Vermigli. May Faith, joined with Hope, prosper all things for you, and may your breast burn with the heavenly love of God. May CHRIST alone be the single rule of mortal life, who will likewise be the sure anchor of your salvation.

units.la: 3. Martij Anno 1560.
units.tr: 3 March 1560.

units.la: IN LIBROS D. P. MARTYRIS IOANNIS FABRICII MONTANI.
units.tr: On the books of Dr. P. Martyr, by Johannes Fabricius Montanus.

units.la: Libri loquuntur.
units.tr: The books speak.

units.la: Si præsens animi latentis index Est oratio, sicut eruditus Rerum nos docuit magister vsus. Si morum documenta sunt libelli, Nostro nil melius probatiusue, Dum vixit, potuit parente fingi, Nil disertius, eruditiusue, Nobis nam genitis parente tanto, (Verum dicere siquidem licebit) Nil syncerius est probatiusq;, Nil politius, elegantiusq;, Nil illustrius explicatiusq;. I nunc liuor edax tuumq; rode Et cor, & digitos, & omne quicquid Infelix rabies vorare suadet. Mirum ni tibi plaudis & triumphas, Inuictus quia miles iste Christi Nunc vitus[?] iacet, & iacet sepultus.
units.tr: If speech is the index of a hidden mind, as the master of things, experience, has taught us, and if little books are teachings of morals, then nothing better or more approved could have been fashioned by a parent while he lived, nothing more eloquent or learned. For we, born of so great a father (if indeed it is permitted to speak the truth), have nothing more sincere or approved, nothing more polished or elegant, nothing more illustrious or clearly explained. Go now, devouring envy, and gnaw your own heart, and your fingers, and whatever else wretched rage urges you to devour. It would be a wonder if you did not applaud and triumph, because that unconquered soldier of Christ now lies vanquished and buried.

units.la: Imponis tibi turpiter scelesté, Saltem reddidit id quod ante fato Se debere sciebat, & sepulchro: Et hoc sponte quidem volensq; fecit, Jam vitæ satur, & satur laborum. Sed qua parte sui perire nescit, Immortale modo perennat ævum. Lætis cœlicolum beatus oris Plusquam gaudia Brentiana carpens, Cui cœlum nihili suum libenter Linquit Martyr, & usque linquet uni. Quod nemo reperire dum, videre Nemo dum potuit bonus, nec unquam Quisquam post alijs videbit annis. Nec nos interea decus parentis, Nec famam celebrare desinemus. Dum convexa poli suos tenebunt Cursus, in statione dum manebunt Sol & Luna, diesq; noxq; : donec Alto flumina se mari recondent: Toto nos etiam legemur orbe.
units.tr: You, Death, basely and wickedly lay the burden on yourself; at least he has given back what he knew beforehand he owed to fate and to the tomb. And he did this willingly, now sated with life and with labours. But in the part of him that cannot perish, he lives on in immortal age, blessed with the joyful faces of the dwellers in heaven, surpassing even the joys of Brenz. To him the Martyr gladly leaves his own heaven of nothing, and will always leave it to him alone. What no one could find while he lived, and what no good man could see while he lived, no one will see in the years to come. Meanwhile we will not cease to celebrate our parent's glory and his fame. As long as the vaults of heaven keep their courses, as long as the sun and moon remain in their stations, day and night, until the rivers hide themselves in the deep sea, we too shall be read throughout the whole world.

units.la: Finis.
units.tr: The end.

units.la: RODOLPHVS GVAL-THERVS RODOLPHO HOspiniano, filio suo dilecto, S. P. D.
units.tr: Rudolph Gwalther to his beloved son Rudolph Hospinian, greetings.

units.la: PRAECLARE admodum Vergilius, qui Andromachen de Ascanio interrogantem hisce verbis inducit: Ecquid in antiquam virtutem animosa, viriles? Et pater Aeneas & auunculus excitat Hector? Vidit enim poeta, generosiores animos a pueris statim maiorum virtute excitari, ut eos sibi imitandos putent, quorum egregia facta publice celebrantur. Et cum omnes magni faciant, quos sibi laudem & gloriam quaesiisse vident, plus tamen maiorum exemplis afficiuntur, quos vel ipsi coram viderunt, vel ab aliis praedicari audiunt. Habes tu mi Rodolphe haec omnia: Quia non tantum patre, verum etiam avo eo natus es, qui vitae honestate cum fide in Christum constanti coiunxerunt. Pater etiam Adrianus in humanioribus & sacris literis eo usque profecit, ut inter eruditissimos locum habere potuerit. Accessit his patruus Ioannes, qui ut eruditione eximius, & ob morum suavitate bonis omnibus charissimus: ita patri suo in morte gloriosa pro Iesu Christo socius fuit indiuulsus. Et hi quidem nunc in Christo beati viuunt & nobis sui memoria te ad virtutem excitant. Quae eo maioris apud te authoritatis esse debet, quod in vivis ad huc habeas domestica exempla, quibus non minus excitari potes: avunculum nimirum, Ioannem Vuolphium, eruditissimum virum & ecclesiae nostrae fidelem ministrum: patruum item alterum, Leonhardum Hospinianum, cuius doctrinam elegantissimam et mores candidissimos, ne ipse quidem Momus reprehenderit. De me, qui fidem meam tibi obstrinxi, cum in sacro fonte Christo initiareris, hoc unum dico, nunquam mihi te & studia tua promovendi voluntatem defuturam, quoad spei de te conceptae respondere perrexeris. Interea breve hoc carmen, quo non tam patris tui memoriam celebrare, quam ex morte eius obortum dolore lenire volui, apud te fidei nostrae pignus esse velim. Vale, 25. Febr. Anno incarnati filij Dei 1563.
units.tr: Virgil put it admirably when he has Andromache ask Ascanius, in these words: "Are you, my boy, stirring yourself toward your ancient courage and manly spirit? Do your father Aeneas and your uncle Hector spur you on?" For the poet saw that the nobler spirits of boys are roused at once by the virtue of their forebears, so that they think they should imitate those whose outstanding deeds are celebrated in public. And although everyone admires those whom they see have won praise and glory for themselves, they are nonetheless more moved by the examples of their ancestors, whom they have either seen with their own eyes or hear praised by others. You, my Rudolph, have all of this: you were born not only of a father but of a grandfather who joined an upright life to a constant faith in Christ. Your father Adrian also advanced so far in the humane and sacred letters that he could hold a place among the most learned men. To these was added your uncle John, who was outstanding in learning and so dear to all good people for the sweetness of his character, and who in his glorious death for Jesus Christ was an inseparable companion to your father. These men now live blessed in Christ, and by their memory they call you to virtue. This ought to carry all the more weight with you, because among the living you still have domestic examples by which you may be no less stirred: namely your uncle John Wolf, a most learned man and a faithful minister of our Church; likewise your other uncle, Leonhard Hospinian, whose most elegant teaching and most upright character not even Momus himself could find fault with. As for me, who pledged my faith to you when you were initiated into Christ at the sacred font, I say only this: my willingness to advance you and your studies will never fail, so long as you continue to answer the hopes conceived of you. Meanwhile, I wish this short poem, with which I wanted less to celebrate your father's memory than to ease the grief arising from his death, to be a pledge of our affection for you. Farewell, 25 February, in the year 1563 after the incarnation of the Son of God.

units.la: IN TVMVLVM D. ADRIANI HOSPI-niani, Altorfianæ Ecclesiæ apud Tigurinos fidelissimi pastoris.
units.tr: IN THE TOMB OF MR ADRIANUS HOSPINIANUS, most faithful minister of the Church of Altorf among the Tigurini.

units.la: Pater filium alloquitur.
units.tr: The father addresses his son.

units.la: Per varios casus, per multa pericula tandem Appulit ad portum nostra carina suum.
units.tr: After many changes and many dangers, at last our keel has reached its harbour.

units.la: Hospes in hisce fui terris, nunc civis Olympi Mens mea cum Christo regna beata colit.
units.tr: I was a stranger in these lands; now my mind, a citizen of Olympus, dwells blessed with Christ in the kingdom.

units.la: Molliter ossa sub hoc tumulo defossa quiescunt, Rursus ad extremum sed reditura diem.
units.tr: Softly my bones rest, buried under this tomb, yet destined to return on the last day.

units.la: At tu, dum licuit dilecti cura parentis, Auribus ista tuis iussa, Rodolphe, cape.
units.tr: But you, while it was permitted, under the care of a loving father, Rodolphus, take these commands in with your ears.

units.la: Esto bonus, fidei & verae pietatis amator, Sit vitae Christus regula certa tuae.
units.tr: Be good, a lover of faith and of true piety; let Christ be the sure rule of your life.

units.la: Illum nec pudeat vita & sermone fateri, Qui vitam pro te tradidit ipse suam.
units.tr: Let it not shame you to confess in life and speech him who himself gave his life for you.

units.la: Hoc avus, hoc patruusque tuus, qui fortiter olim Pro Christo vitam deposuere, monent.
units.tr: This your grandfather and your uncle, who once bravely laid down their lives for Christ, also urge.

units.la: Hoc ego nunc moneo, qui illorum magna laboris Tunc quoque pars fueram, certus & ipse mori.
units.tr: This I now urge, who was also a large part of their labour then, and who myself am certain to die.

units.la: At aliter CHRISTO visum, qui ex ore Leonis Eripuit, vitae & tempora plura dedit.
units.tr: But it seemed otherwise to Christ, who snatched him from the mouth of the lion and gave him more years of life.

units.la: Iamq; grauem senio tranquilla morte solutum In superas ad se transtulit inde domus.
units.tr: And now, released from heavy old age by a calm death, the house above has carried him up to itself.

units.la: Tu si patris, avi, patrui, vestigia serues, Et studijs pergas invigilare bonis,
units.tr: If you keep the footsteps of your father, grandfather and uncle, and continue to labour diligently at good studies,

units.la: Exurget magnum toto tibi nomen in orbe, Et simul æternum, crede, beatus eris.
units.tr: a great name will rise for you throughout the whole world, and at the same time, believe me, you will be blessed forever.

units.la: ΕΙΣ ΑΔΡΙΑΝΟΝ ΞΕΝΟΝ, ΕΚ-κλησιαστὴν ἐν τῇ τῆς Τιγυρινῶν Παλαιοπάγῳ, [?] εὐσεβείᾳ [?] λόγοις [?] διαφερέντι [?] γεγονότα, Κορράδου Γεσνήεου, τῇ [?] κηδείαν αὐτοῦ [?] προσθήκοντι [?], Ἐπιτάφιον.
units.tr: AN EPITAPH ON ADRIANUS THE STRANGER, an ecclesiastic in the Palaeopagus of the Tigurini, distinguished in piety and in words, the kinsman of Conrad Gessner, who attaches his funeral [?] ...

units.la: Ἐν χθονὶ μὴ ξεῖνῳ κηδεστὰ φιλαίτατ' ὑπῆρχες, Γῆεα εἰς καιρὸν πουλυετῆς μεξίου.
units.tr: In a land not foreign you were a most dear kinsman, a long-lived ... for a time.

units.la: Νῦν ἡ θανὼν πολύπαις, ἄλοχον καὶ τέκνα λιλοιπώς Τοιοῦτ... πολίτης ζῆσαι ... ἐξάνιος.
units.tr: Now the dead man, rich in children, leaving a wife and children ... a citizen ... to live ...

units.la: Ἐνθα πέον τε γυνὴ κιχήση ἀδελφειόν τε, Αἷμα τ' ἐξ χειρῶν μάρτυρας ἰναγέας.
units.tr: Where a woman and a brother find him, and blood from the hands, bloody witnesses.

units.la: Εὖ ἡ τόδ' ἀμμιν ἐτύχθη, ὅτι μὴ Μάρτυρα Πέτρου Μῆνας που τέτρας παύσατο τῆδε βίου.
units.tr: It was well for us that he ceased from this life, a martyr of Peter, in the fourth month ...

units.la: Νῦν γὰρ τῆδε φίλοι μελετῶντες ὁμοῦ ἐν λέλτῳ Στυγνὰ ποιοῦσιν ἐπὶ εἰς μόργν ἀμφοτέρων.
units.tr: For now here friends, meditating together in the book, make sad lament over both ...

units.la: Ἠδὲ γὰρ εὐφρενέοντε φίλω, καὶ μάρτυρε κοινῆς Εὐσεβίης ἀμφω τῆς γε παλαιοπάτης.
units.tr: For both were dear friends, and both witnesses of the common piety of the old father.

units.la: IN FILIAM D. PETRI MARTYRIS Vermilij Posthumam, Rodolphus Gualtherus Tigurinus.
units.tr: ON THE POSTHUMOUS DAUGHTER OF MR PETER MARTYR VERMIGLI, by Rodolphus Gualther of Zurich.

units.la: MARIA VERMILIA POSTHVMA.
units.tr: MARIA VERMILIA, POSTHUMOUS.

units.la: Dum nitidam mundi lucem, dum cetera miror,Atque oculis lustro non mihi visa prius.Quaero patrem: Nusquam est: Sed coelos ipse petiit.Quid faciam? Deus ah tu mens esto pater.
units.tr: While I marvel at the bright light of the world and at other things, and survey with my eyes things not seen before, I seek my father: he is nowhere, for he himself has sought the heavens. What shall I do? Ah God, be you my father.

units.la: 6. Martij, Anno 1563.
units.tr: 6 March, in the year 1563.

units.la: EPITAPHIVM CL. V. ac præstantissimi Theologi D. Petri Martyris Vermilij, sacrarum literarum in schola Tigurina professoris, scriptum per M. Balthazarum Susenbetum Eschuegensem Hassum.
units.tr: EPITAPH of the distinguished man and most excellent theologian Mr. Peter Martyr Vermilius, professor of Holy Scripture in the school at Zurich, written by M. Balthasar Susenbeth of Eschwege in Hesse.

units.la: Parua quidem Petri cineres modò Martyris urna Excipit: at magnus vivit in orbe tamen. Testis enim Christi, ceusydus in æthere, lumen Resplendensq;, Dei fulsit in ipse domo. Vidit eum Italiæ primum Florentia natum, Sed locus ecce suos non fuit ullus apud. Mox ad Germanos & ad Anglos mittitur exul, A Maria sæua pellitur inde senex. Rursus & hospitium Germania præbuit illi, Testis ut æterni pergeret esse Dei. Ὑ̓πεσθν[?] at bis sex ubi lustra peregerat, atque Reddens tres annos martyrium absq; metu: Vitæ pertæsus miserę, Christoq; vocanti, E mundo in cœli gaudia lætus abit. Reliquias igitur fragilis modo corporis urna Marmoreo tumulo, concava mandat huic. Illic fatali requiescunt membra sopore, Longis qua mundi sunt agitata malis. Ipsius at nomen fines penetrabit ad orbis Vsque, simul laudis fama perennis erit.
units.tr: Though a small urn now holds the ashes of Peter the Martyr, yet he lives on great in the world. For he, a witness of Christ, flashing light in the heavens, shone forth in the house of God. Florence first saw him born in Italy, yet no place there was his own. Soon he was sent into exile to the Germans and the English; from there the cruel Mary drove out the old man. Germany again offered him hospitality, so that he might go on as a witness of the eternal God. When he had passed twelve lustra, and was rendering his witness for three years without fear, weary of his wretched life and answering Christ's call, he departs joyfully from the world into the joys of heaven. So the hollow urn now entrusts the remains of his fragile body to a marble tomb. There his limbs rest in a fatal sleep, where they were tossed about by the long evils of the world. But his name will reach to the ends of the earth, and his undying fame will be joined with praise.

units.la: DISTICHON, quod annum, mensem, & diem obitus eius ostendit.
units.tr: COUPLET, which shows the year, month and day of his death.

units.la: Petrus, vt effulsit bis sexta luce Nouember, In cœli vectus iubila, Testis ouat.
units.tr: Peter, as on the twelfth light of November he was carried up into the joy of heaven, the witness rejoices.

units.la: PENTAMETER anni quo obijt numerum complectens.
units.tr: PENTAMETER containing the number of the year in which he died.

units.la: Martyr vt astra petet, gens Tigurina dolet.
units.tr: When the martyr seeks the stars, the Tigurine people grieve.
